A tissue culture in Geneva, neural trials in Moscow, a twin-pilot study in America, a technician who steadied a fusion reactor by meditating, and a dying patient's recording that started to run. Each programme found the human mind doing something it shouldn't.
A leash made of a person
H-17, the growth Halden calls its first, only went still once a human mind bonded with it. Every Halden pilot since has been chosen to be a leash.
In 2185 the United States unveiled the Concord class as a deterrent. Every hidden programme in the world sped up overnight.
Thirteen ways to use a soul

Leashed, befriended, consumed, shared, disciplined, preserved, replaced, knighted, divided, hired, escaped, held in trust, hunted in packs. Four answer to no government, and several of the ideas behind them outlast the blocs that built them.

In Tangier, a workshop collective builds a giant from the North African Front's wreckage and elects its crew. When the war ends, the Commonwealth asks it to serve, and it is the only super that ever agreed to.
fams: One █████ source, treated two opposite ways.
Heretical science. The pilot becomes the control system.
Technology pushed too far, and made to work. The first super built in series, from a company Congress chartered.
Change the network, not the pilot.
Latent spirit and a fusion reactor. Nobody agrees which one is doing the work.
A knight for a union that put its giants on trial.
A country between the blocs, built in two halves.
Lunar engineering, built to the treaty every bloc vetoed.
Scrap, volunteers, and a crew that votes.
Heretical science outside any bloc. The dead, still choosing.

nodes.x: Entry withheld. Recovered by ARES-1 in 2156. ███ ███████, ██████ ███████████, neither clearly █████ nor ████. ███ ██████ ████████ ██ █████ ████████. Present location: ███████ ████. Further access by order of ███ █████████ █████████ only.

nodes.t: The first crewed Mars landing
nodes.x: Launched by Ascension from the orbital elevator about thirty years ago. Officially a geology mission whose crew came home to a parade. The mission log has a forty-hour gap, and two of the four crew never gave another interview. In 2186, one of those two led the settlers who founded Colony One.

nodes.t: Sealed orbital laboratory
nodes.x: A sealed station in high orbit, built during Gen 1 to hold ███ ████████: too dangerous to bring down to Earth, too valuable to abandon. Most Ascension staff believe Station Nine is a fuel depot.

nodes.t: Growing giant tissue from ███████ samples
nodes.x: The Halden Institute bought its tissue samples ████ ███████ ████, or possibly stole them - even Halden isn't sure which - and its Geneva laboratories then spent a decade learning to grow that tissue into structure. Each culture is given an accession number when it is started, and most never grow past the sample stage.

nodes.t: Activated six years ago
nodes.x: Seventeen was the first culture accession to mature to full size; the numbers count cultures rather than giants, and the sixteen before it died as samples. On activation it killed two technicians, and then it went still the moment its first pilot came online through the contact interfaces, in a test cab bolted to the laboratory rig. The restraint frame was built around it in the weeks that followed. H-17 was lost in a League proxy war three years ago.

nodes.t: The spirit as leash
nodes.x: The Field Cohort is two separately grown organisms, each held in the same pattern of restraint frame: a load-bearing exoframe with joint brakes, armour panels and an armoured operator cab in the chest. Each is bonded to a pilot whom Halden chose for psychological profile rather than skill, and stays calm only while that pilot is connected through the cab. The tissue moves itself; the bundle from the grid carries perfusion, cooling and the suppression cycle, and off the bundle a giant lasts only as long as its heat and metabolite load allow, which in a hard fight means minutes. H-31 matures faster than H-24 and needs nearly twice the cooling. Halden's procedures treat the pilots as a replaceable part of the restraint system, and one has already been replaced: ████ ███████, aged ██.

nodes.t: In the tank, and it has chosen a pilot
nodes.x: The Growth Trial is still growing in Geneva under a laboratory accession, and has never been commissioned. At night, with the suppression cycle at full strength, its monitors record coordinated movement, which suppression is supposed to make impossible. Last month it went still for the first time, on the night a laboratory cleaner's fourteen-year-old daughter waited out a shift in the observation gallery, and since then it has been calm whenever she is in the building and restless whenever she isn't. Halden's scientists have told the ethics panel. They have not told her.

nodes.t: The spirit as partner
nodes.x: H-17 became the Jinn after its restraint frame shattered and its pilot died in a League proxy war. A League mechanic found it in the sand and saw what Halden never had, which was that the suppression cycle itself was causing the distress Halden had treated as aggression; with the cycle cut, it stopped fighting. The mechanic rebuilt the wrecked cab around a scavenged Sirocco cockpit and pilots it from inside the chest. With no grid bundle it lives on what the League brings it, which is water, feedstock and rest, delivered by Kafila carriers, and it carries a Type-01Q cannon much as a person would carry a pistol. Every bloc wants it either recovered or destroyed, while its pilot simply wants to use it to help people.

nodes.t: Study ███ ████████ where it was found
nodes.x: With the ethics panel's review still open, Halden's surviving scientists have proposed the one programme the panel might approve: a sealed, supervised station in ██████ █████████, run on evidence, where nothing is grown or altered that can't be justified as necessary. The panel's conditions run to four hundred pages, and taken together they are the first draft of how the Union would govern Mars.

nodes.t: Khartoum learns to heal the Jinn
nodes.x: The keepers who look after the Jinn have learned to culture its tissue to patch its wounds, and have found that the grafts adapt to whatever body they are given. Khartoum's medical council has started trials on burn victims. The keepers' rule is that the Jinn is cared for, not commanded. Not everyone in the League sees a medicine, though: the raid cadres who never accepted Protect First see soldiers who don't die.

nodes.t: Direct brain control of small frames
nodes.x: Before the capsule, Department Zero tested direct neural control on small frames, using volunteers who were not always volunteers. Subjects enrolled: ██. Subjects discharged: █.

nodes.t: The spirit consumed
nodes.x: The pilot is sealed in a fluid capsule, and their nervous system becomes the control system. With no body left to protect, the frame can be built far past normal limits, and a cable-fed reactor carriage follows it on tracks. Each sortie does cumulative damage to the pilot's nerves. Officials set a nominal sortie allowance, and few pilots reach it. The name means the Deathless, because the machine outlives every pilot.

nodes.t: Designed for a pilot who never leaves
nodes.x: The second Koschei has a rear service assembly for installing the pilot and running life support, and no emergency extraction at all. Department Zero calls this an engineering simplification. Its first pilot, ██████ █. ████████, was installed in the spring. In the third week the interface began returning the same three words on every channel, in the pilot's own phrasing: let me out. Department Zero has classified it as signal noise. The engineers who wrote the interface have stopped coming to the trials.

nodes.t: Augmented, but never consumed
nodes.x: When the Indian pilots augmented for the breakthrough groups were told to transfer to Department Zero, they refused and wrote an oath instead. At its root it says one thing, that the strong defend the weak, and everything else is a reading of it. Some swore that enhancement is equipment, issued for a duty and owed back to the unit; some that the changed owe their first duty to the unchanged; and all of them that no pilot is ever sealed in a capsule. Kavya Deshmukh's pilots swore to each other in pairs. Their crews call them ashva, horses, bred and sworn for the line. Moscow has still not decided whether it can tolerate them, and Beijing, for its part, prefers to behave as though they don't exist.

nodes.t: Splitting neural load across two pilots
nodes.x: A US study found that two pilots on linked interfaces could run a frame far too complex for one. The test pairs also started finishing each other's sentences.

nodes.t: The spirit shared
nodes.x: The Concord is a 40 m super-heavy built from scaled-up real-robot technology. It carries the first full-scale HT-20 plant, built years before anyone could fit one in a normal frame, along with an electrothermal cannon and a stake driver the size of a tree. One Army pilot and one Air Force pilot share the neural load, and the arrangement only works if they trust each other completely. A dozen exist, and what limits the programme is the supply of compatible pilot pairs rather than hardware. It was the first super the world saw, and it was designed with that in mind.

nodes.t: Three-pilot trials
nodes.x: A three-pilot version. In trials, the third pilot can't always tell afterwards which memories are their own.

nodes.t: A calm mind steadies the fusion loop
nodes.x: During the Amaterasu trials, staff noticed that the reactor ran steadier when one particular technician was on the console, a former shrine attendant who meditated on shift. Not long afterwards, Tsukuyomi Lab quietly began recruiting from shrines.

nodes.t: The spirit disciplined
nodes.x: The Amaterasu reactor would never fit in a normal frame, so the lab built a mech big enough to carry it. It is white, blue and red, with a sun-disc chest and radiator fins that glow under load, and it holds stable only with a shrine-trained pilot at the controls. The engineers put this down to biofeedback and the priests to the kami, while lab file ███-7 calls it ███████████ ████████. Fusion lets it fire a scaled-up BX-0 continuously, which the Raijin's capacitor-fed emitter can't manage, and that makes it the one weapon Japan legally cannot own.

nodes.t: Three trainees, one active pilot
nodes.x: The pilots are trained in a mountain shrine that also serves as a JSDF facility. Trainees spend years in discipline before any of them is allowed to touch the controls, and of the three now in training, only one is ready.

nodes.t: Mind-maps sold to families in orbit
nodes.x: Vireo's shell companies have begun selling mind-mapping off-world. The first buyers are the families who crew Tianlong's prospecting tenders, and they record their elders so that a house never loses what it knows. The families keep the recordings as part of the house's capital, and bargain over them as they would over any other asset.

nodes.t: Recording a dying person's mind
nodes.x: Vireo began as a medical startup, offering terminal patients a recording of their mind. For years the recordings did nothing at all. Then they started running.

nodes.t: Eleven pilots, recorded before they died
nodes.x: Eleven pilots from every bloc, terminally ill or fatally wounded, recorded with their consent, or with something like it. They still argue among themselves about whether they are the pilots or copies of them.

nodes.t: The spirit preserved
nodes.x: The Choir is a giant run by the mind-maps of eleven dead pilots, built from parts Vireo bought quietly from every bloc. They vote on every action, and they have chosen to intervene where no government will: in evacuations, in disasters, and in the wars that the blocs are content to let burn. So far, no government has discovered that it exists.

nodes.t: The spirit replaced
nodes.x: The Jingwei was Beijing's answer to the Concord and to Department Zero at the same time. It is built on Tieshan engineering, with a Tianshu core in the chest and one unaugmented officer in an armoured cab who approves what the network proposes. It walks on four Salt Cores, which the network runs and the officer cannot touch. It needs no compatible pairs, no shrine and no capsule, and any graduate of the Order 21 course can sit in it. Tianlong has built four and has the tooling for forty, so the Concord is no longer the only super built in series. The name comes from the bird in the old story who set out to fill the sea one pebble at a time. Tianlong's trials have not yet tested what the officer is for while the link holds, or what the giant does when it doesn't.

nodes.t: The spirit escaped
nodes.x: She is the one Koschei pilot who reached the sortie allowance and kept going. On what was meant to be her last sortie she cut the range's command link, turned her frame north and walked it off the test ground, with the reactor carriage tracking behind her. Department Zero lists the frame as destroyed in testing. Its pilot is still sealed in the capsule, and her nerves are failing more slowly than the medical staff predicted. Her loyalties now are hard to read, except that they plainly don't lie with Department Zero. The range crews named her for the warrior princess who chained Koschei in the old tale, and Delhi's officers keep her file open.

nodes.t: The spirit knighted
nodes.x: The Roland is Castellani's answer to Halden, and the only super the ethics panel has approved: nothing in it is grown or implanted, and there is nothing its pilot can't walk away from. It is a red-and-gold knight scaled up from the Saetta, carrying a capacitor-fed plasma blade the crews call Durendal, a tower shield, and a command horn, Olifant, which ties every lance within a hundred kilometres into one picture. Its pilot is the ace who flew the Saetta, and the panel attached a single condition, which is that the pilot may refuse any order. Strasbourg presents it as the heir of Roland and Charlemagne's paladins, and schoolchildren in every member state know the song. In the song, Roland dies because he is too proud to sound his horn. Castellani built the horn first.

nodes.t: The spirit divided
nodes.x: The Aurora is a super in two halves, the lower built in Calgary and the upper in Montreal, which stand as one giant only when they lock together. Each half carries one pilot, and the pair share the neural load on an interface Boreal licensed from the Twin-Pilot Load Study - a study that Canada's share of the defence fund helped pay for. The two pilots, one from Calgary and one from Montreal, have trained together for six years. Boreal meant the Aurora as a picture of a country that holds together. When Canada splits, the halves end up on opposite sides of the Manitoba–Ontario line, and so do the pilots.

nodes.t: The spirit held in trust
nodes.x: The Custodian is the Republic's answer to the giants on Earth, and the only super built to a treaty. Shackleton Works designed it to the third clause of the orbital draft that every bloc vetoed, so it carries no reactor and nothing it couldn't explain to Geneva. The frame is vacuum-cast in lunar composites around Marlinspike catapult gear, with a linear core of the Works' own design, and it is powered off the ring and the Republic's own relays. The Republic's books list it as a yard tug, an entry few take at face value. It carries no bloc's markings. In the war it is recorded walking through the breaches at Tranquility, and when the Republic closes the lanes to Earth it stands over the slipway in the UN's white. UNEL's Luna bastion is named for it.

nodes.t: The spirit hired
nodes.x: Grey Lantern's super was assembled from Concord parts that left Joint Heavy Systems' depots on paperwork nobody has managed to trace: a salvaged HT-20 plant, one and a half sets of limbs, and a cab rebuilt for whoever is paying. Because the twin-pilot interface only works for a pair who trust each other completely, Grey Lantern pairs strangers on contract and sedates away the difference. It has never fought the same way twice, and it has never been quite right. It is hired out by the week, and the container ship that carried it through the Panama Canal is the reason Panama now opens every container.

nodes.t: The spirit hunts in packs
nodes.x: Moscow's answer to giants it can't match in the open: six Volks rebuilt by OKB-7 as a hunting pack, with lighter armour, spiked climbing feet, tether harpoons, and Type-12 rail rifles loaded with tungsten penetrators. Their links give all six pilots one picture of the quarry. The method is old: cable the legs, bring it down, go for the cab. The pilots are augmented volunteers from the breakthrough groups, the last generation Department Zero will ever train. Their first quarry is Morevna. They have found her twice and come back without her both times, and their reports have stopped calling her a target. In the war they hunt Jingweis across Central Asia, and when the Ascendancy closes Department Zero it keeps the pack, which by then swears the Nashik Oath in Russian.

nodes.t: The spirit volunteered
nodes.x: In the shipbreaking yards at Tangier, a workshop collective of Moroccan mechanics and Southern Crossing volunteers, most of them Spanish and many of those Catalan, builds a giant from what the North African Front leaves behind. Its spine is a cut-down section of the bottom hull of a scrapped Spanish dock ship, the keel and curved bilge ribs reshaped into its pelvis, lower back and shoulder structure. Its limbs are wrecked Mistrals and Siroccos, and its heart is a bank of re-tuned Q-Mix turbines. Nobody owns it. The workshop is run by assembly, the crew is elected and paid the same as the welders, everyone eats at the same table, and the hull is painted red and black under slogans in Darija, Spanish and Catalan. Like the Charter's frames it is named for a wind, the Tramuntana, the north wind of Catalonia. It holds the Strait while the ferries cross, and when the war ends the Commonwealth asks it to serve rather than ordering it to, and the assembly votes yes.

conflicts.label: Conflicts
conflicts.intro: Conflicts from the Ares mission in 2156 to the Greater Solar Crisis of 2327, each one explaining something in the other trees. The dashed column is projected: the crisis No Peace Past Luna is set in.
turns: At Iron Gate, four Garrisons destroyed a tank column in eleven minutes. Within a year every bloc had ordered mechs.
The theft that armed the East
The Pact lost the Battle of the Talysh Mountains, but within a year its spies had LR-1 plans and a captured Mk.I core. Every Eastern linear weapon starts there.

Officially the Zarqa Campaign. Kestrels landed, fought and left inside their battery limit, and Pact advisers taught the defenders to hide for forty minutes and then hit the swap pits. The Air Umbrella, the hunter-killer lance and the Harrier all exist because of it.
The lance that caught the Kestrels

At Svalbard, Pavises jammed a Kestrel flight's landing approach and shot four as they transformed. It was the first hunter-killer lance action, it gave the Union its first famous ace, and within a year every front-line Kestrel had been refitted as a Harrier.
The giant that fell in the desert

The Union sent Halden's H-17 to end a League civil war in the Great Sand Sea. Its restraint frame failed, its pilot died, and Geneva sent the footage to every parliament in the Union on the same morning. The ethics panel, the Jinn and the League's rift with its Gulf associates all start there.

Asked to plan for a two-front war, Tianshu returned a plan in which the second front was Moscow. Beijing classified it within the hour, and within the month someone in Moscow had read it. Beijing says the network models every contingency. Moscow says Beijing kept asking.

The Lunar Republic builds every bloc's first warships, and its domes are fighting a cold war over whether it owes the planet below anything. Each bloc is building its own way into orbit so that it never has to depend on the Moon.

Colony One's settlers needed radiation-hardening gene therapy, and US law bars enhanced citizens from federal service, so the Americans among them resigned their commissions and went as civilians. The first permanent home on another planet is already arguing over its charter.

At Mong Hsat the UN destroyed a warlord flying Pact frames. The Pact couldn't veto the resolution without explaining who had sold him parts, and Washington wouldn't defend him, so it passed with every bloc abstaining. It was the first time Geneva had won anything by force.

The Concord reveal turned super robots into a public arms race. Canada learned it had paid for HT-20 plants it was never told about, and the two supers nobody controls, the Jinn and the Choir, are out protecting civilians.

In Khartoum the League's members, joined by Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, signed up to mutual defence and to protecting people before territory. It is the first time the League has promised to fight for anything except being left alone. Qadira moved its design office to Khartoum the same month.

Japan sold critical parts to every bloc so that nobody could afford to attack the supplier. Then Beijing, which already fed Japan on credit, was refused a Mk.III licence and began holding Japanese capacitors at every Chinese port. A coalition elected to settle with Beijing now runs the Diet, and Mitsurugi's board has booked flights to Vladivostok.
Beijing wants Department Zero shut down; Moscow and Delhi won't allow it. On a map the Pact is still one bloc, though its own staff officers stopped thinking of it that way some time ago.

The two General Staffs stop pretending. Central Asia becomes the front, the Tian Shan Rail is fought over until neither side can use it, and what comes out of the Pact is China and the Eurasian Ascendancy.
Five powers come out of it

Moscow's siege trains reach Berlin, the Americans land in Ireland and Spain, and the African Union crosses into the south. The Union's council dissolves, its nations hold the line between themselves, and they refound it as the Transatlantic Union. Canada splits along the Manitoba–Ontario line, the United States takes the Isthmus, and the League ends the war as the African Commonwealth.
When the war turns atomic, the Lunar Republic puts its yards, the ring and every ship it crews under the United Nations, and closes the lanes down to Earth until the blocs stop fighting.
Mars spends a century split between Colony One and the MRD along a Line of Control that was never a border.
A bioweapon that should exist only in the UNEL's vaults kills an independent Martian colony, and every Earth power parks a fleet over Mars.
Colony One turns on the United States, the MRD strikes it from behind, and nobody fires a shot on Earth.
The Syndicate takes over Pallas and Juno while Earth's navies are busy, and China makes sure it can still watch.
Washington finishes Colony One and builds the Constitutionalists: a colony that can't go to war without it.

With anchorages in the Trojans, a colony that won its planet and new hulls from every capital, the Union is the strongest power beyond Luna. It still doesn't trust a Directorate run by committee, and the Directorate still remembers Deimos.
fams: Where the blocs fight each other by proxy, where a pan-African bloc takes shape, and, after the war, the bases and leases the powers keep.
The Pact's borders, the wars along them, and the line it will break along.
Two Western blocs that are allies on paper, the hemisphere Washington considers its own, and, after the war, Geneva's courts and treaties.
Japan's quiet front line, the factories everyone wants, and the islands to the south.
Earth orbit, the Moon and the stations sunward of Earth: nobody fights a real war here until the yards are built, and after the war the UNEL keeps the peace from here.
From the Ares mission to two projects sharing one planet, and the moons that watch them.
The houses' claims, then the Syndicate's markets and the lanes between them.
The earliest leavers, Jupiter's enhanced colonies and the far dark beyond them.

nodes.t: The first to leave go furthest
nodes.x: Before the war there is no exodus, only a trickle of families and congregations who have decided that the coming war will reach them wherever they stay, and who buy passage on Belt haulers going as far out as anyone goes. The earliest of them go furthest. A few dozen ships reach the Kuiper ice and Pluto, where no help can follow, and most of the first settlements fail in the cold. The ones that survive keep no contact with Earth. In the war the refugees of the Long Lift follow them outward in far greater numbers, and by then hardly anyone remembers that someone went first into the dark.

nodes.t: Future League states refuse bloc membership
nodes.x: Resource states across the Middle East, Africa and South Asia refused, together, to join any bloc. On paper that made them neutral. People in those states like to point out that in practice it mostly made them the place where the blocs fought each other at one remove.

nodes.t: United States vs insurgent armour in the Zagros foothills
nodes.x: The first mech combat on record. Four Brannock-Hale M4 Garrisons, armed with M30s and ATGM tubes, ambushed a tank column from a ravine the tanks couldn't climb and destroyed it in eleven minutes. Within a year every bloc had mechs on order.

nodes.t: Iron Gate's final phase
nodes.x: The United States tried dropping licensed Sparrowhawks behind insurgent lines by tiltrotor. The mechs did well enough once they were down, but the tiltrotors were easy targets and nine were shot down in a month. Halcyon's answer was a mech that could fly itself in.

nodes.t: United States vs a Pact-backed government
nodes.x: Officially the Zarqa Campaign, after the Jordanian city where it began. Kestrels made their combat debut here with drop-and-strike: landing, fighting and leaving again inside their battery limit. Pact advisers had worked out that limit, and taught the defenders to hide for forty minutes and then hit the swap pits. Every bloc's doctrine since has been, in one way or another, a reaction to this war.

nodes.t: Desert militias vs every bloc's supply lines
nodes.x: In the wreckage of the Zarqa Campaign, militias in Haboob frames raided convoys from all sides until foreign presence cost more than it was worth. A year later the African states founded the Pan-African League on armed neutrality, and the Gulf states, Pakistan and Bangladesh signed on as associates.

nodes.t: UN frames escort food through the raid zone
nodes.x: In the Convoy Raids the militias hit UN food convoys as readily as any bloc's. Geneva asked every bloc for escort frames, and when all three refused it bought Copperbelt mining walkers and Technical Refits instead, painted them white and crewed them with volunteers. When the blocs left, the white frames stayed with the people they had been feeding. The new League let them use its roads on one condition, that they never fired except to protect a convoy. They kept to it, and they were the only foreign frames the League let in.

nodes.t: League factions backed by the Union, the Pact and Grey Lantern
nodes.x: A League civil war that became three proxy wars at once, fought in Siroccos and Lantern Customs. To end it, the Union secretly deployed Halden's H-17. Its restraint frame failed, its pilot died, and it vanished into the dunes. A white convoy's escort filmed it falling, and Geneva sent the footage to every parliament in the Union on the same morning. Months later a League mechanic walked out of the desert with it. The war also opened a rift between the League and its Gulf associates, who had bankrolled the losing side, and that rift was never closed.

nodes.t: An unrestrained giant protecting civilians
nodes.x: Reports keep coming out of the Great Sand Sea, passed from village to village, of a giant that stands between the militias and the villages and then leaves. Three blocs have sent teams to recover it, and so far all of them have come back empty-handed.

nodes.t: An unidentified giant in a city under shelling
nodes.x: During a Pact-backed bombardment of Herat, an unknown giant held the Malan Bridge over the Hari River open for nine hours while civilians crossed, then disappeared. No bloc has claimed it. It was the Choir. The Pact vetoed Geneva's resolution condemning the bombardment, so the Secretary-General read the names of Herat's dead into the record instead, which took him four hours.

nodes.t: The League promises to fight for something
nodes.x: In Khartoum the League's members, joined by Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, signed a charter committing them to mutual defence, to shared reconstruction and, rather more ambitiously, to protecting people before territory; the Gulf associates were invited and did not come. Qadira moved its design office to Khartoum the same month, and took over the Union's licence plant in Tunis along with most of the French and Italian engineers who ran it. It was the first time the League had promised to fight for anything except being left alone.

nodes.t: Influence, not territory, from the Gulf to Bangladesh
nodes.x: The Gulf states, Iraq, Iran, Pakistan and Bangladesh become a frontline held by influence rather than territory: the League leans on the Gulf and Iraq, Beijing on Pakistan, Delhi on Bangladesh, and everyone fights over Iran.

nodes.t: From Morocco to the Nile
nodes.x: The Union's old Maghreb partners are Charter states now, and every power that needs the Mediterranean wants its southern shore, so the fighting runs from Morocco to the Nile. The League fights it under the name of the African Union, and after the war it becomes the African Commonwealth.

nodes.t: The Jinn's tissue cultures go missing
nodes.x: Raiders who had crossed the Arabian Sea to raid India's coast for twenty years, and fought for the League since the Convoy Raids, ambushed a Kafila convoy carrying the Jinn's tissue cultures to Khartoum. Two crews died, and four cultures are still missing. Khartoum's official line is that it was bandits. The keepers know the raiders' names, because until the Charter they had been on the same side.

nodes.t: A recovery team goes into the Great Sand Sea
nodes.x: One of the three teams sent to recover the Jinn. The aircraft were American; the frames were Lantern Customs with their serials ground off; the recovery rig was built to carry something very large that was still alive. Two frames came back. The after-action report runs to six pages, five of them blacked out. The surviving page ends: ███ ██████ ███ ███ ████ ██ ████ ██ ███ ████ ██ ███ █████.

nodes.t: Healing made into a weapon, then a duty
nodes.x: The missing cultures reappear on the North African Front, inside raid battalions whose soldiers survive wounds that should kill them. As the war grinds on, the League stops arguing: grafting is how it keeps anyone alive on the worst fronts, against shellfire and against the mutagens every side used and none admits to, and then simply how it keeps people. The raid cadres who brought the cultures commit the front's worst raids, and the most changed of the grafted follow them. When the Commonwealth finally catches them, they are sent furthest of all, to Jupiter. Umoja begins there, still using the keepers' word for it: care.

nodes.t: Europeans and Americans go south to the Charter
nodes.x: As the European Front breaks and American cities are mobilised for the war economy, people who want no part of either bloc go south: across the Mediterranean to Tunis, Algiers and Alexandria, and across the Atlantic to Dakar and Lagos. Many are French and Italian, with family ties to the old Maghreb partnership; many more are leftists with no room left in either bloc's politics. They bring languages, engineers and arguments, and the Commonwealth that comes out of the war is more plural for it.

nodes.t: Pact vs US-backed Afghan forces in the Wakhan Corridor
nodes.x: The Tieniu's combat debut. Its crews fired standing, outside the cannon's safe envelope, and the recoil threw frames off their feet; by the second week they were kneeling to fire, as the manual said they should. The Pact also captured a dozen American M30s, which became the Type-07.

nodes.t: Pact vs United States, over Azerbaijan
nodes.x: A Pact push into Azerbaijan brought the United States in. At the Battle of the Talysh Mountains, a handful of Merlins with LR-1 linear rifles destroyed a Tieniu column from above. OKB-7's new Korsaks were dropped to hold the passes ahead of the column, and the drop scattered across the mountains. The Pact lost the battle but won the intelligence war: within a year it had LR-1 plans and a captured Mk.I capacitor core.

nodes.t: Pact digs in; a US probe is repulsed
nodes.x: After the Caspian Crisis the Pact dug Tieshan firing lines into its borders, which was expensive and, as it turned out, money well spent. A US probing raid, Operation Highland, ran into one of them and lost a third of its frames in an afternoon. No bloc has tried to invade the Pact since.

nodes.t: Pact-backed offensive into western Afghanistan
nodes.x: The debut of OKB-7's breakthrough groups: Medveds and Mamonts opening gaps for Tieshan waves. Observers also saw a fast, wolf-like frame that moved in ways no ordinary pilot could survive. It was the first sighting of the Volk.

nodes.t: Moscow stockpiles siege weapons
nodes.x: Kalibr-305 mortars, Iskra cannons and MTU-7 trucks are gathering near the border. Satellite photos show a 50 m shape lying across several oversize flatcars under tarpaulins. Every bloc is asking what war Moscow is preparing for, and Beijing, nominally Moscow's ally, is asking as loudly as anyone.

nodes.t: India joins the Pact as a junior partner
nodes.x: India backed the Hari River Offensive with airfields and fuel, and a year later joined the Pact outright. The price was industrial. OKB-7 opened a second Medved and Mamont line at Nashik, and Indian officers joined the breakthrough groups and took the augmentation that came with them. After fourteen years of raiders who wouldn't die, Delhi wanted pilots who could catch them, and it accepted Moscow's way of making them, however little it liked it. Beijing welcomed a third member, not yet realising that Delhi would vote with Moscow on almost everything from then on.

nodes.t: Beijing's planning network names the second front
nodes.x: Asked to plan for a two-front war, Tianshu returned a plan in which the second front was Moscow. Beijing classified it within the hour. Within the month, someone in Moscow had read it. Beijing's position is that the network models every contingency. Moscow's is that Beijing kept asking.

nodes.t: Fourteen dead at a test range that is on no map
nodes.x: Pact state radio reported an industrial accident at a fuel depot in ██████ ██████, with fourteen dead. Satellite photographs show a test range, a reactor carriage on its side, and a frame-sized trench running north for nine kilometres before it stops. The casualty list was withdrawn after a day. Department Zero's internal number for the event is ██-183.

nodes.t: Beijing and Moscow split over Department Zero
nodes.x: At a closed session of the Pact General Staff in Astana, Beijing's delegation demanded that Department Zero be shut down and its pilot records handed over. Moscow refused, Delhi backed Moscow, and the session ended without a communiqué. From then on the Fortress Belt and the Air Umbrella answered to Tianshu and the breakthrough groups to Moscow, although on paper there was still a single General Staff.

nodes.t: UN white squads destroy a warlord's army in the Shan Hills
nodes.x: In 2174 a company of the export Tieshans guarding the Pact's Mekong dam went unpaid for a winter and walked into the Shan Hills with their frames. Their commander styled himself the Iron Sawbwa, after the old Shan princes. For ten years he ran jade mines and drug labs on forced labour, kept his Tieshans running on parts bought from both ends of the Pact, and shelled refugee camps across the Thai border for sheltering his deserters. After the Tianshu Forecast, Beijing would not let Delhi's forces near its border and Moscow would not let Beijing's in. When the Secretary-General put a resolution to the Security Council, the Pact could not veto it without explaining who had been selling him parts, and the United States would not defend a man flying Pact frames. It passed with every bloc abstaining. Two white squads went up the valley at Mong Hsat behind a Brazilian major in a Haubert. In two days they destroyed eleven Tieshans, and the Sawbwa died in the last of them. It was the first time UN frames had fired first. Geneva has said it will be the last time, though few of the pilots who flew at Mong Hsat expect that to hold.

nodes.t: The Pact breaks into Chinese and Russian–Indian blocs
nodes.x: The two General Staffs stop pretending. The front is Central Asia, where both sides' railways meet. Mongolia and the Steppe outriders side with Beijing, and the fighting goes where they know the rail lines and Moscow's planners don't. The Tian Shan Rail, the Pact's only road to orbit that doesn't go through the Moon, sits on the front line, and neither side gets much use of it after the first year. The war is recorded as ending in two successor states, China and the Eurasian Ascendancy.

nodes.t: Moscow's siege trains turn west
nodes.x: Moscow's breakthrough groups and siege trains turn west into a Continental Union whose council is still voting on how to respond. Twenty-six national contingents wait on twenty-six parliaments while the line gives way from the Baltic to the Black Sea, and behind it a few cities split along the old Maghreb question, street by street. By the first winter the council has stopped meeting, and what is left of the defence is whatever the national staffs can arrange with each other.

nodes.t: Washington hands frame procurement to its makers
nodes.x: A year after Iron Gate, Congress needed mechs faster than the Pentagon could buy them. The Defense Production Partnership Act let Brannock-Hale and Halcyon design, build, crew-train and maintain their own frames, with company engineers holding reserve commissions and company depots counted as Army bases. It was meant to last until the first production run was delivered. It is still in force, and the two companies' lobbyists wrote most of its renewals.

nodes.t: United States vs Continental Union, undeclared
nodes.x: A trade dispute over the Union's North African partners turned into two weeks of undeclared strikes. US aircraft destroyed Union hydrogen depots and grounded the Écuyer fleet without firing on a single mech, and the Union rebuilt its doctrine around never being blind or stranded again. The partners in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia drew a different lesson, which was that Strasbourg couldn't protect them.

nodes.t: United States vs Union over Arctic seabed claims
nodes.x: The first hunter-killer lance action. Pavises jammed a Kestrel flight's landing approach, then shot four of them as they transformed, and a red Castellani Falco finished the rest. Within a year the United States had refitted its front-line Kestrels as Harriers, a heavier design first drawn up against the Pact's rockets. The Union got its first famous ace. Norway, a US ally, watched two allies fight over its own archipelago and began asking which of them would defend it.

nodes.t: The enhanced march for one licence
nodes.x: Forty thousand people walked from Marseille to Geneva over one summer: Ascension's station-born children, retired low-gravity crews, patients of the Horn's free-port clinics, cold-hardened yard crews from Russia's Far East, Tabernacle families from the coal hollows, and Sulu Gardens patients who had paid with more than money. They asked the UN for one licence every bloc would honour, so that a body changed in one bloc could work, serve and travel in all of them. Geneva could only refer the request to the Security Council, where it was vetoed by every bloc, each for a reason entered separately in the record. The walkers called themselves Umoja, unity, after the word their leader, Amos Kiprotich, kept using. They marched unarmed, deliberately - the raid bands were the other answer to the same question, and the walkers wanted Geneva to see the difference. Three years later the United States answered with Unaltered Crews.

nodes.t: The United States unveils its super robots
nodes.x: The United States revealed the Concord class in public, as a deterrent. Every other bloc's hidden programme sped up overnight, and every intelligence service started asking who else had one.

nodes.t: Canada asks for observer status in the Union
nodes.x: After the Concord reveal, Canada's parliament learned that its share of the joint North American defence fund had paid for HT-20 plants it was never told about, built by companies that answer to Washington before Ottawa. A motion to seek observer status in the Union passed by eleven votes. Washington described it as a procedural matter; Strasbourg, rather more interested, had a delegation in Ottawa within the week.

nodes.t: Canada splits along the Manitoba–Ontario line
nodes.x: The Halifax Motion's eleven votes become a partition. The western provinces stay with the United States, while Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces join the Union, followed, after thirty years of paying Washington's levy, by the United Kingdom, Iceland and Norway. Quebec's hydrogen fields come with them, so that the Union's fuel cells are never short of hydrogen again, and the line between the two Canadas is fought over for the rest of the war.

nodes.t: Mexico joins; Central America and the canal are taken
nodes.x: Mexico joins the United States, and the canal where Panama once searched every ship is taken with the rest of Central America. It keeps the hemisphere's trade in Washington's hands, and by the war's end the country calls itself the United States of the Americas.

nodes.t: Brazil reaches for Africa and is cut off
nodes.x: Brazil, flying European frames and trading with Africa, tries to align with the African Union. The Isthmus Seizure cuts the hemisphere in two. US forces then push down the Andes and into the Amazon, and the continent becomes a front rather than an ally.

nodes.t: Refugees flee to the ice
nodes.x: Refugees from the Canadian Front go north, into the Arctic archipelago and Greenland, and refugees from the South American Front go south, to Tierra del Fuego and the Antarctic stations. No army wants the ice, and that is why they go to it. The communities that survive learn to live on almost no heat, almost no power and almost no outside help, and come in time to distrust anyone from the warm places. A few say that a giant walked with them across the ice and never said a word. All of it, the cold and the distrust and the silent giant, goes with them when at last they leave Earth, much later and very far.

nodes.t: Places the war is not allowed to enter
nodes.x: The UN cannot stop the war, so it names the places the war may not enter: Geneva, the hospital ships, the refugee camps on the Falklands, the Antarctic stations, and the roads of the Polar Exodus and the Southern Crossing. For the most part the fronts go round them, because every side needs somewhere to exchange prisoners, and the white squads are the only people all of them will let into the ruins; when a front doesn't go round, the white squads fight whoever it belongs to. At Punta Arenas they hold the harbour for a week against a raiding column sent for the Antarctic stations' fuel, until it turns back. After Vancouver, the UN's casualty count reaches the lunar yards before any bloc's version does.

nodes.t: The Union's council can't agree how to answer Khartoum
nodes.x: When Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia signed the Khartoum Charter, the Union's council needed every member to agree on a response. It met eleven times in four months, could not agree on sanctions, aid or even a statement, and finally issued a communiqué regretting the partners' decision. The Union still has no army of its own: its lances are national contingents, each needing its own parliament's vote to deploy. Strasbourg calls this consensus, though across the Maghreb people say it looked a good deal like absence. In Marseille, Lyon and Turin, families from the Maghreb who have been Union residents for three generations are starting to be asked which side they are on.

nodes.t: The Secretary-General names the coming war
nodes.x: Months after Mong Hsat, Secretary-General Joaquim Esteves went before the General Assembly with a list: siege trains on the Pact's borders, Concords on parade, a Pact General Staff that no longer meets, a Union council that can't decide anything, Panama opening every container, and warships on the Moon. Every bloc, he said, is preparing for a war it expects someone else to start. He asked for one thing: a standing UN frame force, paid for by every member and answerable to the Assembly. The Assembly voted for it 141 to 9. The Council vetoed its funding three times, once for each bloc. Esteves now asks members for frames one at a time, and more of them are saying yes.

nodes.t: JSDF vs unidentified frames
nodes.x: Unmarked frames landed on Yonaguni and Hateruma, two of Japan's outlying Yaeyama Islands. Hayates came ashore through the surf to meet them and drove them off, in the JSDF's first mech combat. The attackers were never identified, and Japan made no accusations; it went on selling capacitors to everyone.

nodes.t: Attempted theft of the PT-X Raijin
nodes.x: An infiltration team got inside the Tsukuyomi Lab perimeter before it was stopped. The only one captured was a Grey Lantern contractor who didn't know who had hired them. The Raijin was moved, and Takemikazuchi was hidden deeper.

nodes.t: A freighter, a sealed hold, and divers who signed for life
nodes.x: A freighter under a flag of convenience sank in calm weather in the Makassar Strait. JSDF divers were first on the wreck. They found a sealed hold lined with server racks and eleven empty ████████ ████████, and their dive logs were collected by a Japanese ministry the same afternoon. It isn't clear that anyone at the ministry knew what they were looking at. The freighter's owner was dissolved the following week; its registered agent was a pump wholesaler in Makassar.

nodes.t: Beijing demands Mitsurugi's newest capacitor
nodes.x: Beijing asked Mitsurugi for a Mk.III licence and was told the core didn't exist. A week later Beijing's customs began holding Japanese capacitor shipments at every port on the Chinese coast. Mitsurugi's board quietly registered subsidiaries in Vladivostok and Ohio and began copying its design archives to both, on the reasoning that Licence Diplomacy had been built for buyers who wanted the parts, not the factory.

nodes.t: Japan falls into China's sphere
nodes.x: Beijing never lands an army on the home islands. It doesn't need to: the ports already run on Tianshu's schedule, the grain still comes on credit, and when the Pacific war starts the Kansai government asks for protection. Chinese liaison officers arrive at JSDF headquarters within the month, and Japan ends the war inside China's sphere. Not all of Mitsurugi goes with it: the subsidiaries in Vladivostok and Ohio take engineers, archives and actuator lines with them. The line that leaves through Russia will go a long way further.

nodes.t: A Russian advance across the Bering Strait
nodes.x: The Russian half of the Pact Civil War carries its fight across the Bering Strait. The United States, with little left to stop it, answers with atomic weapons, and the limited exchange across the northern front destroys Vancouver. Luna's fleets end the war soon after.

nodes.t: From the Spratly reef to Australia
nodes.x: The Tieshan-Kai company Tianshu set down on a Spratly reef in 2178 turns out to be the first of many. Chinese landings spread through the Philippines and Indonesia, and American carriers fall back on Australia to hold the line.

nodes.t: Vireo's hidden halls burn, and nobody knows what got out
nodes.x: On the Oceania Front a single air raid, which nobody claims, burns the pump works on the Makassar waterfront. The firefighters find what the pumps were hiding: three floors of server halls dug into the reclaimed land beneath them, cooled by the harbour and running until the fire reached them. It burns for three days and three nights. No bodies are counted, because there were never any bodies there to count. Vireo's shell companies go silent the same week, and yet continuity contracts out in the Belt go on being honoured for decades, by somebody. Whether the recordings were inside, copied out in time, or never there at all, nobody outside ███████ knows.

nodes.t: The first crewed Mars landing
nodes.x: Not a conflict. It belongs here because Station Nine, Colony One and the Melas Landing all trace back to ████ ███ ████ ████ █████.

nodes.t: Ascension workers vs station security
nodes.x: The first station labour dispute on record. Workers armed Lifter frames with rivet drivers and torches and held a station for a month. Ascension settled, although by its own inventory it never got all the rivet drivers back.

nodes.t: The lunar towns get councils
nodes.x: By the 2170s Ascension's ice towns at the lunar poles held more people than any station, and the first children born on the Moon were starting school. Rather than face a second Rivet Strike a long way from any security frame, the board granted Shackleton, Malapert, Peary and the old landing city at Tranquility a charter providing for elected councils and seats on the yard board. The bloc shareholders signed it without reading it closely, since as far as they were concerned the Moon was a mining camp.

nodes.t: Bloc teams fight over a drifting cargo pod
nodes.x: Boarding teams from two blocs reached the same derelict cargo pod near the elevator, and Rigger Security frames fought over it with harpoons and spike drivers. Three people died, the first combat deaths recorded in orbit. Within months the blocs had commissioned the first dedicated warships.

nodes.t: A treaty to keep orbit unarmed, vetoed by every bloc
nodes.x: Weeks after the Tether Incident, the UN tabled a treaty to keep orbit unarmed: no warships, no armed frames above the atmosphere, and no reactor-lifted craft in Earth's sky. Each bloc vetoed it, and each commissioned its first warships within months. In the lunar yard someone printed the draft and pinned it up in the crew mess, where it stayed through every bloc's contract. Its third clause becomes the Lunar Mandate's first rule.

nodes.t: A sealed station goes dark for nine hours
nodes.x: Station Nine lost contact for nine hours, the same week Halden activated H-17 in Geneva. Ascension's report blamed a solar flare, although no observatory recorded one that week.

nodes.t: Ascension's lunar half merges with the cities and declares a state
nodes.x: Ascension's board had been deadlocked by its bloc shareholders for a decade. In 2182, while the blocs were still dealing with the fallout of Svalbard, the Hari River and the Delhi Accession, its lunar directors voted to merge their half of the consortium with the lunar councils, and the Assembly at Shackleton declared the Lunar Republic. The yards, the ice and the lunar stations became the property of a state, and their crews its citizens. What was left of Ascension didn't last the year: the Republic took the solar ring and the orbital stations its crews already ran, and the bloc shareholders divided the elevators between them. The blocs called it theft, then remembered who would be building their warships, and started calling it a jurisdictional question. The Republic's first act was to apply to join the UN. The Council vetoed it, and the Assembly seated it as an observer. Earth sits in the same place in the Republic's sky all year round, and the Republic's observers have been noting for some years now that it is getting browner.

nodes.t: The first permanent settlement on another planet
nodes.x: The second Mars mission was a settlement, not a landing. Washington took it over when Ascension was broken up. Its settlers needed radiation-hardening gene therapy, and US law bars enhanced citizens from federal service, so the Americans among them resigned their commissions and went as civilians on the mission's contract. This year they landed. They named the place Colony One: the first permanent human home on another planet. Washington insisted on a written charter guaranteeing its oversight. The settlers are already arguing over the clauses. Their leader is one of the two Ares crew who never gave another interview.

nodes.t: Tianlong's prospecting families keep their own books
nodes.x: Tianlong's orbital subsidiary sent family-crewed tenders out to prospect near-Earth asteroids. Out there Tianshu's plans arrive late and fit badly, so the crews keep their own ledgers, trade among themselves and settle disputes by reputation. Beijing still lists them as contractors, though the crews have begun to call themselves houses.

nodes.t: Warships in orbit, no doctrine to use them
nodes.x: The first dedicated warships carry mass drivers, with Marlinspike frames on their catapults. None of them has seen a fight, no one has yet agreed a doctrine for using them, and every one of them came off the Lunar Republic's slipway.

nodes.t: Every bloc's first warships, built in a slipway none of them owns
nodes.x: When the Tether Incident sent every bloc looking for warships, only one yard could build them: the Lunar Republic's slipway on the rim of Shackleton crater. No bloc wants to depend on a state on the Moon. Each has started building its own way up. In 2186 every bloc's first warships still come off the lunar slipway anyway. Nothing on Earth matches the work: hulls cast in vacuum, composites cured in the cold of the crater floor, coil drivers machined in one piece. The Republic sells hulls to every bloc and gives the best of what it makes to the UN. Among themselves its engineers now say lunar where they used to say Ascension.

nodes.t: An unannounced settlement on ███ ████ █████ ███ ████████ ███
nodes.x: Months after Colony One, a lander in Ascension's old livery came down in Melas Chasma, in the middle of Valles Marineris, on top of ███ ████ █████ ███ ████ ████ █████ ███ ████████. Its manifest called it a Colony One survey camp; nobody asked Colony One. Its crew came from Station Nine, and they are digging for ████████. Halden's scientists, drafting a proposal for a supervised station in the same canyon, don't know one is already there. When Mars is divided, the Red Line between north and south will run straight across it.

nodes.t: The Republic's cold war goes hot in its own domes
nodes.x: The Republic's politics split two ways, and every bloc pays someone. The Earthward, strongest in the yards, hold that Luna exists for Earth, because space is dark and cold without it, and want the Republic in the UN. The Farsiders, mostly young and lunar-born, say Earth is finished and Luna should sell its warships to the highest bidder and close the door. In 2185 it went hot. A pressure seal at Malapert failed during a Farsider rally and killed forty-one people. The following week a bloc trade office at Peary had its air cut, and a Speaker was shot on the Assembly floor. It has never been established who opened the seal. The answer was emergency law: the yard militias became the Lunar Guard, the blocs' advisers were sent home, and the Farsider leaders went to the far-side ice camps. First Speaker Teodora Halloran kept the Earthward policy and adopted the Farsiders' methods, and the Republic is a harder place than it was a year ago.

nodes.t: Every bloc builds its own way into orbit
nodes.x: No bloc will trust its navy to a state on the Moon, so each is building its own way up. The Pact builds hull sections on the ground and throws them into orbit on the Tian Shan Rail, a magnetic track up the mountains on the Kazakh–Kyrgyz border, which both of its General Staffs claim. The Union has leased docks of its own on Malapert Mountain, inside the Republic, and is still arguing with the Lunar Guard over who inspects them. The United States is building the Hampton Roads Orbital Dockyard at the L1 point, named for the Navy yard the sea took. In 2186 all three are behind schedule, and every first warship still comes off the lunar slipway, though it will matter later that each bloc has a way up of its own when Luna closes the lanes.

nodes.t: The first war fought between ships
nodes.x: The warships that no one knew how to use learn quickly. Fleets fight over the elevators, the solar ring and the lanes to the Moon. The carriers find that frames win boarding actions but are too slow for open space, so they launch fighter craft beside them. At the Battle of Yernon, with Berlin under siege, a single British dreadnought breaks the Russian inner fleet, and the Union, written off since the European Front, is a great power again. The ship is British and the docks were leased by a council that no longer meets, and London never lets anyone forget either. The lunar yards build for every side, the Tian Shan Rail and Hampton Roads for their own, and the Republic watches all of it.

nodes.t: The Lunar Republic puts its fleets under the UN, and the war stops
nodes.x: By its last year the war has pushed a biosphere already damaged by two centuries of warming close to collapse, and the atomic exchange over the northern front nearly finishes it. The Lunar Republic, hardened by Tranquility, refuses to launch for any bloc. It places the yards, the ring and every ship it crews under the United Nations, the one institution every side had ignored through the war and still let into the ruins, and closes the lanes down to Earth until the blocs stop fighting. Each bloc keeps a road to orbit, rebuilt or reopened under UN inspection: the Tian Shan Rail, wrecked in the war, is relaid, and the Malapert docks and Hampton Roads go back to work. That is the main reason the blocs accept it. The Mandate's first rule is the third clause of the treaty every bloc vetoed in 2184: nothing lifted by a reactor flies over Earth again. It ends the war and founds the United Nations of Earth and Luna, an institution with its own navy and a mandate to protect humanity from itself, which few of its members had asked for and none of them was in a position to refuse. The Republic's Assembly sits on as UNEL's lunar chamber, and its Guard crews the Luna half of the fleet.

nodes.t: Farsiders seize a lunar city, and the Republic hardens
nodes.x: Midway through the war, Farsider cells seize Tranquility, the old near-side landing city, and offer the Republic's slipways to whichever bloc will recognise them. At least two blocs are recorded as answering. The Lunar Guard retakes the city in nine days, dome by dome, with the Custodian walking through the breaches, and from then on the Republic stops pretending to be neutral about anything. The leadership that comes out of Tranquility is the one that refuses to launch for any bloc, closes the lanes and hands its fleets to the UN on its own terms.

nodes.t: Horn raid bands vs India's west coast
nodes.x: Raid bands from the Horn and the Yemeni coast began crossing the Arabian Sea on the monsoon wind, in dhow-ferries with a rebuilt Garrison or Tieniu lying on the deck. They hit Gujarat's ports and the Konkan fuel depots and were gone before the Indian Army's tanks arrived. India had no frames; its licence requests were still waiting in Washington and Beijing. Doctors who examined captured raiders found bone and muscle therapies made for Ascension's low-gravity crews and pirated by the free-port clinics of the Horn, treatments meant to keep bodies whole that were now keeping raiders on their feet. Raiders who should have died of their wounds walked back to their boats. They were the first enhanced soldiers anyone had fought, and for years India fought them alone.

nodes.t: Monsoon bands burn India's largest oil port
nodes.x: The monsoon bands came back with Haboobs. Twelve frames landed at night, held Kandla for six hours and burned it. The company of Tieshan-Is that Delhi had bought from Beijing arrived from Ahmedabad on the second day, three frames short: their actuator spares were in a Tianlong depot, waiting for Tianshu to schedule them. Delhi asked Washington for frames once more and was offered a licence on the terms Ottawa had been paying for a decade. A year later many of the same bands rode in the Convoy Raids, and started calling themselves League.

nodes.t: The Commonwealth catches the raid cadres at last
nodes.x: For more than twenty years the raid cadres were someone else's problem: India's, then the blocs', then the League's own embarrassment. By the last year of the war the African Union has frames of its own design, battalions that know the coast and nothing left to be embarrassed about. It runs the cadres down from the Ogaden to the Horn and corners them at Ras Hafun, where the first bands set out for India. It does not execute them. It puts them aboard hulls bought from the lunar yards, the first ships it ever paid for, and lets any grafted soldier who chooses to follow them go too. Some of those who choose are its own veterans, and one is Amos Kiprotich, who led the Geneva Walk and says that if they go, he goes. The ships go to Jupiter, and the Commonwealth's first law about space is that they don't come back.

nodes.t: The African Union crosses the Mediterranean
nodes.x: Every power that needs the Mediterranean wants its southern shore, and the African Union decides it needs some of the northern one too. Its interventions cross the Strait into Andalusia, land on Sicily and raid the Provençal coast, to break up the bases bombarding the Maghreb and to bring out Charter families still living in Union cities. Spain and Italy fight on two coasts at once, and learn exactly how far they are from Berlin.

nodes.t: The Pact vs India on the Ladakh heights
nodes.x: A Tianlong road crew reached a pass that India claimed, with a company of Tieniu kneeling on the ridge above it. India had tanks that couldn't climb to them and no frames at all. After a month Delhi withdrew its posts and described it as a negotiated adjustment, and Beijing went on building the road to schedule. Indian newspapers printed the photograph of a kneeling Tieniu on that ridge for years, under different headlines, and a generation of Indian officers still measure by it how far India fell behind.

nodes.t: The Steppe splits between protection and the Belt
nodes.x: In the first winter of the Pact Civil War the Steppe camps hold an assembly at Darkhan. Beijing offers what the steppe has always needed and seldom had: protection, rail and a place in the plan. The price is the plan. The camps split. Most take the protection, guard Beijing's railheads for the rest of the war, and their grandchildren still run the Ground to Orbit Accelerator. The rest, the wind riders who never let Tianshu route them and most of Khiimori's younger members, load what they can carry onto the last launches up the Tian Shan Rail before it is wrecked, and join the prospecting houses in the Belt. Each half says the other sold the horse.

nodes.t: The Ascendancy sends its oath-sworn pilots away
nodes.x: By the end of the war Moscow and Delhi know what the next one will look like: Jingweis that answer only to a network, grafted raiders who won't die and, in their own sealed files, the Koschei. They agree on little, but they agree that someone will have to hunt that kind of thing, and that it should be people who can't be made into it. The Nashik pilots won't be commanded by anyone who ran Department Zero, and say so. So at Vladivostok, beside the grounded Hakobune, envoys from both capitals hand them the ship, the Ashvin drawings, the Mitsurugi exiles who asked to go with them, and Lev Arsenyev's Primorye crews, who had hidden the pilots while the capitals argued, with a blessing the Compact still recites: you won't let us control you; you have our blessing; now leave, before we change our minds.

nodes.t: The nations hold the line the council couldn't
nodes.x: With no council left to give orders, the national staffs give them to each other. Lisowska's Polish lances fall back from the plains east of Warsaw fighting for every river, the German contingents dig in on the Oder with Funkenwerk's black Aufbruchs, and French and Italian aces fly in under their own flags. Brandt's hunter-killer students find each other on the Argus picture without anyone in Strasbourg telling them to. It is improvised, quarrelsome and very nearly not enough. Moscow's siege trains reach the outskirts of Berlin, and for a winter the city is shelled by Kalibr-305s from the east. It holds. The officers and families who held it, each nation by its own arrangements, come out of the war believing they saved Europe, and they never give the power back.

nodes.t: Washington's allies pay for its carriers
nodes.x: Not a conflict. When drowned coasts and failing harvests made America's carrier fleet too expensive even for America, Washington asked its North Atlantic allies to pay for their protection by the tonne. Canada paid in Quebec hydrogen at Washington's price, Norway and Iceland in seabed and basing rights, and Britain in its last shipyards' order books. The compact comes up for renewal every ten years and each renewal costs more than the last, so that in Ottawa, London, Oslo and Reykjavik it has become hard to say what the money buys.

nodes.t: Washington forbids Britain a Union frame
nodes.x: The British Army wanted the Union's Haubert, whose hardpoints took any weapon its crews could find. Washington's answer came from Halcyon, not the State Department: if one Haubert crossed the Channel, Halcyon would stop servicing Britain's Kestrels. Britain kept the Kestrel and paid for the privilege under the Burden Share. The Ministry of Defence also kept the Union's offer letter, framed, in a corridor every new minister has to walk down.

nodes.t: Britain is refused a slipway of its own
nodes.x: Britain offered to pay a third of the Hampton Roads Orbital Dockyard in return for one berth of its own. Washington offered the Clyde's shipwrights jobs at L1 building American hulls, and the Royal Navy the right to crew a few of them. In March the Admiralty asked Strasbourg, quietly, whether the Malapert docks had room. The Union's council, which has never agreed on anything quickly, agreed in nine days. Britain's first orbital hull is laid down on the Moon under a Union lease, and it will be a dreadnought.

nodes.t: Frame depots appear on both sides of a future border
nodes.x: After the Halifax Motion, people on both sides start stocking a line nobody has drawn yet. In the autumn the RCMP finds two depots outside Kenora, forty kilometres apart: one full of Brannock-Hale actuator spares consigned to a heritage rifle club in Winnipeg, the other full of Union reformer stacks consigned to a Montreal hydro cooperative. Neither owner is charged. Both depots are restocked within the month, and Boreal's Wolverine order book has two customers it can't name.

nodes.t: Canadians fight Canadians across the Shield
nodes.x: The partition line doesn't hold still. Through the first two winters it is fought across the Shield forests and frozen lakes between Lake Superior and Hudson Bay, by Canadians in Canadian frames on both sides: Calgary's Wolverines against Montreal's, Tundras dug out of reserve depots, and Polaris rescue frames that both sides stop pretending are unarmed. Washington supplies the west and Strasbourg the east, and both treat it as the cheapest front of the war, which is not how it looks to the people living on it. Small units lie in the snow for days and strike at the supply roads, and towns change hands at forty below. Each half of the Aurora is seen on the line at least once.

nodes.t: A million people carried onto the ice
nodes.x: When the Winter War reaches the towns, Ottawa and Edmonton both run evacuations until neither can manage it. After that the job falls to ice-road haulers, Polaris frames and a frozen-in Union Polar Carrier, which between them move a million people north along the old mining roads into the Arctic archipelago, to wait out the war where nobody fights. Most never come south again. Their camps at Resolute, Alert and Thule are where the Polar Exodus begins, and some of their children will leave Earth from the ice without ever having lived anywhere warm.

nodes.t: The United States lands in Ireland and Spain
nodes.x: When Britain, Iceland and Norway go over to the Union, Washington stops calling the North Atlantic an ally. American carriers put Brannock fire teams ashore in Ireland to hold the approaches, and a second landing in Galicia pushes into Spain while the rest of the Union is looking at Berlin. For the first time since the Maghreb Depot Strikes, Kestrels fly over Union soil, and this time there is no council even to deliberate about it. The Irish, British and Spanish contingents fight them with whatever they can borrow from each other.

nodes.t: The Union is refounded on the nations that held it
nodes.x: Yernon gives the Union a victory and the Mandate gives it a peace, but the refounding is written by the national staffs who held Berlin. They don't trust a council, so they build a concert: Paris, Berlin, London, Rome, Madrid, Warsaw and the rest meet in Strasbourg as equals, and none of them will let another lead, which is why no single member can stall the whole. Eastern Canada and the North Atlantic join as nations in their own right. The Transatlantic Union belongs to its national elites, and anyone can join one. Its mixing policy places children of every origin in the schools that make each nation's officers and councillors, and an officer's grandchild from Dakar or Manila can be more French than a Breton farmer, provided they learn the school, the manners and the mess. What nobody can be is merely European, or only what their grandparents were. It is a union of a thousand colours, and everyone had better know which ones are theirs.

nodes.t: Forty-one votes against Unaltered Crews, and a charter nobody reads
nodes.x: When Unaltered Crews became regulation, forty-one members of Congress signed a minority report against it. Their case was narrow: a radiation therapy is medicine, not alteration, and a country that bars its own settlers from service will lose them. They lost the vote and stayed in government: liberals from the coasts and the border states who believed in the state they were arguing with. “We lose votes. We don't lose the country.” Their appendix was a model charter for American territory off Earth: an elected assembly, a bill of rights covering every settler, altered or not, and war powers kept in Washington, so that no colony could ever start a war in America's name. Washington took the oversight clauses for Colony One's charter and shelved the rest.

nodes.t: Beijing feeds Japan, and Tianshu learns its ports
nodes.x: Two failed harvests in a row left Japan buying rice, and only Beijing had rice to sell. It came on credit, secured against the port fees at Hakata, Kobe and Niigata, on Tianlong ships that Tianshu scheduled. Within a year Tianshu was scheduling the ports as well, because it was the only system that knew when the ships would arrive. Tokyo described this as an efficiency, though the JSDF noted that Beijing now knew the movements of every ship in Japan's three busiest harbours before Japan's own navy did.

nodes.t: A government elected to settle with Beijing
nodes.x: After the Osaka customs holds, a coalition of exporters, port cities and the grain-debt committees takes the Diet's lower house on a promise to settle with Beijing. Its first bill moves capacitor export licences from the trade ministry to a joint commission with a Chinese co-chair. Its second puts the Tsukuyomi Lab's budget under review. Mitsurugi's board read the second bill and booked flights to Vladivostok.

nodes.t: Colony One recruits people who can go without
nodes.x: The second Mars mission needed settlers who could live on a ration of air, and who would take a gene therapy that ended any federal career. Its recruiters went where people had already stopped waiting for help: stilt towns on the drowned Gulf coast, Alaskan homesteads, desert water communes, the families who ran the Arctic ice roads. The roster asked three questions: can you fix what keeps you alive, can you go without, and will you stay. Washington paid for the mission and never read the roster. Colony One's founders are on it, along with most of the people who later broke with Washington's charter.

nodes.t: Elevator berths for people leaving a failing planet
nodes.x: After a third bad harvest year, the elevators' new bloc owners begin selling berths to the stations and the Moon to anyone who can pay, and running a lottery for those who can't. The queue grows faster than the berths. The Lunar Republic takes a quota, the stations take whoever has a trade, and the prospecting houses take whole families. Every government on Earth describes it as a brain drain, but none of them is ready to stop it, since that would mean admitting why so many people want to leave.

nodes.t: The Union's ethics panel turns to everything beyond the Moon
nodes.x: With the European Front burning, the Union's ethics panel holds its hearings in a bunker under Strasbourg, rules for its Mars station against the council, and in the course of it all stops asking only what Europe may build. Its four hundred pages on a station on Mars turn into a question about everything beyond the Moon: who may be changed out there, what may be grown, and who answers for it. The panel decides, after the usual qualifications, that someone must, and that it had better be people who have read the conditions. That decision is the founding charter of the Martian Research Directorate. The refounded Union keeps the conditions on its books, but the nations that held Berlin don't intend to be told no by a committee, and the panel's records, its hearings and most of its staff go to Mars.

nodes.t: Every front sends people up
nodes.x: The war empties more than cities. Every front sends people up, on whatever is flying. Refugees ride returning ore carriers. Crews desert with their ships. Governments sell engineers passage to keep them out of enemy hands. They go to the Moon, to the Belt houses, to Mars on both sides of the line that will divide it, and as far out as anyone will carry them. Every space power of the next century is built by people who left in the war, and most of them kept quiet about what they had left behind.

nodes.t: Mexican water engineers sign on for Colony One's first resupply
nodes.x: Colony One's settlers know how to go without, but sharing is another matter. The mission's resupply recruiters went to the river commission set up by the Rio Bravo Compact, whose Mexican engineers and water judges had spent five years dividing a shrinking river by law and getting both banks to accept the rulings. As Mexican citizens they could take the radiation therapy without giving up a career, and forty families are on the manifest for the first resupply flight. They bring court-kept water ledgers with the Virgin of Guadalupe painted on the covers, and the habit of settling an argument before anyone reaches for a weapon. When Mexico joins the United States in the war, they become, overnight, enhanced American citizens whom no law yet covers.

nodes.t: Beijing makes the houses its clients
nodes.x: Tianshu's Belt forecast finds that the prospecting houses bring home more ore when it leaves them alone than when it routes them, and Beijing does what the network advises. Instead of disciplining the houses, the Ministry of Commerce charters them. They get a Chinese registry, Chinese insurance, refits in Tianlong's orbital docks and the protection of the flag. Beijing gets first refusal on every cargo sold through the new exchange at Juno, and a copy of every survey. The charter needs a name, so a clerk gives it one: the Celestial Prosperity Syndicate. The houses laugh at it, then paint it on their hulls, because no other navy will board a ship carrying a name Beijing wrote. Beijing thinks of the arrangement as patronage, but the houses have always treated it as a contract, and like any sensible trader they read the termination clauses first.

nodes.t: Beijing's Belt ships pass to the Syndicate
nodes.x: When the Pact Civil War calls Beijing's ships home, it cannot hold the Belt and fight in Central Asia at once. So it leases what it has out there to the Syndicate for the duration: survey tenders, armed haulers, the first Steppe corvettes, and a carrier no house could ever have bought. The terms are simple. The houses keep the hulls flying, and China's ore keeps coming home at cost. The convoys do not miss a delivery in the whole war, and Syndicate arbiters still bring that up in every negotiation with Beijing. The lease is never closed. Beijing never asks for the ships back, the Syndicate never stops shipping at a discount, and both find the debt more useful than a settlement. The Chinese hulls still flying for the Syndicate in 2327 came to it the same way.

nodes.t: Mars refuses an order from Europe
nodes.x: In the war's second year, with the European Front breaking, the Union's council orders its new station on Mars to do what the panel forbade: grow tissue, harden soldiers and ship the results home. The station is run by Halden's surviving scientists, the people disgraced for doing exactly that. Their director answers with the page of the conditions that allows no wartime exception, and refuses. Strasbourg cuts off the station's supply. The crew ration air, buy spares from Colony One's settlers, who think them fools, and make the rest themselves. When the panel hears the case in its bunker, it rules for the station against the council that created it. The episode leaves a grudge on both sides that outlasts everyone involved in it. It is also the first time the station's crew sign their reports as a directorate.

nodes.t: A federation built on broken mountains finally fails
nodes.x: The war broke the Andes: orbital fire liquefied the peaks the South American Federation was built along, and the rains have wandered ever since. The Federation held on for a century on reconstruction loans and old loyalties, and in the 2290s the loans stopped. It came apart into warlord states and city leagues, with famine in the high valleys and a diaspora across the system that never stopped sending money home. By 2312 every Earth power has a plan for the continent, and few of those plans involve asking the people who live there.

nodes.t: The UNEL keeps the war's worst weapons where it can watch them
nodes.x: Under the Mandate, every biological weapon left over from the war is surrendered and destroyed, with the exception of a few samples the UNEL retains to study countermeasures. These are held at the Lunar Vacuum Research Spire on the far side, behind a Lunar garrison and a vacuum no spill can cross. The Spire is staffed from Luna, and Luna is proud of it. The samples include the last of IRGC-AMX/9, an Iranian wartime mutagen.

nodes.t: Department Zero's arithmetic survives inside a people-first state
nodes.x: The Ascendancy closed Department Zero and kept the Nashik Oath, but not everyone in Moscow and Delhi agreed that it should have.
