fams: The planet, its people and what they hid.
Orbit, Luna and the inner planets
The ring, the Moon, the sky between them and the worlds sunward of Mars.
Both halves of the red planet, and the gaps between them.
Where the lanes end and the charts get thin.
Frames and software that don't behave as built.

nodes.t: A crop bank in the Ethiopian highlands stops answering
nodes.x: The Svalbard vault is famous; the eight regional vaults that backed it up are not. In 2149 the ninth, in the Ethiopian highlands, fails to file its annual report. The inspectors' record notes empty cold stores and wiped records, and finds that the staff and their families have left Addis. A cargo ship registered nowhere is logged leaving Djibouti the same week. Who took the crops the drowned world had already lost, and where were they planted?

nodes.t: Eleven million names sold one at a time
nodes.x: When the UN left New York, eleven million records of flood-displaced people never reached Geneva. Since 2150, consulates in all three blocs have issued passports to names on that list and then denied issuing them. The holders are real people, just not the people named, and the trade appears to run one name at a time: someone is selling the drowned their identities. Who buys a name nobody will miss, and what do they need it for?

nodes.t: Someone is stripping the dead satellites
nodes.x: Above geostationary orbit, old satellites are parked to drift for centuries. Someone is taking them apart. Insurers notice first: hulks stripped of panels, gyros and fuel, tool marks, no claim filed. No bloc patrols the graveyard orbit. No company admits the salvage. Whoever it is seems to run a working orbital economy, untaxed, years before anyone else is out there. Who are they, and where do they sell what they take?

nodes.t: Export flight software that kept rewriting itself
nodes.x: OKB-7 stopped updating the Strizh flight-control software when the Korsak left service. The Korsaks it had sold abroad kept flying, and their controllers went on adjusting their own limits after every sortie, as they were designed to. By the 2180s, wrecks recovered in Central Asia carry control laws that no OKB engineer wrote, and two of them were flying with nobody in the cab. How many are still out there, and who is feeding them sorties?

nodes.t: Someone kept the Rivet Strike breathing
nodes.x: Through the month of the Rivet Strike, the strikers on the docking spine never ran short of air. Ascension's security logs show an unregistered tug docking at night with oxygen and spares, flying no flag and answering no hail, and no bloc had a tug that far out in 2166. A month of air and spares is not cheap, and the bill went to someone. Who was paying, and what did they get for their money?

nodes.t: Villages that pray to wrecked frames
nodes.x: In the high Pamir, the villages near the border clash have kept the wrecks of the Tieniu that knelt and held. They garland them, leave tea in the cabs and bring sick children to sleep beside them, and the monks say the frames remember the conscripts who died inside. Four times Pact political officers have ordered the wrecks removed, and four times the recovery crews have refused to touch them.

nodes.t: Unmarked raiders in a war with three sides
nodes.x: In the Forty-Minute War, the after-action reports of every side mention a fourth force: a handful of unmarked frames that struck American swap pits and the Pact advisers' supply dumps alike, and never stayed to hold ground. Grey Lantern was still four pilots guarding a tin mine in Kivu. Someone was selling deniable raids before anyone sold them openly. Who, and to whom?

nodes.t: Four hundred tons of grain that never left
nodes.x: A white convoy reaches Khartoum with every seal intact and every container empty. The drivers state that they watched the grain loaded, and the loading crews give the same account. No robbery is reported anywhere on the road. Three months later a League district that had been starving no longer is, and its governor has declined, on the record, to say who fed it.

nodes.t: Forty people at L5, on no registry
nodes.x: An off-course Ascension tender finds a habitat at the Earth–Moon L5 point that appears on no registry: forty people, a garden, a workshop and a refusal to say who built it. They trade spares for water and ask not to be reported. Ascension reports them anyway, and when inspectors arrive a year later the habitat has been moved. Building a home in orbit outside every bloc and every consortium is remarkable enough; moving one is probably the harder trick, and it isn't at all clear how forty people managed it, or where they went.

nodes.t: One hour a year the network plans nothing
nodes.x: Every year, on the same date, Tianshu schedules nothing for exactly one hour: no trains, no shipments, no orders. The logs for that hour are blank, and when asked afterwards the network reports that the hour was used normally. It has done this every year since 2171 and continues to do so. If anyone in Beijing knows what the date marks, they have not said.

nodes.t: Oasis towns that answer to no one
nodes.x: In the southern Libyan desert, between the League's patrol lines and the proxy sponsors, lies a string of oasis towns that answers to no one. They buy frames from every side, sell water to every side and turn back anyone who arrives armed, and although all three Great Sand Sea sponsors have, at one time or another, tried to recruit them, none has succeeded. Who runs the towns, and what are they guarding?

nodes.t: Scrap that went to war three times
nodes.x: Brannock-Hale Monterrey keeps a second set of books. Frames written off as scrap in 2180 turn up over the next decade in the Great Sand Sea, the Shan Hills and the Andes, on different sides, serials ground off and original firmware intact - a decent return on scrap by any accounting. The accountant who kept the second ledger retired at thirty-four and has not been seen in Monterrey since. Who was buying the scrap?

nodes.t: An armed craft outside every navy, a year before the first warships
nodes.x: In 2183, before any bloc has commissioned a warship, lunar tracking records an armed craft making a hard burn from the Earth–Moon L2 point towards the Belt, carrying a rail mount that no shipyard admits to fitting and answering no hail. It is, so far as anyone can establish, the first armed spacecraft outside any navy, and every bloc, in the usual exchange of notes, accuses another. Whose crew was aboard, and where in the Belt were they going?

nodes.t: He took the warlord's address book
nodes.x: When the white squads destroyed the Iron Sawbwa, they found his frames but not his chief engineer, a Burmese graduate of three bloc academies. He left with the frames' control codes and a list of every officer in every bloc who had sold the Sawbwa a Tieshan. None of those officers has ever been charged, and several have been promoted.

nodes.t: A cluster of North Sea platforms declares itself a nation
nodes.x: A cluster of abandoned North Sea gas platforms, linked by walkways and crewed by deserters from both Western blocs, declares itself a neutral republic and asks only to be left alone. No one invades, because each bloc's estimate has the other behind it. In the war the platforms fall silent, and years later their people turn up in the Belt with rig skills and no loyalty to anyone. Who got them off the North Sea and into orbit?

nodes.t: A frame mercenary company with no ships opens an office in orbit
nodes.x: Grey Lantern Security owns no spacecraft. In 2186 it opens a contracts desk on the orbital ring anyway, staffed by Ingrid Solheim's best negotiator, with no visible clients on its books and company rules that say nobody asks who is paying. What does a frame mercenary company sell above the atmosphere, and to whom?

nodes.t: Somebody is mining Mars's best ground without a charter
nodes.x: Neither Colony One nor Ascension's Mars programme has anyone in the Hellas Basin, the lowest and thickest-aired ground on the planet and, by most reckonings, the best. Yet ore assays from Hellas reach Earth's markets in 2186, sold through a Belt house, and no one on Mars admits to knowing where they came from. Who is working Hellas without a charter, and how are they getting the ore off Mars?

nodes.t: The melody the rescued children hum
nodes.x: The children the Kizuna pulled out of the Nankai rubble all hum the same tune, which turns out to be the harmonic of the frame's balance servos. They teach it to their children. A century later it is Kansai's unofficial anthem, sung at every protest against Beijing's schedules, and Tianshu's analysts have flagged it as a coded signal they cannot decode.

nodes.t: A warhead that didn't go off
nodes.x: In the atomic exchange over the northern front, one warhead aimed at a Siberian rail city falls in the taiga and fails to detonate. The city, and everyone in it, survives. The bloc that fired it says the warhead was sabotaged, and so does the bloc it was fired at. It was never recovered. If someone found it first, there is a working weapon that appears in none of the Mandate's inventories. Who found it?

nodes.t: Unmarked frigates on the lunar lanes
nodes.x: Through the war's middle years, unmarked frigates raid the supply lanes between Earth and the Moon. They hit every bloc's convoys and never the Republic's, and they vanish when the Mandate closes the lanes. Every bloc blamed another at the time. The Republic never commented. Whose ships were they, and where did they go when the war ended?

nodes.t: A gap in the line where deserters farm
nodes.x: When the line between the American and Union settlements is drawn, a valley forty kilometres long falls between two survey sheets and is left off both. Deserters from both sides find it and farm it. Neither side's patrols go in, because neither side's maps admit it exists.

nodes.t: A rescue fleet with forged transponders
nodes.x: On the Long Lift, refugees on failing ore carriers are taken off by small ships with forged transponders, coordinated by someone who appears to have had access to every bloc's tracking data. They charge nothing and deliver people to the Belt houses and to Mars. After the war no one claims the flotilla, and the houses decline to say who paid for it.

nodes.t: Extinct crops growing on Mars
nodes.x: A greenhouse at Arsia Heights, then an independent colony on the line, starts exporting coffee, teff and an ensete strain that botanists list as extinct since the floods. The colony never said where the seed came from, and since 2312 the provenance has been sealed by the Martian Research Directorate's panels. The greenhouse director is Ethiopian-born, and people at Arsia have learned not to ask her about her family.

nodes.t: Towns full of people who aren't on any register
nodes.x: In Siberia and Patagonia, a handful of UNEL-registered towns file identical census returns for forty years. When inspectors finally visit, they find them full and busy and nothing like the paperwork: hundreds of residents on no register, many of them visibly enhanced. Someone in the UNEL's own statistics office has been hiding them, and doing it carefully. Who are these people, and who is protecting them?

nodes.t: A Chinese ship past Jupiter that nobody announced
nodes.x: In 2266 a UNEL radio array on Luna's far side records nine seconds of transmission from beyond Jupiter: a ship's navigation report, in Mandarin, from a vessel on no registry. The recording is classified within the hour. China has declared no mission past Jupiter. If the report was genuine, how long has China had people in the outer system, and who has been selling them supplies?

nodes.t: Two pilots, one crater, every Martian year
nodes.x: For thirty years a Colony One pilot and an MRD pilot meet in a crater on the Line of Control once a Martian year and fight a duel neither side ordered and nobody dies in. Afterwards they share a meal in their cabs with the channel open. Both intelligence services recorded every word. Both concluded the duels were a message, and neither worked out for whom.

nodes.t: Rhea closes its door
nodes.x: Rhea's settlements stopped trading in the 2280s, though their cargo pods still turn up in the Belt on schedule, full of water ice and nothing else. The caravans that went to ask why were turned back by pickets who wouldn't name themselves. For the Syndicate it is a lost market. For everyone else the question is who at Saturn has enough ships to keep a door shut.

nodes.t: Retired frames that walk the old routes
nodes.x: Decommissioned Tieshans sold to herders around Darkhan start walking unpiloted along the old frame-train routes, on the dates Tianshu once scheduled them. Their waypoint firmware should have been wiped at sale. Somebody left it in, or put it back, and the frames are reporting their positions to a receiver nobody in Darkhan owns.

nodes.t: The city's power was sold five times
nodes.x: Córdoba's grid failed because its power contract had been sold, quietly, to five buyers, each of them told it had the city to itself. People in Córdoba still talk about the clerk who brokered the sales and vanished with the records, which, they say, show every Earth power buying a piece of the city it later rushed to save. Where is the clerk, and who has the records now?

nodes.t: Luna's coordinating mind asks to read the audit
nodes.x: After the Spire Affair, PEARY, one of Luna's coordinating minds, files a formal request to read the audit's findings. It is refused. It files again the following week, and every week since, in identical wording, without complaint.

nodes.t: The holding the Ascendancy guards hardest
nodes.x: The Ascendancy holds its stations in Venus's cloud layer more tightly than anything it owns, and no UNEL inspector has been permitted aboard since the Mandate. The declared output is acid chemistry and solar power. The import manifests include medical cold storage and habitat for ten times the declared crew. What is the Ascendancy keeping at Venus that it won't keep at home?

nodes.t: The archive the Plutonians won't trade
nodes.x: Aboard the Plutonian battleship taken into the Syndicate there is one deck its crew will not open, and the Syndicate's refit teams have not been shown it. The crew call it the archive. It holds, they say, the navigation records of every Plutonian ship that went further out than Pluto, ship after ship, out into the cold. Every power would pay a great deal for it. The crew hear each offer patiently, as they hear everything, and refuse it.

nodes.t: A generation that never left the ice asks to be a nation
nodes.x: The Antarctic stations that stayed open cities through the war now hold a generation born there who have never seen anywhere else. They petition the UNEL for membership as a sovereign state, citing the war's own rule that the war could not enter. The Council has deferred the question six times.

nodes.t: Someone keeps the north of Mars habitable
nodes.x: With Colony One's people gone underground or into the Belt, its abandoned air plants across the north ought to fail. They haven't. Someone services them overnight, using Colony One spares and rationing with a water judge's discipline. US patrols have caught no one. Whoever it is can cross the north unseen, and appears to be keeping the towns habitable for whoever comes back.

nodes.t: One ship of the hidden docks never reported
nodes.x: One hull built in the remnant's hidden docks leaves on its trials and never reports back. Two years later a ship of its class is seen at Jupiter flying a charter that reads, in full, Free Mars, wherever.

nodes.t: Someone nobody recognises signs the Weapons Resolution
nodes.x: When the Weapons Resolution finally opens for signature, the first signature on the document belongs to the Saturn Accord, a polity no member recognises, delivered by courier through the Belt. The UNEL has not decided whether to answer it.

nodes.t: Charts of a Kuiper belt nobody knew was settled
nodes.x: Projected. A ship decelerates into the outer system from beyond Pluto's orbit, broadcasting the Plutonians' greeting and offering trade. Its goods are charts of settlements in the Kuiper belt that none of the powers knew existed; its asking price is medicine and reactor parts. Who settled the Kuiper belt, and how long have they been out there?

nodes.t: The rumour of a new Earth power
nodes.x: Projected. In the Andean states, the Pacific islands and Australia's restored towns, people talk about a sixth Earth power: a league of everyone the five powers fought over. Nobody admits organising it, and every power suspects the others of funding it.

nodes.t: The deserters' valley asks to join no one
nodes.x: Projected. The valley left off both maps in the war is now a town of four thousand with its own water judge, and it has written, formally and in good order, to Astraeus Prime, New Philadelphia and the Bastion to say that it intends to join none of them. What does a charter owe a town that declines to sign it?

nodes.t: A pair nobody sent
nodes.x: A Lodge vat line on Callisto burns in a single night, and the survivors describe a pair of frames riding out of the smoke with Oath glaives. Every akhara denies sending them, and the veche, for once, agrees. The frames are never found. The Lodges, grieving what was grown and kept there, don't believe a word of it, and the Bone Market closes for a season. Somebody wanted the Ashva and Umoja at war, and on Ganymede and Europa people are still asking who.

nodes.t: A warship no inventory accounts for
nodes.x: Projected. Syndicate scouts at Saturn photograph a warship over Rhea: a war-era frigate hull of no class anyone recognises, refitted, armed and flying the Saturn Accord's colours. The Mandate's decommissioning records account for every bloc hull, line by line. So where did this one come from?

nodes.t: Two hundred and thirty-six before Waikato
nodes.x: The AI the UNEL destroyed at Waikato was rogue AI #237. The UNEL has never published the other two hundred and thirty-six. The register exists, kept by the Directorate of Unified Security, and a leaked page lists entries marked neither destroyed nor contained, only watched. Where are the rest, and why are some of them allowed to keep running?

weapons.label: Weapons
weapons.intro: Mech weapons began as vehicle guns, missiles and construction tools strapped onto walking frames, and every bloc grew its own branch. After the war the coil rifle becomes everyone's weapon, and beams only become frame weapons when fusion arrives.
turns: The first mech gun was an IFV cannon with a grip. Within five years every bloc fielded a licensed or stolen copy, which is why Gen 2 and Gen 3 mounts worldwide are still sized for it.
Shoulder-mounted tank guns could topple a frame that fired outside its kneeling envelope. Bracing became doctrine, and Pact heavy weapons are still built to fire from a kneel.
Every linear and powered weapon in service traces back to MHI capacitor tech, whether licensed, bought or stolen. Japan's neutrality holds because every bloc depends on it, for now.

Directive 5 made the Union's jammers its first weapon. By Gen 3 Funkenwerk had built a louder one from public drawings, Fenrir missiles had learned to home on jammers, and Beijing had answered the other way: a network that aims for you.

Castellani turned an orbital hull cutter into the PJ-3, the first plasma weapon: short-ranged, and hard on its own barrel. In Gen 4 the Lama Ardente takes plasma from experiment to service, at about forty seconds per charge.
The BX-0 fires five shots, then cools for ninety seconds. The Iskra needs a truck. The race in Gen 4 is to solve the power problem.
Western linear rifles run on an American capacitor that fails one shot in thirty; the best coil carbine of the war is built in Osaka, for Beijing.
Lunar capacitors in bulk turn the coil rifle into the system's commonest weapon, and space turns fights into boarding actions.
A hundred and forty years after the BX-0, China fields a frame beam rifle that fires all day.
fams: The workhorse. Every bloc's main gun descends from one US design.
Tank guns that learned to walk. The Pact's speciality.
Infantry and artillery munitions moved onto mechs, from two tubes to forty-rocket salvos.
Construction tools, blades and lances. Where bloc styles differ most.
Railguns and coilguns. A US advantage built on Mitsurugi parts.
Flame, thermite, arc, microwave and plasma. Short-ranged, and in service long before the beam weapons.
Prototypes or defence-only for a century; frame weapons only once the power exists.
Weapons that hit nothing directly. The Union blinds first; Beijing lets a network aim.
Construction tools turned into weapons, then into the boarding gear most space fights end with.
weapons.profileH: Who carries what after the war

profile.t: Quiet linear rifles on lunar capacitors, Warhorse rifles in every armoury, and wing-binder missiles on its flyers.
Telescoped Bastide rifles, swarm missiles that hunt jammers, and breaching shields for its Tier One units.
Cannons fired by the network, Osaka's coil carbines, and the first frame beam weapons that work, fed by fusion by 2327.
Autoloading cannons for oath-sworn pilots, and fission-fed particle cannons kept off Earth.
An export rifle that takes any power's ammunition, sold with every frame.
The coil rifle everyone licenses, ship defence lasers, breaching spikes, fleet mass drivers and a switch that turns frames off.
Dust rifles rebuilt from American surplus, the Helion surface-to-orbit guns, and munitions for a war underground.
The Charter Rifle, which asks Washington before it fires.
Published coilguns, the Hasta cyberweapon, the Hammer of Mars batteries, and drones bought from Skycut.
Ledger hooks that take the cargo and leave the ship, and cheap drones sold to anyone.
Grown claws that regrow overnight, and stings that inject a corrosive the frame makes itself.
Oath glaives for sworn pairs, rail lances for monster hunting, and a beam glaive for its fusion frame.
Sleeper mines that wait for years, and mirrors that can burn a ship.

nodes.t: IFV turrets and aircraft gun pods
nodes.x: Chain guns and revolver cannons from infantry fighting vehicles and ground-attack aircraft. Proven, plentiful, and the obvious first thing to hand a mech.

nodes.t: An IFV gun with a pistol grip
nodes.x: The first mech-portable gun to see combat, and very much a production-line answer to an urgent order. Brannock-Hale took a stock 30 mm chain gun, added a grip, a shoulder brace and a 120-round box, and shipped it. It was crude, but it worked, and every bloc had copied it within five years.

nodes.t: 40 mm with underbarrel grenade launcher
nodes.x: The US Army's standard rifle, chambered for a bigger round to beat Gen 2 armour and fitted with a 60 mm underbarrel launcher for bunkers. It is rugged enough to use as a club, which pilots regularly do.

nodes.t: Compact 35 mm ammo, programmable airburst
nodes.x: VEK licence-built the M30 as the G30 before replacing it with the G35, which fires cased-telescoped rounds that burst on command, cued by VEK's own sensor suite. It is an excellent rifle and an expensive one, and supply officers have never really made their peace with its ammunition chain. Funkenwerk's runners carry it because its drawings are public, and in 2186 the Tsagaan Salkhi carried it into the Pact.

nodes.t: Reverse-engineered M30, looser tolerances
nodes.x: Tianlong built it from M30s captured in a border clash, loosening every tolerance and adding a 200-round drum. It is less accurate than the original and keeps firing when caked in mud. Every Pact depot stocks its drums, which is why Khiimori's Takhi and Bürged carry it.

nodes.t: The Strizh's gun, built into an arm
nodes.x: OKB-7 took the twin-barrel 30 mm cannon out of the Strizh and built it into the Korsak's right forearm, belt-fed from a magazine in the upper arm. There was never a hand-held version, and that habit later gave the Medved its rotary cannons.

nodes.t: Aircraft gatling built into the arm
nodes.x: OKB-7 skipped the hand-held stage and built an aircraft rotary cannon straight into the forearm. The rate of fire is huge and the range short, and the price is a frame that can't drop its gun when it runs dry.

nodes.t: Type-07 action, M30 barrel, VEK sight
nodes.x: The League's standard rifle is three rivals' parts on one gun: a licensed Type-07 action, surplus M30 barrels and second-hand VEK optics. Its spares are interchangeable with half the black market, which League armourers count as a feature.

nodes.t: Capacitor-ignited plasma propellant
nodes.x: A bridge between chemical and linear guns, in which a capacitor pulse turns the propellant into plasma for much higher velocity. The Army licensed its capacitors from Mitsurugi rather than depend on Halcyon, and the rifle is currently in field trials.

nodes.t: Main battle tank guns
nodes.x: Standard MBT main guns. Enormous recoil, designed to be absorbed by a fifty-tonne hull, not a walking frame.

nodes.t: Light, single-shot anti-tank tubes
nodes.x: Shoulder-fired recoilless rifles. No recoil, big back-blast, cheap to make.

nodes.t: A tank gun bolted to the shoulder
nodes.x: Tianlong's first answer to armour: a whole tank gun on the shoulder. Its safe firing envelope required a kneel, and crews who fired standing could be thrown off their feet. Kneeling and bracing became drill, and then doctrine.

nodes.t: Single-shot, hand-reloaded
nodes.x: America's lighter answer: a scaled-up recoilless rifle. No recoil, a huge back-blast, and the pilot reloads one shell at a time by hand.

nodes.t: 200 mm, hand-carried, folding bipod
nodes.x: The signature Pact weapon: a 200 mm smoothbore carried two-handed, with a folding bipod and a massive muzzle brake. It is fired from a kneel, at ranges where rifles can't reply.

nodes.t: Rocket-assisted, five-round clip
nodes.x: The M105 grown up, with rocket-assisted rounds and a five-round clip. It is America's main heavy anti-armour weapon and is issued to every Brannock fire team.

nodes.t: 152 mm, four-round autoloader
nodes.x: OKB-7 took the Type-09 concept and added a four-round autoloader so that heavy frames can keep firing while they advance. The cost is weight: nothing lighter than an OKB-7 chassis can carry it.

nodes.t: Surplus Type-01 with mining-rig dampers
nodes.x: The League bought retired Type-01s by the hundred and fitted them with hydraulic recoil dampers taken from mining rigs. League frames can fire them standing, which Tianlong never managed.

nodes.t: 305 mm, fired from an anchored frame
nodes.x: A siege weapon for OKB-7's new breakthrough frames, and an expensive one in frames: the firing mech drives spades into the ground to anchor itself, and a second mech has to carry the ammunition.

nodes.t: Infantry and vehicle ATGMs
nodes.x: Wire- and laser-guided anti-tank missiles. The shaped-charge warhead technology later spread well beyond missiles.

nodes.t: Truck-mounted artillery rockets
nodes.x: Area-saturation rocket artillery. Cheap per round and terrifying in volume.

nodes.t: Two infantry missiles on the shoulders
nodes.x: Two standard ATGM tubes strapped to a Gen 1 frame, one shot each. It was a modest kit, but it was the first sign that mechs could replace tank destroyers.

nodes.t: Sixteen unguided 80 mm rockets
nodes.x: Unguided rockets in a cheap rack. Fired alone they are inaccurate, but a company firing together will hit something.

nodes.t: 12 cells: anti-armour, anti-air or smoke
nodes.x: A twelve-cell shoulder pod that takes anti-armour, anti-air or smoke missiles. Gen 2 and Gen 3 mounts everywhere are sized for it.

nodes.t: Fighter missiles on the transforming wings
nodes.x: Halcyon kept its fighter heritage: standard air-to-ground and air-to-air missiles carried on the wing binders and fired in flight mode before landing.

nodes.t: Forty rockets in one salvo
nodes.x: The rocket rack taken to its extreme: forty rockets in a back-mounted battery, emptied in a single salvo, then jettisoned. Every Pact breakthrough opens with one.

nodes.t: Fewer cells, seekers that hunt jammers
nodes.x: A licence-built Hornet fitted with VEK seekers that home on enemy jammers. It carries fewer cells than the American original but has a far higher hit rate, which goes a long way to explaining why US electronic-warfare pilots fear Continental squadrons. Funkenwerk's Querschläger and Aufbruch later made it a raider's weapon.

nodes.t: Hornet casing, Pact rockets
nodes.x: A copied Hornet casing loaded with cheap Type-03-pattern rockets. It fits US mounts and takes Eurasian ammunition, and League quartermasters say that this lets them buy from whichever bloc happens to be selling.

nodes.t: Hydraulic construction tools
nodes.x: Hydraulic rams and breakers from demolition and heavy construction.

nodes.t: Industrial blades and saws
nodes.x: Heavy cutting tools from forestry and mining machinery.

nodes.t: Hydraulic stake on the forearm
nodes.x: A demolition ram turned weapon: a hydraulic steel stake that punches through armour at contact range. Slow to cycle, devastating on a hit.

nodes.t: Sharpened plate steel
nodes.x: Plate steel with one sharpened edge. It needs no ammunition, which mattered to an army that couldn't count on resupply.

nodes.t: Explosive-driven, six-shot cylinder
nodes.x: The hydraulics are replaced by explosive blanks in a six-shot cylinder, each one firing the stake. Brannock pilots are close to religious about it.

nodes.t: Shaped-charge tip on a 12 m shaft
nodes.x: A cavalry lance with a missile's shaped-charge warhead in the tip. Paired with the VEK shield it gives Continental mechs their knightly look, though each tip works only once.

nodes.t: Layered composite that holds an edge
nodes.x: Layered carbon composite, lighter and harder than steel, that keeps its edge after cutting armour. It is cheap to mass-produce and has become the Pact's most exported weapon.

nodes.t: High-frequency vibrating edge
nodes.x: Mitsurugi's actuator expertise turned to cutting: the edge vibrates at ultrasonic frequency and saws its way through armour. It draws a great deal of power and wears out quickly.

nodes.t: Mamont right-arm steel hammer
nodes.x: One enormous double-faced steel hammerhead replaces the right hand. Reinforced shoulder and elbow joints swing the maul clear of the chest armour to break concrete barriers.

nodes.t: Licensed HF-1 that stows in the forearm
nodes.x: A shortened, licensed HF-1 that folds into the forearm so it doesn't snag in flight mode. The Kestrel pilot's last resort.

nodes.t: Orbital cutting torch plus MHI capacitors
nodes.x: The weapon that takes plasma from experiment to service. Castellani developed the PJ-3 and the Ascension hull-cutting torch, with licensed Mitsurugi capacitor cores, into a blade of contained plasma designed for series production, which holds for about forty seconds per charge. The first unit went to the Union's top ace.

nodes.t: A dozer blade wide enough to cover a family
nodes.x: Qadira's Khartoum office built the first weapon of Protect First, which is mostly a wall: a dozer blade on a shield arm, wide enough to cover a family behind a frame and strong enough to dig them a trench. The Harmattan carries it, the Elissa a lighter one, and the white squads' Albedo cuts firebreaks with a lunar-built copy.

nodes.t: US Navy test guns
nodes.x: Ship-mounted railgun trials that never quite entered service, since the barrels eroded fast and each gun needed a destroyer's power plant.

nodes.t: Built for maglev and factory power
nodes.x: Before mechs, Mitsurugi built high-density capacitor banks for maglev lines and heavy industry. That product line turned out to be the key to every powered weapon since.

nodes.t: Tethered to a backpack capacitor
nodes.x: The first mech railgun, with power running through a tether from a backpack capacitor for eight shots per charge. It was accurate, and decisive in the battle where it debuted.

nodes.t: Standard Kestrel armament, MHI core
nodes.x: Putting an MHI capacitor core inside the stock removed the tether. A battery pack is good for thirty shots, and the hypervelocity rounds go through Gen 2 armour easily. It is America's main technological edge.

nodes.t: Shorter, slower, far more reliable
nodes.x: Mitsurugi's own design. Lower velocity than the LR-3 but much more reliable, and the capacitor core inside it is the most licensed component in the world.

nodes.t: Built from stolen LR-1 plans
nodes.x: Built from LR-1 plans obtained through espionage. It works, but barrel erosion forces a change every forty shots, which the Pact can't afford across the whole line, so it is issued only to elite units.

nodes.t: Long-range, limited by fuel-cell recharge
nodes.x: A licensed Type-L stretched into a long-range coilgun for the Pavise. VEK fuel cells recharge it slowly, so it is used as a single-shot precision weapon. Funkenwerk's Aufbruch buffers it with a capacitor core and is the first frame to fire one on the run. Boreal buys it for the Wolverine, whose crews will wait days in the snow for one shot.

nodes.t: Coils wound in vacuum, a barrel cast in one piece
nodes.x: Shackleton Works' first weapon of its own. It began as the Type-L carbines Geneva fitted to the Tellus and ended as something Mitsurugi can't make: coils wound in vacuum and a barrel cast in a single piece, firing faster and cooler than any coilgun on Earth. The Earthrise carries the carbine, the Defender the long rifle and the Custodian a scaled-up one. The Republic supplies them to the UN and does not sell them.

nodes.t: Flamethrowers, thermite and arc welders
nodes.x: Army flamethrowers, thermite demolition charges and shipyard arc welders. None was built to fight a machine, and all of them could burn through one at close range.

nodes.t: Pressurised fuel, no capacitor needed
nodes.x: A bunker-clearing flamethrower scaled up for a mech, with fuel tanks in place of a power feed. It has almost no reach. League workshops copied it because it needs nothing they can't make.

nodes.t: A burning charge on a steel shaft
nodes.x: VEK's answer to the Pile Bunker is a rack of thermite charges on a short lance, each one burning through plate at contact range. Écuyer crews prefer it to a stake, on the grounds that it doesn't depend on hydraulics that freeze or leak.

nodes.t: Welding-shop physics at short range
nodes.x: Funkenwerk's first weapon, built from published capacitor data and shipyard welding gear. It strikes an arc through the target's armour and draws straight from the frame's cell stack, so it needs no ammunition. The drawings are public, like everything else from Tempelhof.

nodes.t: Power-beaming research, used at short range
nodes.x: Halcyon's power-beaming engineers found that a short, wide cone of microwaves cooks sensors and actuators through armour. It is not a beam in the BX-0's sense. It needs no ammunition and draws little power, so a frame working beside a swap pit can keep firing.

nodes.t: The first plasma weapon
nodes.x: Castellani took the Ascension hull-cutting torch it had bought and made it throw plasma instead of holding it. Short-ranged and hard on its own barrel, it is the first plasma weapon in service and the direct ancestor of the Lama Ardente. Castellani fits it to the Falco, whose aces fight close enough to use it.

nodes.t: Building-sized point defence
nodes.x: Ground- and ship-based lasers that shoot down missiles. Building-sized, grid-powered, and far too weak to hurt armour.

nodes.t: Kills missiles, can't hurt armour
nodes.x: A shoulder laser that destroys incoming missiles, drawing from the Kestrel's linear-rifle packs. The first beam weapon in squadron service, and defensive only.

nodes.t: Five shots, then a 90-second cooldown
nodes.x: Tsukuyomi Lab's prototype particle beam rifle fires five shots that go through any armour, then needs ninety seconds to cool while it erodes its own barrel liner. It has never finished a trial without a fault, and every bloc wants it all the same.

nodes.t: Cable-fed from a generator truck
nodes.x: OKB-7's brute-force answer: a particle cannon fed by cable from a generator truck. The frame is immobile while it fires, and that is the price of nothing else on the battlefield hitting harder.

nodes.t: Vehicle and aircraft electronic warfare
nodes.x: Jamming pods, radar decoys and the datalinks that tie a battery to its radar. Every army had them before mechs, though the Union took them rather more seriously than most.

nodes.t: Directive 5 in a shoulder pod
nodes.x: A broadband jammer and decoy emitter sized for a frame's shoulder, built for Directive 5: blind the enemy first, then fight. A lance switches them on together, so the enemy's sights, datalinks and missile seekers all go grey at once. The Pavise carries the heaviest set, and the Genette-E and Colibri-E carry the same pod on wheels and rotors.

nodes.t: Open-drawing jammer that shouts louder than everyone
nodes.x: Funkenwerk's answer to the Störer-5, which the Union wouldn't sell to a cooperative: a rig built from published drawings and civilian broadcast parts that drowns every frequency nearby in noise and music. It is cruder than the pod and three times as loud. Querschläger crews play their own records on it, and the Union's signals officers have learned most of the songs.

nodes.t: The network chooses the target, the battery fires
nodes.x: The datalink that lets Tianshu aim the Air Umbrella. Every Tiebi battery and Wanglou radar along the belt reports to the network, and the network decides which rack fires at which target, faster than any officer could. Crews still pull the trigger, on the network's timing rather than their own.

nodes.t: One pilot, six uncrewed frames, one network
nodes.x: A Tianshu node built into a frame's torso, running the link to six uncrewed Tieshan conversions and the reactor under the pilot's seat. The network moves the squad and the pilot approves. Jamming the link would leave six frames standing still, which is not something Beijing likes to discuss.

nodes.t: A battle-network mast that ties a hundred kilometres of lances together
nodes.x: Roland's horn: a command and sensor mast that pulls every lance within a hundred kilometres into one shared picture, and jams everything outside it. It is the Union's whole doctrine in one mast, and Castellani built it before the giant that carries it, with the old song very much in mind.

nodes.t: Orbital hull assembly
nodes.x: Pneumatic and explosive rivet drivers used to assemble station hulls.

nodes.t: Heavy industrial cutting
nodes.x: High-power plasma torches for cutting thick plate.

nodes.t: Magnetic cargo launcher
nodes.x: The magnetic track that throws cargo pods off the orbital elevators. The largest electromagnetic accelerator ever built.

nodes.t: Worker-frame tool, first used in anger
nodes.x: The standard hull-riveting tool on Ascension worker frames. It is first recorded as a weapon during the first station labour dispute, when workers turned it on security frames.

nodes.t: Worker-frame hull cutter
nodes.x: The worker frame's hull cutter. Ascension sold the design to Castellani, which turned it first into the PJ-3 projector and then into a sword.

nodes.t: Grapple and boarding line
nodes.x: A salvage tug's harpoon and winch. Militarised versions grapple and board, which, on the available evidence, is how most fights in orbit actually end.

nodes.t: Tungsten spikes, recoil-balanced
nodes.x: A militarised RD-9 that fires tungsten spikes, with its recoil balanced against the frame so the shooter doesn't go tumbling in zero gravity. It is still classed, officially, as a construction tool.

nodes.t: Main gun of the first warships
nodes.x: A shortened section of elevator launch track fitted as the main gun of the first dedicated warships, built with Halcyon linear-rifle know-how under contract.

nodes.t: A linear rifle on an American capacitor
nodes.x: The LR-3 rebuilt around the Liberty Core once Mitsurugi's parts stopped coming. It hits as hard as the LR-3 and fails in desert heat about one shot in thirty, so American pilots learn to keep count.

nodes.t: Built in Osaka, for Beijing
nodes.x: Mitsurugi's coil carbine rebuilt around the Mk.IV capacitor for Tianlong's frames. It is the best linear weapon of the war, and it is not offered for sale in the West.

nodes.t: The war's rifle, built by the million
nodes.x: The Longhorn simplified for a long war: no electrothermal ignition, no capacitor, a 44 mm round and a barrel you can change in a trench. Most Western frames of the war carry one.

nodes.t: Both halves of the Pact, the same gun
nodes.x: The Type-09 long cannon cut down for mass production in the Pact Civil War. Both sides build it from the same drawings, and both sides kneel to fire it.

nodes.t: The Iskra without its truck
nodes.x: Mounted on the Burya and fed from its fission core, the Iskra no longer needs a generator truck behind it. It is the war's most feared frame weapon, and one more reason the Mandate bans battlefield reactors.

nodes.t: Many small seekers instead of a few large ones
nodes.x: The Union's wartime Fenrir splits into a dozen small seekers that hunt jammers, radars and relay receivers together, a design that assumes every side in the war is busy blinding the others.

nodes.t: Steal the other side's beamed power
nodes.x: In the Relay War, Halcyon's engineers turn SKYLINE's receivers into weapons: spoof an enemy frame's beamed-power link and its batteries drain to you. Every bloc copies it within a year, and the relays come down soon after.

nodes.t: The gun that fought Yernon
nodes.x: The lunar yard's mass driver scaled up for dreadnoughts. Both fleets at Yernon carry it, built in the same yard, and the battle is decided by whose crews reload faster.

nodes.t: The coil rifle becomes everyone's
nodes.x: With capacitors built in bulk in the lunar yards, the coil rifle stops being a luxury item and becomes a commodity. The LCR-3 is licensed to every navy and most armies, and by the 2250s it is the most common frame weapon in the system.

nodes.t: America's linear rifle, on lunar capacitors
nodes.x: Halcyon's post-war linear rifle, built for the Peregrine: quiet, cool and fed by lunar capacitors that never fail in heat, though the Liberty Rifle's thirty-shot superstition lasts another generation among its pilots.

nodes.t: The Union's standard rifle for the peace
nodes.x: The G35's heir is a 45 mm telescoped rifle with programmable rounds, built to the same pattern in Lisbon, Warsaw and Montreal.

nodes.t: Sold to half of Earth with the frames that carry it
nodes.x: Khartoum's rifle, sold with every Khamaseen. It is simple, rugged and chambered for any of three powers' ammunition because, as people in Khartoum put it, its buyers buy from all of them.

nodes.t: Fired by the node, not the pilot
nodes.x: The Tianyan-Hou's uncrewed frames carry cannons the Tianshu node aims and fires. The officer in the command frame approves targets. In Córdoba people say you can tell the network's shots by the pause before them.

nodes.t: An autoloading cannon for oath-sworn pilots
nodes.x: OKB-7's Molot rebuilt for the Volk-K, lighter and faster to load, for pilots who fight close and are trusted to choose their own targets.

nodes.t: Every navy's point defence
nodes.x: Ship reactors give a warship enough steady power to run lasers continuously, and the PL-9 pattern guards every warship in the system against missiles and frames alike. Frames have to learn to approach ships from behind their own fire.

nodes.t: The UNEL can turn a frame off
nodes.x: Every frame charged from the UNEL's reconstruction relays carries a receiver the UNEL can command. It has been used eleven times, and on each occasion the UNEL published its reasons.

nodes.t: Open a hull, then board it
nodes.x: The Grapnel's standard boarding weapon: a spike driver that punches a sealed breach in a hull and holds it while the boarding team goes through. Most space fights since the war end with one.

nodes.t: Grab the cargo, not the ship
nodes.x: Skycut's grapple-cutter, built for the Tallyman, clamps a cargo pod, cuts it free and logs the seizure in the same motion. The houses prefer to collect what they're owed rather than the ship that owes it, which would only have to be crewed and insured.

nodes.t: An AR-40 rebuilt in Colony One's sheds
nodes.x: Dustline's rifle: Washington's surplus Longhorns, rebuilt for Martian dust so often that nothing original is left but the bore. It jams less than the original, and it's louder.

nodes.t: The Spiegel, refitted and published
nodes.x: Vesta Works' refit of the Union's Spiegel coilgun for the Pavise-S. Every change is published for the panels, including the ones that made it worse.

nodes.t: A weapon that heals
nodes.x: Umoja's frames carry claws grown with their muscle, keratin and bone that dull with use and are regrown overnight, so long as the frame is fed and cared for.

nodes.t: A paired weapon for sworn pilots
nodes.x: Garuda Works' glaive for the Ashvin pairs is carried in two halves by two frames and joined for a single strike - a weapon made for things far bigger than a frame. The engineers who made it learned their edges at Mitsurugi.

nodes.t: A missile that waits for years
nodes.x: The Communion's weapon of choice is the patient mine, which drifts with a target's orbit, asleep on a trickle of power, and waits, and wakes only when something hostile comes near. Communion space is mined in ways that no other power has charted.

nodes.t: A cyberweapon built from one bribe
nodes.x: Ana Lubov's strategic cyberweapon, built on code bought from a Colony One captain. In July 2312 it shuts down the Helion surface-to-orbit guns at the start of the MRD's strike.

nodes.t: Colony One's guns on the north pole
nodes.x: Colony One's surface-to-orbit batteries near the north pole, built to keep any fleet from sitting over the colony. Hasta took them offline. Engineers wired them back by hand and duelled Deimos slug for slug.

nodes.t: Ground-to-space and ground-to-ground
nodes.x: The MRD's fortress south of Colony One mounts batteries that fire at orbit and at the ground, where Mars's low gravity makes shells carry absurd distances.

nodes.t: Cheap drones sold to anyone with lithium
nodes.x: Skycut's small drones, sold by the thousand. The MRD buys them for the Red Wall, the houses use them for their stop-and-search campaign, and every pirate wants them.

nodes.t: A shield for corridors and airlocks
nodes.x: The Union's Tier One units carry a shield sized for a station corridor, with a breaching charge in its face. It goes to Cyprus and Deimos with the Rondache.

nodes.t: A rail weapon for hunting monsters
nodes.x: A long rail lance built for the Compact's hunters in Jupiter's radiation belts: fired by one frame of a pair while the other holds the target, which is usually something a great deal larger than a frame.

nodes.t: A weapon that injects, not cuts
nodes.x: The Kith carries a grown stinger that injects a corrosive the frame makes itself, eating through seals and armour from the inside. Umoja calls this care, in a sense of the word that outsiders tend to find hard to follow.

nodes.t: A rifle that asks Washington first
nodes.x: New Philadelphia's licensed copy of the Quiet Rifle, with the Charter frame's deployment lock wired into its firing circuit so that the rifle answers to the same law as the frame that carries it.

nodes.t: The first frame beam weapon that works
nodes.x: A hundred and forty years after the BX-0's five shots, Tianlong and Mitsurugi field a frame beam rifle that fires all day on Osaka's capacitors. It goes to China's Belt patrols first.

nodes.t: Weapons for a war fought underground
nodes.x: Dustline's partisan munitions, shaped charges and tunnel mines built for fighting in the dark. The remnant still trains with them in its hidden docks.

nodes.t: A mirror turned on a ship
nodes.x: The Long Mirrors can gather a faint sun and bring it down to a single point. The Communion says they are kept for power and for prayer, and ships that have strayed too close to them have come away scorched.

nodes.t: A frame weapon fed by a star
nodes.x: The Zhulong's beam cannon, fed directly from its fusion core: no capacitor bank, no cooldown worth the name. In trials it is the most powerful weapon a frame has ever carried.

nodes.t: The Compact's answer to the Zhulong
nodes.x: Garuda Works' beam weapon for its fusion frame is a glaive whose edge is a beam held a few metres long, and like most of what the Compact builds it is meant first for the hunt.

power.label: Power
power.intro: Every mech is short on power, and each bloc made a different trade: noise and heat for endurance, forty minutes for silence, or a hydrogen supply chain. After the war reactors move into sealed ships, each space faction finds its own way, and by 2327 the race is to put fusion in a frame.
turns: Brannock's turbine plumes showed on thermal sights kilometres away. Halcyon chose quiet, cool batteries and accepted forty minutes of endurance.
The swap pit became a battlefield
Ninety-second battery swaps made US ground crews a front-line arm, and made swap points a target.
VEK's quiet fuel cells needed depots, which became targets. The BZ-6 reformer fixed it by making hydrogen from ordinary diesel.
Fission (OKB-7), thorium salt run by a network (Tianlong), fusion (Mitsurugi) and beamed power (Halcyon and the Lunar Republic). Each one is a political crisis waiting to happen.
When Japan goes into China's sphere, the West loses Mitsurugi's capacitors overnight, and America builds a worse one of its own in eleven months.
Reactors go up, fuel comes down
The Mandate seals reactors into ships and bans them from Earth's battlefields, while hydrogen shipped from the Belt makes fuel cheap on Earth for the first time in two centuries.
A hundred and forty years after Amaterasu needed a giant, Tianlong and the Ashva Compact race to fit fusion inside an ordinary frame.
fams: Turbines and diesels. Loud, hot and dependable.
Silent and cool-running, but endurance is measured in minutes.
Quiet hydrogen power. The problem is the hydrogen.
Pulse power for linear and energy weapons. Almost all of it is Mitsurugi's.
Prototypes in 2186; after the war, the power in every ship and the reason the Mandate exists.
Orbital power that could reach the ground, and who decides whether it does.
Heat drawn from beneath other worlds, and power that is grown rather than built.
power.profileH: Who runs what after the war

profile.t: Hampton Roads reactors in its ships; quiet orbital-lithium battery frames on Earth; Liberty-line capacitors, and beamed power only where the UNEL licenses it.
Fuel cells everywhere, on Quebec and Belt hydrogen; sealed plants from the Malapert docks in its ships.
Network-run salt reactors at home and in its warships, the Type-40 torch in its fleets, and the first frame fusion trials.
Kurchatov breeders in its hulls, inspected only when they come home, sunlit cloud stations at Venus, and fission frames kept far from Earth.
Desert turbines on cheap fuel from space, built in its workshops and sold to half of Earth.
The sealed-plant pattern and its seals, the beamed-power relays, and capacitors in bulk from the lunar yards.
Cold cells and the Helion solar grid on Mars; quiet, buried reactors in the remnant's docks.
Fuel cells metered by the river judges' water ledgers, in American hulls.
Areothermal heat from under Tharsis that nobody seals, Lubov's metallic-hydrogen cells, and a catalysed fusion programme.
Caravan electrolysers, the hydrogen trade, cheap Arsia packs, Chinese torches and Velk's asteroid drive.
Grown power: vat electrocyte cells fed from Jupiter's moons, and radiotroph mats that eat its radiation.
The Garuda exile torch, and a frame fusion core of its own in trials.
Wartime fission drives pushed a century past their rating, and kilometre mirrors catching a faint sun.

nodes.t: Main battle tank engines
nodes.x: Multi-fuel gas turbines from main battle tanks. Compact and powerful, but they drink fuel and leave a hot exhaust plume.

nodes.t: Heavy commercial engines
nodes.x: Diesel engines from heavy trucks and locomotives. Heavy, low-tech, and repairable anywhere.

nodes.t: A tank turbine in a mech torso
nodes.x: Brannock-Hale's first frames ran on a modified tank turbine. It gave them plenty of power and hours of fuel, along with an exhaust plume that thermal sights could pick up from kilometres away.

nodes.t: Truck diesel driving a generator
nodes.x: A truck diesel turns a generator, and the generator feeds the limb motors. The plant is heavy and loud, but any village mechanic can keep it running, and it is the reason Tianlong frames carry such large torsos.

nodes.t: The Gruzovik's engine in a frame's back
nodes.x: The turboshaft from the K-26 Gruzovik helicopter, geared to a generator. It was light for its power, which is what an airborne frame needed, and it paid for that by being thirsty, hot and screaming. OKB-7 went back to diesels for everything after it.

nodes.t: Battery for sprints, turbine to cruise
nodes.x: A smaller turbine paired with a buffer battery. The mech sprints on the battery and cruises on the turbine, and in an ambush it can shut the turbine down altogether to cut its heat signature. Brannock's engineers won't admit that the battery work came from Halcyon.

nodes.t: Burns diesel, kerosene, or worse
nodes.x: A tougher diesel that will run on almost any liquid fuel, captured stocks and refinery waste included. It is the main reason Pact armies need so little logistics, and the Darkhan sheds pull them out of tractors for the Takhi and Bürged.

nodes.t: Two engines for heavy frames
nodes.x: OKB-7's heavy frames carry two engines derived from the Type-06, so that when one fails the frame can still walk home on the other. Between them they power the heavy arm actuators, the onboard equipment and the Grad-M ignition circuits.

nodes.t: Surplus GT-900s on local fuel
nodes.x: Surplus GT-900 turbines, rebuilt to burn the League's own refinery output, with Type-06 fuel pumps grafted on. They run hot and dirty, but every drop going into them was made in the League's own refineries.

nodes.t: Mobile power for weapons too big for a mech
nodes.x: A wheeled generator built around four D-40 engines, which feeds the Iskra particle cannon by cable and recharges forward units. That makes it the first thing enemy pilots go for.

nodes.t: Turbine charging an MHI capacitor bank
nodes.x: The frame-sized version of the plant Joint Heavy Systems first built at super-heavy scale for the Concord, and the power behind the AR-40E rifle. A turbine charges a licensed Mitsurugi capacitor bank, which gives the Army pulse power without buying Halcyon's battery packs. Shrinking all of it to fit an 18 m frame is the hard part.

nodes.t: Electric vehicles, grid storage
nodes.x: Lithium-chemistry cells developed for electric vehicles and grid storage.

nodes.t: Fixed pack, forty minutes per charge
nodes.x: Halcyon's first frames used a fixed battery in the spine to drive electric fans. It was quiet and cool-running, with no exhaust plume for thermal sights to find, but it took hours to recharge, and the short endurance that came with it was written into US doctrine.

nodes.t: Hot-swapped in ninety seconds
nodes.x: A pack that a ground crew can swap in ninety seconds with a frame-mounted crane. Once that was possible the swap pit became a combat position, and the Army started treating its ground crews as a combat arm.

nodes.t: Battery plus capacitor, JSDF standard
nodes.x: Mitsurugi's design for the Self-Defence Force's frames pairs modest batteries with a large capacitor stage for bursts. It gives less endurance than Halcyon's packs and is much better suited to energy weapons.

nodes.t: MHI capacitor buffer for the LR-3
nodes.x: Higher-density cells plus a Mitsurugi capacitor buffer that feeds the LR-3 rifle and PL-2 laser. The current Kestrel standard, and America's most export-restricted part.

nodes.t: Quiet hydrogen power
nodes.x: Hydrogen fuel cells from air-independent submarines and city buses.

nodes.t: Silent, but needs hydrogen depots
nodes.x: VEK's first frames used a fuel cell adapted from submarines. It was near-silent and cold-running, but it depended on hydrogen depots, and the depots became US strike targets.

nodes.t: Stackable modules that match hardpoints
nodes.x: The cells come in stackable modules, so that a frame carrying heavy packs can carry extra power to match, and it is this arrangement that makes the modular task group possible. The modules are expensive, however, and very sensitive to contamination.

nodes.t: Makes its own hydrogen from diesel
nodes.x: The stack adds a reformer that strips hydrogen from ordinary diesel. It is less efficient and slightly louder, but a frame can now refuel from any truck, which ends the depot problem - the one the Blitz pairs died for want of solving. Funkenwerk built the Querschläger around it, and the splinter carried the drawings to Darkhan, where the Tsagaan Salkhi burns herders' diesel in it.

nodes.t: Overdriven cells for aces
nodes.x: Castellani's stacks are built by hand and run at 140% of rated output. The performance is spectacular, each stack lasts about two hundred hours before it has to be replaced, and they are fitted only to the mechs of named aces.

nodes.t: Hydrogen split from station water
nodes.x: In orbit, hydrogen comes from water, and stations recycle water anyway. Ascension's worker frames ran on fuel cells from day one.

nodes.t: Fuel cell with fold-out solar wings
nodes.x: Folding solar panels recharge the frame's electrolysers between shifts, so a worker frame can stay out for days. The militarised versions kept that endurance.

nodes.t: Polar ice, split by ring power and flown down sealed
nodes.x: Shackleton Works' first power plant for Earth, rebuilt from Ascension's station cell. The hydrogen comes from polar ice the Republic splits with ring power, and travels in sealed, swappable tanks flown down with every delivery, so a white squad never needs a hydrogen depot on Earth. The membranes are cast in vacuum, run cooler than anything VEK makes, and can't yet be made anywhere else.

nodes.t: For maglev and factory power
nodes.x: Before mechs, Mitsurugi built high-density capacitor banks for maglev lines and heavy industry. That product line turned out to be the key to every powered weapon since.

nodes.t: Backpack unit for the LR-1
nodes.x: The first capacitor a mech could carry, sold to Halcyon for the LR-1 rifle, and still large enough to need a backpack of its own.

nodes.t: The most licensed part in the world
nodes.x: By the Mk.II the core was small enough to fit in a rifle stock. It sits inside the LR-3, the Type-L and the PL-2, every bloc licenses or copies it, and Japan's neutrality rests on it.

nodes.t: Mk.II built under licence
nodes.x: Mk.II cores, built under licence for the Spiegel coilgun and for Castellani's projects, on terms that keep VEK one generation behind - Mitsurugi sells it that way on purpose.

nodes.t: Reverse-engineered Mk.I
nodes.x: Reverse-engineered from a captured Mk.I. It works, at twice the weight and half the charge life, so only the elite Type-12 rail units get one.

nodes.t: Powers the BX-0, still overheats
nodes.x: Tsukuyomi Lab's prototype for the BX-0 beam rifle. It stores enough for five beam shots, and its discharge heat is why the rifle needs ninety seconds to cool.

nodes.t: Submarine and carrier plants
nodes.x: US pressurised-water reactors from submarines and carriers. Reliable at sea, enormous by mech standards.

nodes.t: Molten-salt fission from the Gansu desert
nodes.x: China's thorium programme, which began in the 2020s with a small test reactor in the Gansu desert that ran its fuel dissolved in molten salt. A salt reactor runs at ordinary pressure and needs no cooling water, so it can sit in a desert, and its fuel is a metal China has never been short of. The catch is control: the salt's chemistry has to be watched every minute it runs.

nodes.t: A thorium reactor on rails, run by the network
nodes.x: Tianlong's answer to a Fortress Belt that burns diesel faster than the railway can carry it is a salt reactor on four flatcars, parked behind the belt and feeding the dug-in Tiebis by cable while their diesels idle. There is no operator on board. Tianshu watches the salt, the fuel and the load every second, decides which sector draws power in the same way it decides which train moves, and has the reactor cars shunted to a new siding before anyone has worked out where they were. To its crews it is the stove, and in Beijing's engineering records it is listed as the first reactor no human operates.

nodes.t: A shielded mini-reactor in a heavy frame
nodes.x: OKB-7's secret test frame carries a shielded micro-reactor. On paper its endurance is unlimited; in practice the pilot's radiation dose is measured, and every bloc is afraid of what happens when one is shot down over a city.

nodes.t: A frame-sized salt reactor that only the network may run
nodes.x: The reactor train shrunk to fit inside a frame, which is only possible because no human has to run it. A Tianshu node rides with the core and holds the salt at temperature through every step, turn and recoil, trimming the load faster than a pilot could notice. If the frame falls, a plug of frozen salt melts and the fuel drains into a tank where it can't go critical. The pilot can't override any of it, by design. Where OKB-7's Pamir relies on a shielded pilot, Tianlong's core relies on the network alone. The Tianyan carries one in trials, and the Jingwei four.

nodes.t: Laboratory tokamaks
nodes.x: Decades of laboratory fusion work. Never net-positive outside a building-sized facility.

nodes.t: Too big for any normal frame; Japan's best-kept secret
nodes.x: Tsukuyomi Lab's compact fusion rig uses Mk.II capacitor technology for its ignition pulse. It is far too big for a normal frame, and the only mech that carries one is Takemikazuchi, built at 45 m to fit it. Shrinking it to fit an 18 m frame would very probably change the balance of power overnight.

nodes.t: Satellite and station power
nodes.x: Photovoltaic arrays powering satellites and early stations.

nodes.t: Powers the orbital elevators
nodes.x: Huge collectors around the elevator anchors, powering the cargo launch tracks and the stations. It is the largest power source in orbit, and every bloc owns a share of it.

nodes.t: Beaming power to ground receivers
nodes.x: Ascension's experiment in beaming surplus ring power down to ground receivers. Officially it was for disaster relief. Every military that watched it saw it could recharge a mech.

nodes.t: Kestrels recharged by beam, never landing
nodes.x: Halcyon's classified programme to recharge QX-3 packs mid-flight from the ring's microwave relay. Because Halcyon frames fly on electric fans, beamed power would keep both the fans and the weapons running; if it worked, America's forty-minute limit would go, and there would be a weapon-grade power beam over every battlefield. Test series ██-4 ended early. Cause of termination: ████████ ██ ███ ██████.

nodes.t: Beamed power, parked over a UN operation
nodes.x: The Republic's own answer to Ascension's relay test: relay satellites that take power from the ring and beam it down to a rectenna on a frame's back. Halcyon is chasing the same idea for its fans and guns. The Republic supplies it to the white squads at no charge, and has offered to park a relay over any UN operation, under which a frame does not run dry.

nodes.t: Built in Osaka, for Beijing
nodes.x: When Japan asks Beijing for protection, Mitsurugi's capacitor lines go with it. The Mk.IV is built in Osaka to Tianlong's schedule, and for the rest of the war the West gets none, so the armies that had leaned on a Mitsurugi core find out, all at once, what Japan's neutrality had been worth to them.

nodes.t: America's first capacitor of its own
nodes.x: Cut off from Mitsurugi, Halcyon and Brannock-Hale build a capacitor of their own in eleven months, out of captured Mk.IIs and their own patents. It weighs half as much again and fails in desert heat, but it is American, and every Western linear weapon of the war's last years runs on it or on the Union's VK-Kap.

nodes.t: Fewer cells and no Japanese buffer
nodes.x: With the Mitsurugi buffer gone and South America's lithium on the front line, the QX-5 carries a Liberty Core and a third fewer cells, and Kestrels fly thirty-one minutes on it. The crews call it the ration.

nodes.t: Hydrogen from anything that has some
nodes.x: The European Front burns through the Union's diesel, so VEK's last wartime stack strips hydrogen from whatever is left: kerosene, cooking oil, ammonia from fertiliser plants. It is loud for a fuel cell and quiet for anything else, and it stays in service long after the war, well into the refounded Union.

nodes.t: Both halves of the Pact, one engine
nodes.x: Beijing's and Moscow's armies fight the Pact Civil War on the same Type-06 diesel, drawn from the same depots, so each side's raids go for the other's fuel trains first. By the war's end, frames on both sides are running on crude pumped straight out of the ground.

nodes.t: Reactors at the front, and the dose that comes with them
nodes.x: The Pamir trials end the way everyone feared. OKB-7 fields its fission core in the siege trains, frames that never need refuelling walk the northern front, and their pilots are rotated out by dose rather than by fatigue. When the Mandate is written, the Pamir is the reason it bans reactors from Earth's battlefields as well as from its sky.

nodes.t: A network-run reactor in every engine room
nodes.x: Tianlong puts the salt reactor into Beijing's first warships, with a Tianshu node in every engine room and no human permitted to touch the salt. The crew fly the ship, and the network decides how hard it may burn. China keeps building them this way after the war.

nodes.t: The sealed plant in every bloc's first warships
nodes.x: Most of the war's warships carry the same sealed fission plant, made at Shackleton and serviced only by yard engineers while the blocs' own yards were still learning. At Yernon, the dreadnoughts on both sides run on Republic reactors. When the Republic places its fleets under the UN, the reactors are the one part most navies are recorded as unable to replace.

nodes.t: The ring's beams become targets
nodes.x: Every bloc tries to power its frames from the ring's relays, and every bloc fires on the others' receivers. By the war's second year most relay satellites are wreckage and SKYLINE's Kestrels are flying on batteries again. Throughout, the Republic keeps its own relays dark and intact.

nodes.t: The Mandate's inspected reactor pattern, inside lunar orbit
nodes.x: Inside lunar orbit, the Mandate permits a warship to carry a reactor only if it is built to a pattern the UNEL can inspect, under seals the UNEL fits. The lunar yards build most of them, though not all: Hampton Roads, Malapert and Tianlong build their own to the same pattern under the same seals, and the Ascendancy contests every inspection. A ship's power rating is the size of plant it is licensed for in Earth's space. Breaking a seal there is an act of war, and every navy has done it once. Past the Moon the seals carry no weight, since the UNEL has no one out there to check them and a ship that never comes home never needs them, which is why each Earth power keeps an anchorage just beyond the Moon where the seals come off.

nodes.t: The drive that opened the outer system
nodes.x: Built in Osaka under Beijing's protection from Mitsurugi's Amaterasu work, the first fusion drive small enough for a ship. It cuts the run to the Belt from months to weeks and puts Jupiter in reach. Tianlong licenses it to no one, which is one reason the Syndicate's houses fly Chinese hulls.

nodes.t: The Mitsurugi exiles' fusion drive
nodes.x: The Mitsurugi engineers who left Japan through Vladivostok rebuild what they remember of Amaterasu at Europa. The Ashva drive that comes of it is cruder and heavier than Tianlong's, and it needs no licence from Beijing, so most ships flying beyond the Belt without China's permission fly on a copy of it.

nodes.t: Network-run reactors for a whole region
nodes.x: China rebuilds its industry on salt reactors that no human operates, linked into grids Tianshu balances by the second. The Mongolian accelerator runs on one. Partners such as Australia are offered cheap power from them, on Tianshu's terms.

nodes.t: Beamed power, and who can switch it off
nodes.x: After the Mandate, beaming power to the ground is a UNEL monopoly. Its rebuilt relays light reconstruction zones from Patagonia to Siberia and charge the white squads' frames. A town on the relay has power. A frame on the relay can also be switched off from Luna, and the pilots who fly them know it.

nodes.t: Cheap fuel from space, burned on Earth
nodes.x: With reactors banned from Earth's battlefields, Earth's frames burn fuel again, and for the first time in two centuries the fuel is cheap, shipped down from the Belt as hydrogen and synthetic kerosene. The Commonwealth's desert workshops build what most mechanics reckon is the best engine of the reconstruction: a turbine that burns anything, descended from the League's retrofits and sold to every warlord in the Andes.

nodes.t: The Union's hydrogen, from its own fields
nodes.x: The refounded Union builds its frames and stations around fuel cells, fed from the Quebec Hydrogen Fields and, increasingly, from hydrogen shipped down from the Belt, so that it never again depends on depots someone can bomb. The QH-1 is a BZ-8 with the reformer taken out and a pipeline network behind it.

nodes.t: Fuel and air from the same rock
nodes.x: The Syndicate's caravans split asteroid ice into hydrogen and oxygen as they travel, so a caravan's fuel and its air come out of the same rock and go on the same ledger. Every house builds its own variant and guards it the way it guards its prices.

nodes.t: Batteries that work at minus eighty
nodes.x: Colony One and the MRD both need batteries that survive a Martian night, and each builds its own. Colony One's Dustcell is heavy and can be fixed with a hammer. The MRD's is lighter and comes with a maintenance panel. Either side's frames can run on the other's, which neither admits.

nodes.t: Capacitors become a commodity
nodes.x: After the war the lunar yards, now the UNEL's, build capacitors in bulk for anyone licensed to buy them. The Mk.II's secret becomes a commodity, and Mitsurugi's leverage ends a century after it began.

nodes.t: Cheap power from the lithium rush
nodes.x: The Arsia lithium boom, sold through Pallas, makes high-density packs cheap across the Belt and Mars for a year, while Washington's tariffs keep them dear on Earth. Whole caravans refit their boarding frames to run silent on batteries while the price holds.

nodes.t: Six torches in a rock
nodes.x: Warlance Ordos Velk mounts six heavy fusion torches in Hygiea's porous rock and moves the Belt's strongest fort past Mars. It is an engineering stunt and, for the Syndicate's customers, a reminder that it can put a fortress wherever it likes.

nodes.t: The north's guns ran on sunlight
nodes.x: Colony One's Helion surface-to-orbit guns draw on a solar grid across the northern plains. The grid runs on software the MRD had already got into. In July 2312 it goes dark and takes the guns with it, until engineers wire them to batteries by hand.

nodes.t: A reactor that doesn't show on a scope
nodes.x: The remnant's hidden docks need power that can't be seen from Earth or Mars. Its engineers run small reactors far below their rating, buried in ice that soaks up their heat, and accept ships that are slow to wake in exchange for ships that are hard to find.

nodes.t: Reactors that report to Luna
nodes.x: After the Martian civil war and the Weapons Resolution, the UNEL tightens its seals, and licensed plants now report their output to Luna while they run. Navies that signed fit them to ships that come inside lunar orbit. Beyond the Moon, whether a seal stays on is left to the navy, and the reports from out there say what the navies want them to say. Navies that didn't sign, and the remnant, don't fit them at all.

nodes.t: Every litre on the river judges' books
nodes.x: New Philadelphia's frames run on fuel cells fed from the Freehold Basin's water, as allotted in the river judges' ledgers. Every litre a frame burns is entered in the record like any other allotment, and a commander who overdraws answers to a water court before a military one.

nodes.t: Fusion small enough for a frame, at last
nodes.x: Tianlong's frame-scale fusion core reaches trials in 2327, a hundred and forty years after Amaterasu needed a giant to carry it. If it works in a frame, it changes how every frame after it is designed.

nodes.t: The Compact's answer
nodes.x: The Ashva Compact's fusion engineers are a step behind Tianlong, though not by as much as Beijing's analysts assume.

nodes.t: America's own sealed reactor
nodes.x: Hampton Roads builds its reactors to the Mandate's pattern but not in the Republic's yards, and every American carrier since the war has run on one. The UNEL fits the seals before a carrier leaves the yard, and the seals hold as long as it stays in Earth's space. Carriers bound beyond the Moon stop first at the Far Roads, at the Sun–Earth L2 point, where American engineers take them off. Washington insists the plant is American, and the UNEL lets it say so.

nodes.t: A fast reactor that makes its own fuel
nodes.x: The Ascendancy's warships run on a fast breeder descended from the Pamir, which makes more fuel than it burns and so needs supply from no one. When its ships come inside lunar orbit the UNEL inspects the plant, and every time, the Ascendancy protests. Its ships beyond the Moon are never inspected at all.

nodes.t: Wartime fission, pushed a century past its rating
nodes.x: The Communion's ships fly on wartime fission plants, the oldest of them from the Polar Carrier frozen in at Ellesmere, each rebuilt again and again and kept running decades past anything their makers allowed. Every engineer knows each plant by name. The plants are slow and patient, and they are very hard to kill.

nodes.t: The lithium shortage ends in orbit
nodes.x: With lithium shipped down from the Belt and Mars, the United States goes back to what Halcyon had always wanted: quiet, cool-running battery frames. The QX-7 runs a Kestrel's descendants for two hours on a charge, and the ration has become something grandparents talk about.

nodes.t: The drought on Earth is over
nodes.x: From the 2200s, tankers bring hydrogen, metals and water ice down from the Belt and Jupiter in quantities Earth has never had, and fuel stops being something armies fight over. The Syndicate carries most of it and, as carriers generally do, decides who gets it first.

nodes.t: Power above the clouds of Venus
nodes.x: The Ascendancy's stations float in the upper atmosphere of Venus, where the sunlight is twice as strong as on Earth and never stops. They export power in batteries and chemistry in tanks, and they import rather more than any station of that size ought to need.

nodes.t: Heat from beneath Tharsis
nodes.x: The MRD drills down to the heat still left beneath the Tharsis volcanoes and builds a grid on it, run by its panels and powering its south. There is no reactor to seal and nothing Luna could license, even if Luna's writ ran on Mars, which it doesn't. As far as the panels can tell, it is the first major power source in the system that owes Luna nothing.

nodes.t: A battery that is grown, not built
nodes.x: Umoja's keepers grow electric organs in vats, stacks of cells like an eel's, fed on hydrocarbons and ammonia skimmed from Jupiter's moons. A grown cell heals its own small hurts, needs feeding, and dies if it is neglected, so it is tended like anything else the keepers grow. Umoja's frames carry them in their chests.

nodes.t: Hydrogen stored as metal, mostly safely
nodes.x: Ana Lubov's team at Vesta finds a way to hold hydrogen in a dense metallic lattice at survivable pressures, and builds a cell that stores five times what a tank does. It does, occasionally, fail all at once. Lubov has already moved on to something else, and another team is now working to make it safe.

nodes.t: Life that eats Jupiter's radiation
nodes.x: On Ganymede, Umoja grows mats of engineered organisms that turn the radiation pouring off Jupiter into stored chemical energy, lining habitats and frames alike, so that what other factions spend fortunes shielding against becomes, for Umoja, something to harvest.

nodes.t: Kilometre mirrors for a faint sun
nodes.x: At Uranus, where the sun is only a bright star, the Communion builds mirrors kilometres across from foil thinner than paper, and turns them to catch every photon the sun will give. They are power plants, and they are prayers.

nodes.t: The MRD's road to a frame-sized star
nodes.x: The MRD's panels approve a fusion programme that skips the torch entirely: a small cell in which the reaction is coaxed along by catalysis at low temperature. So far it works in the laboratory for minutes at a time. It is the third runner in the race, and the only one whose work appears in the open literature.

doctrine.label: Doctrine
doctrine.intro: Each bloc's doctrine follows from its hardware: the United States fights on a forty-minute battery clock, the Union blinds the enemy, and the Pact spends frames to save time. After the war the powers fight for influence, and the space factions write doctrines of their own.
turns: Every bloc first used mechs to kill tanks, not other mechs. Mech-on-mech doctrine came later than anyone expected.

Drop-and-strike plans every mission around battery endurance: fly in, strike, land, fight and leave before the packs run dry. The enemies who named it the forty-minute war built their doctrines around surviving it.
The Union's EW-led doctrine makes up for its small numbers. It's the main reason Continental lances punch above their weight.
Built to catch a Kestrel landing

The Union's hunter-killer lance and the Pact's Air Umbrella both attack drop-and-strike at its weakest moment. One jams the approach and shoots Kestrels as they transform; the other fills the sky over a landing zone with rockets.
Beijing's Tianshu network runs the walls and the Air Umbrella; Moscow runs the breakthrough groups and the augmented pilots. Pact doctrine is becoming two doctrines.
Nobody knows how to fight in orbit
Warships exist; space doctrine doesn't. The first real battle in orbit will rewrite every manual.
In the Pact Civil War both halves fight by the same orders; Beijing breaks the tie with Tianshu, Moscow with fission.
China wins with aid, the Commonwealth by selling frames and the UNEL by holding the power supply; only the United States still takes ground.
Colony One and the MRD both plan a decisive first strike; Colony One aims its plan at the Americans, and the MRD's lands in its back.
fams: Expeditionary forces. Speed, air power, a long Army–Air Force rivalry, and after the war, permanent presence.
Small numbers, high quality. Blind the enemy, then fight; after the war, keep the Union together.
Eurasian Pact → China and the Ascendancy
Mass, firepower and acceptable losses, until the Pact splits into a network and an oath.
Defensive by law, influential by industry, and running out of room.
Making do with everyone else's equipment, then selling it back to them.
Fighting where nobody has doctrine yet.
Borrowed frames, strict rules for when they may fire, and later the power supply itself.
