Colony One, the MRD and the Constitutionalists: three answers to one planet.
The Syndicate's houses, who fight to keep trading.
Umoja, the Ashva Compact and the Communion, too far from Earth to fight like it.
doctrine.profileH: Who fights how after the war

profile.t: Quiet patrols on two hours of battery, and permanent presence wherever it takes ground.
Soldiers who are also integration officers, and anchorages of its own beyond Luna.
A network that runs its wars, aid that buys influence, and a doctrine for frames that never run out of power.
Pilots augmented as equipment owed to the unit and sworn to each other; fission sieges kept off Earth.
Influence without occupation: shelter first, sell the frames, keep no bases.
The sealed peace, held through the power supply, and witnesses who fly unarmed into no-fly zones.
Hold the north, plan the decisive first strike, and when that fails, go underground.
A force that defends New Philadelphia and cannot go to war without Washington.
Engage at range, break contact, return; fortify the line and open any war with a cyber strike.
Fight only to keep trading; wage economic war by inspection; guard the exchanges, not territory.
Kin defence for the habitats, and the Lodges' grown command for war.
Riding out wherever the weak are threatened, and monster hunting, its oldest form.
Patience: mine the approaches, sleep through the years, and outlast.

nodes.t: Armour holds, air power strikes deep
nodes.x: Pre-mech US doctrine: armour holds the front while air power strikes deep behind it.

nodes.t: Helicopter and tiltrotor assault
nodes.x: Infantry delivered by helicopter and tiltrotor behind or around the enemy front.

nodes.t: Mechs as mobile anti-tank guns
nodes.x: The Army's first mech doctrine, and a cautious one. Pairs of Brannock frames with M30s and ATGM tubes waited in terrain that tanks couldn't cross, ambushed the armour as it came past, and then fell back on friendly tanks rather than trying to hold anything themselves.

nodes.t: Frames slung under heavy-lift tiltrotors
nodes.x: Halcyon's early ground frames were slung under tiltrotors and dropped behind enemy lines. The method worked well enough, but the tiltrotors were easy kills on the way in, and losing them is what pushed Halcyon towards a frame that could fly itself, and so towards transformation.

nodes.t: Four-mech teams replace tanks in rough terrain
nodes.x: The Army's standard team is four Brannock frames: two rifles, one Hornet pod and one M140 bazooka. In mountains, forests and cities, where a tank struggles to turn round, fire teams have now taken over the tanks' job outright.

nodes.t: Fly in, land, fight, leave inside forty minutes
nodes.x: Kestrels fly in, strike with their wing stores, land and fight on the ground with LR-3s, then transform and leave before the batteries run out. Every plan is written backwards from the forty-minute clock, and the enemies on the receiving end call it “the forty-minute war”.

nodes.t: Army holds the ground, Air Force strikes
nodes.x: After years of rivalry between the services, a joint mandate: Brannock fire teams seize and hold a swap point, and Kestrels strike from it. The mandate settled who does what, though not who commands, and the services are still arguing about that.

nodes.t: Forward battery points as combat positions
nodes.x: Battery-swap pits sit within reach of the front, and the ground crews who run them are trained and armed as combat troops. They need to be, since enemy planners now go after the pits before they go after the mechs.

nodes.t: Kestrels that never need to land
nodes.x: A draft doctrine written for SKYLINE, the beamed-power programme, in which Kestrels stay airborne for hours rather than minutes. None of it works without SKYLINE, and it still isn't clear whether SKYLINE works either.

nodes.t: Two ordinary soldiers, not one altered one
nodes.x: America's answer to the Volk and to the rumours about Koschei. By regulation every US pilot serves unaltered, and recruits are screened for implants before they reach a frame. Halcyon and Brannock-Hale advertise their frames as built for ordinary people, and the Concord's two-pilot crew is held up as proof. In Washington, the language of biological purity has started to creep into speeches about patriotism.

nodes.t: Reconnaissance-in-force tradition
nodes.x: European armoured cavalry: fast reconnaissance units that find and fix the enemy for the main force.

nodes.t: Jamming and signals intelligence
nodes.x: Cold War electronic warfare: jamming, deception and signals intelligence.

nodes.t: Licensed frames scouting ahead of tanks
nodes.x: The first Union mechs were licensed Brannock frames, and the cavalry put them to work screening ahead of the tank columns, where their height and sensors let them see rather farther than any vehicle could.

nodes.t: One frame, reconfigured per mission
nodes.x: Because every Union frame shares the standard hardpoint, a lance of three VEK frames can be re-equipped overnight for assault, defence or reconnaissance, as the mission requires. It is how the Union, which has never had the numbers of the larger blocs, makes up the difference.

nodes.t: Blind first, fight second
nodes.x: Union engagements open with electronic attack, in an order the manuals set out with some care: jam the sensors, spoof the data links, and only then attack, while the enemy is still blind. EW frames lead the formation rather than following it.

nodes.t: EW frame, coilgun sniper, lance knight
nodes.x: Written specifically to defeat drop-and-strike. An EW frame jams the Kestrels' landing approach, a Spiegel sniper shoots them as they transform, and a lance-armed frame finishes them once they are on the ground.

nodes.t: Named aces in Castellani prototypes
nodes.x: The Union gives its best prototypes to its most famous aces and publicises their kills. It is partly for morale and partly propaganda, and partly a way of persuading reluctant member states, in committee, to approve more spending.

nodes.t: Every programme answers to a panel that can stop it
nodes.x: When the Union's parliament learned, from footage Geneva sent to every member on the same morning, what Halden had sent into the Great Sand Sea in its name, it placed every defence research programme under an ethics panel with the power to halt it. Halden's Geneva laboratories are the panel's first case, and the hearings are still running. The Union accepts that it is slower for it, and its parliament has shown no wish to change that.

nodes.t: Echeloned mass offensives
nodes.x: Offensives in successive echelons, each wave exploiting the gap the last one opened.

nodes.t: Fire as the decisive arm
nodes.x: Artillery as the arm that decides battles, used in enormous concentrations.

nodes.t: Six weeks of training, many frames
nodes.x: The Pact accepted early on that its Tianlong frames were outclassed, and chose to field so many of them that the enemy runs out of ammunition first. Pilots get six weeks' training, and the losses are counted in conscripts.

nodes.t: Frames dropped behind the front
nodes.x: Deep battle from the air. Korsaks were dropped by parachute to seize passes and bridges ahead of the Tieniu waves and hold them until the column came up. At Talysh the column never arrived. The order is still on the books, though no frame has been dropped under it since.
nodes.z: 2171 · the airborne divisions go back to light tanks

nodes.t: Ride ahead, carry everything, never wait
nodes.x: The doctrine the Takhi was first built for and the Tsagaan Salkhi later perfected: a handful of fast frames that scout, strike and supply themselves, spread across a hundred kilometres of steppe and answerable to their own camp rather than to a depot. Tianshu routes the trains, but it is the wind riders who decide where the trains will be needed. When the wind riders leave for the Belt during the war they take the idea with them, and it becomes the Syndicate's rapid doctrine: speed, dispersal and self-supply, a long way from any depot.

nodes.t: Mechs as direct-fire artillery
nodes.x: Type-01 cannons could only be fired braced, so Pact mechs formed kneeling firing lines in the manner of artillery batteries. It began as a technical workaround and became the image most people still have of the Pact.

nodes.t: Rockets, then cannons, then blades
nodes.x: Three waves: the first empties Grad-M batteries, the second kneels and fires Type-09s, the third closes with carbon blades. Each wave is timed to arrive as the one before runs dry.

nodes.t: Dug-in kneeling lines on the borders
nodes.x: Type-09 lines in prepared positions along the borders, with the mechs dug in to the shoulders. They are very hard to dislodge, and they are the reason no bloc has invaded the Pact. Tianshu began by scheduling the belt's trains and now decides which sector the reserves go to.

nodes.t: OKB-7 heavies open the gap
nodes.x: OKB-7 heavy frames with demolition mauls and supporting cannons lead and punch a hole for the waves behind. The first change in Pact doctrine that values quality over numbers.

nodes.t: Engineered elites for the best frames
nodes.x: Conscript losses made elite pilots precious. The answer is Department Zero, a secret institute that augments pilots with implants and conditioning. Officially it doesn't exist, and it is run from Moscow. Beijing's planners accept cybernetic links but refuse anything that rewrites the pilot, and say so at every staff meeting.

nodes.t: Massed AA rockets against Kestrels
nodes.x: Built to defeat drop-and-strike. Type-03 racks loaded with anti-air rockets fire massed volleys over the fortress belts to deny the Kestrels anywhere to land. It is cheap and crude, and it works. The batteries are cued by Tianshu, Beijing's planning network and the most automated command system any bloc has fielded.

nodes.t: Mongolian crews who scout ahead of the frame trains
nodes.x: Tianshu can route a frame train across Mongolia, but it can't see the pasture, the washed-out crossings or the herders who know both. Since the Fortress Belt went in, Mongolian and Kazakh crews have scouted the rail lines in stripped-down Tieniu, living in their frames for weeks at a time between depots. They are austere and communal, and they are the least predictable part of Tianshu's plans, because they treat a frame like a horse and won't leave a lame one behind. In Beijing's paperwork they are the Steppe detachments.

nodes.t: Kalibr-305 and Iskra against cities
nodes.x: Draft doctrine for breaking fortified cities with siege mortars and cable-fed particle cannons. It assumes a long war, which is what worries the other blocs most.

nodes.t: The network proposes, the officer approves
nodes.x: Tianshu began as Tianlong's rail scheduler for the frame trains, grew into the planner behind the Fortress Belt, and learned to cue the Air Umbrella. Under Order 21 it drafts every operational plan from sensors, depot stocks and rail timetables, and officers approve or amend it. Officers who amend too often are retrained. Tianshu also grades them for reliability, and the criteria are listed only as ████████ ██ ███ ███████, ███████ ███████. Moscow's staff officers call it command by forecast.

nodes.t: Constitutional self-defence
nodes.x: A long-standing legal limit: Japanese forces exist only to defend Japan.

nodes.t: Trade as national strategy
nodes.x: Decades of national strategy built on high-value manufacturing exports.

nodes.t: Mechs first fielded for earthquakes
nodes.x: Japan's first mechs were rescue and recovery frames, built for earthquakes and tsunamis, and the public had come to trust them long before the military armed them.

nodes.t: Coasts and islands, with the navy
nodes.x: Self-Defence Force frames defend the coastlines and outlying islands, deployed from amphibious ships with naval fire support and equipped with Type-L carbines and HC-2 hybrid cells.

nodes.t: Sell to everyone, depend on no one
nodes.x: Japan's real defence doctrine is to license critical parts to every bloc, so that none can afford to attack the supplier. It holds for as long as no bloc decides it would rather seize the factory.

nodes.t: JSDF units run MHI prototypes
nodes.x: Selected JSDF units take Mitsurugi prototypes into live exercises and, now and then, a real incident. It gives Japan the fastest test cycle in the world, and it explains why so many of its prototypes end up in combat.

nodes.t: Armed pickups and militia
nodes.x: Irregular warfare built around armed pickup trucks and local militia.

nodes.t: Refusing bloc membership
nodes.x: A shared refusal to join any of the major blocs.

nodes.t: Surplus Gen 1 frames as militia fire support
nodes.x: The League's first mechs were surplus Gen 1 frames brought in to support the militias, the mech equivalent of a gun on a pickup. They taught a generation of pilots to improvise.

nodes.t: Disperse, hide, strike, vanish
nodes.x: Small groups hide among the dunes and in the sandstorms, strike convoys and depots, and then scatter. The League rarely wins a pitched battle, so it has sensibly learned not to fight them.

nodes.t: No foreign bases, ever
nodes.x: League states deny bases to every bloc, and keep enough mechs between them to make any incursion costly. Kept out in the open, the blocs fight their proxy wars here instead, through whichever local side will take their frames.

nodes.t: Organised around interchangeable parts
nodes.x: League battalions mix frames from every bloc and are organised around which parts will interchange. The idea is borrowed from the Continental modular approach, though in the League it is driven by supply rather than choice.

nodes.t: People before territory
nodes.x: The Khartoum Charter's doctrine, written after the Jinn sightings. Frames are positioned to shield populations rather than to hold ground, and a battalion's first duty in any fight is evacuation. The Gulf associates call it soft, and the Charter states tend to answer that people still live in the Great Sand Sea.

nodes.t: Policing, not warfare
nodes.x: Security on early stations was policing: no heavy weapons, no military chain of command.

nodes.t: Ship-to-ship tradition
nodes.x: Centuries of ship-to-ship combat doctrine, none of it written for orbit.

nodes.t: Hired protection
nodes.x: Private firms hired to guard assets in unstable regions.

nodes.t: Armed worker frames after the labour dispute
nodes.x: After the first station labour dispute, Ascension crews armed their worker frames with rivet drivers and torches and formed militias, and the consortium was never able to take the frames back.

nodes.t: Harpoon, breach, seize
nodes.x: Most fights in orbit end with a harpoon and a cut hull, since neither side wants to destroy the station it is fighting over. On the evidence so far, worker frames do this better than military ones.

nodes.t: Small elite teams, the best of every bloc
nodes.x: Grey Lantern Security fields small teams built from the best frame each bloc makes. It copied the US fire-team structure, but not its rules of engagement.

nodes.t: Fire only to protect
nodes.x: The white squads' first rules of engagement, written for the convoy escorts. Under them a white frame fires only to protect a convoy, a camp or itself; it does not pursue, and it does not hold ground for anyone. Squads train to fight as mixed units whose frames share no parts, and their mechanics are expected to learn every bloc's wiring.

nodes.t: Protect, then pursue
nodes.x: Rewritten after Mong Hsat. When the Security Council names a threat to civilians, a white squad may go after it instead of waiting for it, and may finish it. Esteves describes it as the narrowest possible exception; among the squads who flew at Mong Hsat it is known as the Sawbwa rule.

nodes.t: First warships, no proven doctrine
nodes.x: The first dedicated warships carry mass drivers and mech catapults, but no one has yet fought ship-to-ship in orbit. Every bloc is borrowing from old naval thinking and hoping, with no real evidence either way, that it applies.

nodes.t: Drop-and-strike on a ration
nodes.x: When the Mitsurugi parts stop coming, the Kestrel's forty minutes drop to thirty-one. The Army rewrites drop-and-strike around the shorter clock, with smaller objectives, swap pits pushed closer to the front and no second pass.

nodes.t: Hold the Americas, whatever it costs
nodes.x: The war's American doctrine. Ironside divisions hold the Central American and Canadian fronts while the Air Force strikes where it can, and for the first time the Army is writing doctrine around holding ground rather than taking it.

nodes.t: Blind the enemy's power, not just its eyes
nodes.x: The Union extends Directive 5 to the war's beamed power: jam the relays, spoof the receivers, and leave the enemy's frames to run dry. Through the Relay War it proves the Union's most effective weapon, and it is the main reason the relays eventually come down.

nodes.t: Two halves of one army, using the same manual
nodes.x: In the Pact Civil War both sides fight by the same orders, with the same frames, drawn from the same depots, and whoever breaks the shared doctrine first will win. Beijing breaks it with Tianshu and Moscow with the Burya.

nodes.t: Siege trains that never stop for fuel
nodes.x: The Siege Doctrine with fission frames: Buryas and Iskra-Fs in front of the siege trains, needing no fuel convoys and never stopping to wait for one. It is the doctrine the Mandate is written to end.

nodes.t: The network fights the whole war
nodes.x: Tianshu stops proposing operations and starts running them, front by front, with officers approving its plans in bulk. Beijing wins its half of the Pact Civil War this way, and keeps the arrangement afterwards.

nodes.t: Build for the protector
nodes.x: When Japan asks Beijing for protection, licence diplomacy comes to an end. Mitsurugi builds to Tianlong's schedule, and the Self-Defence Forces become a coastal guard inside China's sphere.

nodes.t: Protect First, on a front
nodes.x: Khartoum's war doctrine on the North African Front: hold the ground the refugees need, shelter them first and fight second. The migrants of the Southern Crossing still talk about which frames opened their bays to them.

nodes.t: Name the places the war may not enter
nodes.x: The UN cannot stop the war, so it names places the war may not enter and holds them with borrowed white frames. When a front doesn't go round an open city, the white squads fight whoever it belongs to.

nodes.t: Whose crews reload faster
nodes.x: Yernon teaches the first lesson of fleet action: when both fleets have bought the same guns from the same yard, battles go to the crews that reload, repair and manoeuvre faster. Every navy drills it for the next century.

nodes.t: Two hours in the air, and silence
nodes.x: With orbital lithium, American frames get their endurance back. Quiet Patrol keeps battery flyers over a region for hours at a time, which is the persistent air presence the Army wanted in 2186, arriving about a century late.

nodes.t: Stability is manufactured
nodes.x: The doctrine of the reconstruction garrisons is decisive force followed by permanent presence. It holds the Andean border through the Federation's collapse, and in 2312 it is the doctrine that takes Bolivia and then Phobos.

nodes.t: Soldiers who keep the Union together
nodes.x: The refounded Union expects its soldiers to serve as integration officers as well as fighters: they settle disputes, enforce the mixing policy and, when ordered to, break up movements judged to threaten the Union. Toronto in 2312 is Directive 20 in practice.

nodes.t: Aid first, influence always
nodes.x: China's post-war doctrine runs in a set order: send aid, run the logistics through Tianshu, ask for nothing up front, and let dependence do the rest. It wins Australia and half of South America without a shot being fired, and Beijing holds them loosely.

nodes.t: Augmentation is equipment owed to the unit
nodes.x: The Ascendancy builds its forces on the state's reading of the Nashik Oath. Augmentation is equipment, issued by the unit and owed back to it, never something a pilot consumes, and pilots are sworn to each other and to the state. It keeps the Oath's root, that the strong defend the weak, but reads the weak as its own people first. The Ascendancy sees it as the opposite of Department Zero, and is proud of the difference.

nodes.t: Rescue frames as a kind of resistance
nodes.x: Japan's civil defence flies rescue frames for floods and earthquakes, and in Kansai the same crews organise the protests against Beijing's schedules. Tianshu cannot tell where one job ends and the other begins.

nodes.t: Sell the frames, keep no bases
nodes.x: The Commonwealth's post-war doctrine is to supply and never occupy. It sells frames to half of Earth and keeps no foreign bases, and its influence comes from the people its frames once sheltered.

nodes.t: Inspect the reactors, hold the relays, as far as the Moon
nodes.x: The UNEL's doctrine after the Mandate is to keep the peace by controlling what powers everyone else. It inspects every sealed reactor that comes inside lunar orbit, holds the beamed-power relays, and keeps its fleets where every power can see them. Beyond the Moon it has no such hold, and does not claim otherwise.

nodes.t: Most space fights end in a breach
nodes.x: Ships with defence lasers are hard to kill from outside, and their cargo is generally worth more intact. Space doctrine has settled, for the most part, on closing in behind the enemy's own fire, breaching and boarding, and navies, houses and pirates all fight this way.

nodes.t: Survive first, fight when you must
nodes.x: Colony One's doctrine for a century on the Line of Control. Keep the air plants running. Keep the militia ready. Treat every MRD survey as a probe. The frames are built to be fixed in a tunnel.

nodes.t: A fight you survive beats a battle you win
nodes.x: The MRD's doctrine was written by officers trained in the Union's lance schools and approved by its panels: engage at range, break contact before the losses mount, reassess, and return. Force is treated as a regrettable necessity, and rationed accordingly.

nodes.t: Fight to keep trading, and leave if fired on
nodes.x: The Syndicate's caravans are fleets and markets at once, and their doctrine is accordingly commercial: avoid combat, trade wherever possible and leave the moment shots are fired, unless an example needs making - in which case it is booked as a cost of doing business.

nodes.t: Care is the reason to fight
nodes.x: Umoja fights only for kin, and kin is whoever it has cared for. It is the councils' doctrine, the keepers' word carried out to Jupiter: Umoja's frames heal, need feeding, and are crewed by people bound to them. Since the Ganymede Split it governs how Umoja defends its habitats rather than how its Lodges make war. To outsiders its idea of protection can be hard to tell apart from possession.

nodes.t: Sworn pairs against things bigger than frames
nodes.x: The Compact's oldest form of riding out is the hunt for what Jupiter's moons and other powers' programmes produce: giants, rogue machines and worse. The akharas that swear pairs hunt in pairs and never alone, as the first Ashvins did, while the others hunt however their honour tells them.

nodes.t: Wait, and let the dark do the work
nodes.x: The Communion's doctrine is time. It mines the approaches, sleeps through the years and wakes when something hostile comes near, and its frames are built to idle in the cold for a decade at a stretch. In the long watch, it is usually the enemy who tires first.

nodes.t: What is grown obeys
nodes.x: The Lodges' doctrine, and since the Ganymede Split, Umoja's in any fight that matters. A body or frame that was grown can be commanded, and a Lodge war band is commanded to the cell: grafts that harden under fire, muscle that keeps fighting after the pilot is unconscious, stings ordered to spread. It is strength through strength, against Kin Defence's strength through cultivation, and it fights like the raid bands it came from: disperse, strike, heal, strike again.

nodes.t: The strong go where the weak are threatened
nodes.x: The Compact's root doctrine, the Oath in motion. Wherever the weak are threatened, whether by giants, strays, a Lodge war band or an Earth power's patrol, an Ashva rides out, with or without leave and with or without a pair. There is no warrant, no hearing and no appeal; honour is the only check, and honour is the rider's own judgement. Riding out has saved habitats no one else would reach, and it has started fights the Ascendancy has had to finish, sometimes against the Ashva themselves.

nodes.t: Act beyond Luna without a colony
nodes.x: The lesson the Union's councils drew from the Martian crisis: hold anchorages of its own, on Deimos's doorstep and in the Trojans, so that it need never again depend on a colony to act in space. In 2312 it takes the Trojans in a day.

nodes.t: Fly unarmed into the no-fly zone
nodes.x: At Mars in 2312 the UNEL sends unarmed observers, with crews chosen for their nerve, to wait at the edge of the no-fly zone and fly in to record who fires. It is later written up as doctrine, on the reasoning that a witness counts for a great deal when every power knows the UNEL publishes what it sees.

nodes.t: Everything in place before the first shot
nodes.x: Colony One's war plan for the MRD. Agents across the line. Explosive drones in hired warehouses. Enemy spies eliminated. The first strike is meant to decide the war. In July 2312 Colony One aims it at the Americans instead.

nodes.t: Hold the line, strike their systems
nodes.x: The MRD's doctrine for the crisis: fortify the Line of Control, win the independent colonies by consent, and open any war with a cyber strike on the enemy's defences. It never intends to cross the line, and in 2312 it doesn't.

nodes.t: Economic war without a shot
nodes.x: The Syndicate's answer to American tariffs is to stop and search every unescorted American merchant ship in the Belt, seize cargo on whatever pretext the inspectors can write up, and never fire. It is the Merchant Marine doctrine turned into a weapon.

nodes.t: Hide the weapons, burn the records, blend in
nodes.x: When the fleet falls, Colony One's ground forces cache their weapons, destroy their own personnel records and melt into the population. The remnant teaches the doctrine in its hidden docks, in case Mars needs it again.

nodes.t: A force that cannot fight alone
nodes.x: The Constitutionalists' founding doctrine is written into their charter and into their frames alike: their forces exist to defend New Philadelphia, and they go to war only with Washington's consent and under Washington's code.

nodes.t: Guard the trade, not the territory
nodes.x: The Syndicate guards its exchanges at Pallas, Juno and Ceres with frames paid for out of the trades they protect. It holds no territory it can't move, and it moves Hygiea to prove the point.

nodes.t: When power no longer decides doctrine
nodes.x: Projected for the fusion frames: a frame that needs no fuel, battery or relay can stay in the field as long as its pilot can. Tianlong's doctrine writers are drafting what that means, and every doctrine on this page was written around a power limit.

vehicles.label: Vehicles
vehicles.intro: Tanks, jets and helicopters didn't disappear when mechs arrived: they're cheaper, lower and harder to see than an 18 m frame, so every line adapted. After the war Earth's vehicles burn fuel again, and each space faction rebuilds sealed Earth vehicles for its own ground.
turns: Garrisons ambushed a TL-80 column from a ravine tanks couldn't climb. Designers answered with roof armour, high-angle guns and hull-down tactics. Crews learned to stay hull-down and let the frames give themselves away first.
A mech can see over every ridge, but everyone can see a mech. Low vehicles became the ambushers: hull-down tanks, recon cars in hedgerows, and gunships just below the crest line.

A Kestrel is a ground frame that can fly, and a poor dogfighter. Fighters escort the drops, other fighters hunt them, and jets with hours of fuel fly the support missions a forty-minute battery can't.
Capacitor cores, electrothermal guns and point-defence lasers were built for frames, and they're now going into tanks, fighters and gunships. The BH-110 Regulator and the Kite IV are the result.

Beijing's Tiejia-V has no crew and a reactor no human runs. The Lunar Republic beams power to a truck. OKB-7 puts a particle cannon on tracks. The newest vehicles carry the frames' technology further than the frames do.
The Relay War teaches every army that a vehicle drinking beamed power can be starved or spoofed. Fighters get fuel tanks back, and the Union builds tanks and jets whose job is to kill relays.

Reactors leave Earth's battlefields under the Mandate, and hydrogen and kerosene pour down from the Belt. China's crewless tank goes back to diesel, and the Commonwealth sells a turbine that burns anything to half the world.
Every world needs its own wheels
The space factions start with sealed Earth vehicles and replace them with their own: crawlers for Martian tunnels, tugs for the Belt, heated halls on tracks for the far dark.
In 2312 the Americans revive the Hound for the altiplano and drop rovers onto Mars, while the MRD moves its batteries along the Red Wall by night.
fams: Escorts, hunters, and jets that can stay longer than forty minutes.
Under the crest line, where a mech can't follow.
Small enough to lose. Jammers, raiders and the network's eyes.
Rovers, crawlers, tugs and walkers for places with no air.
vehicles.profileH: Who drives what after the war

profile.t: The Provost for holding ground, Condor and Egret airlifters for the reconstruction, the Hound and Kite revived for Bolivia, rovers dropped onto Mars and patrol cars in the Bastion, and a hauler for the Keystone.
The Gardien on Quebec hydrogen for integration duty, and Boreal East's haulers for the hydrogen fields, after a war fought by killing the enemy's relays.
A crewless tank on diesel once the reactors went, Lianxin aid convoys that power the towns they stop in, Kansai's rescue carriers under protection, and jets and swarms that never run dry.
The Vityaz-D on diesel for oath-sworn crews, after the fission siege tanks of the war, and cloud skiffs between the stations at Venus.
The Kafila-M and Rahma: carriers on the Desert Turbine, sold with every frame and given away when the buyer can't pay, descended from the war's ambulance columns.
Relay trucks the UNEL can switch off, firebreak tankers for a planet still burning, and the heirs of the white convoys into the Open Cities.
Sealed American Drovers at first, then Dustline's Burrowers for the tunnels, and the partisans' tunnel carts after 2312.
The Charter Carrier, an American IFV that only starts with Washington's code.
Rebuilt Funkenwerk scout cars, then Vesta's Surveyors, tractors that move the Hammer batteries along the Red Wall, and a field laboratory for the fusion cell.
Belt tugs that push rocks and tow ships, and cargo walkers for asteroids too small to drive on.
Kin Carriers grown on salvaged frames and fed on ammonia, later lined with mats that eat Jupiter's radiation.
The Nashik chariot rebuilt as a rescue rover for Io, and hunt crawlers that carry sworn pairs into the radiation belts.
Ice crawlers descended from the Canadian haulers that carried refugees north, and the sledges that set up the Long Mirrors.

nodes.t: America's main battle tank
nodes.x: Brannock-Hale's main battle tank: gas turbine, 125 mm gun, composite armour, and the fire-control system that later went into the Garrison. On open ground it was the best tank in the world.

nodes.t: Roof armour and a sensor mast after Iron Gate
nodes.x: After Iron Gate the Army knew what happens when the enemy fires from above, and the A3 was its answer: roof armour against plunging fire, a sensor mast to see over ridges, and a gun that elevates far enough to reach a mech's torso. Crews were trained to stay hull-down and let the frames give themselves away first.

nodes.t: The first tank designed to fight mechs
nodes.x: The first American tank designed from the start to fight mechs: a low hull, heavy roof armour, a high-angle 125 mm gun, and a roof-mounted Hornet pod for shots at hip actuators. A Marshal II platoon costs about as much as one Teamster and, on open plains, spots a frame long before the frame finds it. Brannock fire teams still own rough ground; on the flat, the Marshals have the better of it.

nodes.t: Point-defence laser borrowed from the Harrier
nodes.x: Hornet pods and Grad-M salvos made the roof the weak spot again. The A2 mounts a PL-2-derived laser on the turret to shoot down incoming missiles, fed from a capacitor buffer the turbine charges.

nodes.t: An electrothermal gun on a tank
nodes.x: A Marshal successor built around the HT-20 plant and an enlarged AR-40E electrothermal gun, which hits about as hard as a linear rifle from a hull only 2.4 m tall. The Army's mech lobby considers it a waste of capacitors, and the tank lobby's reply is usually the unit cost, which comes to about a quarter of a Pathfinder's.

nodes.t: “Iron Armour”: cheap, low, exported by the thousand
nodes.x: Tianlong's mass-production tank, small and simple, and sold across Africa and Arabia. At Iron Gate an insurgent column of them became the first armour ever destroyed by mechs. Thousands remain in service.

nodes.t: Taught to fight beside the Tieniu
nodes.x: After Iron Gate the Pact went on building tanks, and set about teaching them to work with mechs. Tiejia platoons guard the Tieniu's legs and flanks while the frames kneel to fire, and a raised gun mount lets them reach a frame's torso at close range. They are cheap, plentiful and easy to crew.

nodes.t: Autoloader, reactive roof armour, export favourite
nodes.x: It is built in the same factories as the Tieshan, on the same multi-fuel diesel. Reactive armour on the roof stops the plunging fire that kills older tanks, and the autoloader cycles quickly enough to hit a mech before it ducks back behind a ridge. It has become the most exported tank in the world.

nodes.t: Fights in the gaps between kneeling Tieshans
nodes.x: Order 11 waves leave gaps between the kneeling frames, and the TL-19 was designed to fill them: low and fast, with top-attack missiles in the turret and a Type-07 action as its coaxial gun. Under the current establishment every Tieshan company has a Tiejia platoon assigned to protect its legs.

nodes.t: Turretless Tiejia hull, raid supply carrier
nodes.x: People in the League still tell how it began: surplus TL-92s bought cheaply, their turrets cut off, and the hulls turned into armoured carriers for fuel, ammunition and frame parts. The frames do the fighting and the Kafila keeps them running between strikes, and it is often said that one convoy of them keeps the Jinn alive.

nodes.t: TL-99 hull with a refurbished shoulder cannon
nodes.x: The League's own tank: a surplus TL-99 hull carrying a Type-01Q cannon on mining-rig recoil dampers. It fires on the move, which no Tianlong vehicle ever managed with that gun, and it hides in dunes a Sirocco couldn't crouch behind.

nodes.t: Light enough for mountain bridges and landing ships
nodes.x: Japan's defensive tank, built light for mountain roads and amphibious ships. Mitsurugi's suspension work on it fed into the balance-control research behind every later MHI frame.

nodes.t: Wheeled, fast, shipped with the Hayates
nodes.x: Japan replaced the Type-78 with an eight-wheeled combat vehicle that sails on the same landing ships as the Hayates. On island roads it outruns a frame, and its coil gun, derived from the Type-L, gives any intruder's mech reason to think twice. In the island garrisons' telling, the Hayates hold the beach and the Type-11s hold the roads behind it.

nodes.t: Air-droppable light tank
nodes.x: A light tank built to go under a tiltrotor with airborne infantry: thin armour and a 105 mm gun.

nodes.t: Re-roled as a mech ambusher
nodes.x: Once the Sparrowhawk had taken over the air-drop job, the Army went looking for a new one for the Ranger. A low, fast tank with ATGMs in the turret can hide where an 18 m frame can't, and wait there for a Tieniu to walk past; Ranger crews have taken to calling this fighting from the ankles.

nodes.t: A purpose-built mech hunter
nodes.x: Two metres tall, quiet on hybrid drive, with a mast sight and top-attack missiles aimed at hip actuators. Hounds work in pairs ahead of a fire team, finding enemy frames and forcing them to stop and deal with something they can barely see.

nodes.t: The fire team's hidden fifth member
nodes.x: Hounds are data-linked to Teamster fire teams, so a Hound can fire Hornet cells at targets a Teamster has marked, and the other way round. The after-action numbers show that fire teams trained with a Hound pair lose fewer frames than teams that aren't, and that has quietly settled the Army's argument about whether tanks still matter.

nodes.t: Wheeled recon with a telescoping sensor mast
nodes.x: The Union's reconnaissance car: fast, quiet, with a mast that raised its sensors eight metres.

nodes.t: Eyes that can't be seen
nodes.x: A mech sees farther from 17 m up, but it can also be seen from almost everywhere, and the Union drew the obvious conclusion. The Genette-B went passive, with no radar, a lower mast and thermal sights, so that it could sit in a hedgerow and watch what the Écuyer screen could only guess at.

nodes.t: Ground jammer car
nodes.x: Directive 5 opens every engagement with electronic attack, and the Genette-E delivers it from closer than any aircraft is prepared to go. It creeps to within a few kilometres of the enemy line, switches on, and moves on again before anyone can find it.

nodes.t: A decoy that looks like a lance
nodes.x: Built for the hunter-killer lance, the Genette-L is a car that broadcasts the radar and radio signature of a Pavise, so that enemy Kestrels see three lances where there is in fact one. Its crews accept being shot at, on the condition that the car keeps moving.

nodes.t: Infantry fighting vehicle, 30 mm turret
nodes.x: America's infantry carrier: six dismounts in the back and a 30 mm chain gun on top. That chain gun, given a pistol grip, became the M30, the first mech weapon.

nodes.t: Up-armoured to keep up with mechs
nodes.x: Infantry still clear buildings and guard frames at rest, and they need to arrive with them. The A4 added armour and a frame-height periscope so its crew could follow a Garrison pair through ground the old Drover had always avoided.

nodes.t: Fire-team carrier with reload racks
nodes.x: One Drover II rides with each four-mech fire team. It carries dismounts, M140 reloads and spare stake-driver cylinders. It is why a Brannock team can fight a full day without pulling back.

nodes.t: Armoured swap-pit carrier with a battery crane
nodes.x: A Drover II hull with the M1100's flatbed: four QX-3 packs under armour, a fold-out crane, and a 30 mm turret for when the pit comes under attack. Kestrels land beside it, swap packs in ninety seconds and leave again. Pit crews reckon it is the most shot-at vehicle in the Army.

nodes.t: A swap pit with no crew
nodes.x: Enemies go for swap pits before they go for mechs, so the Army has been testing a Pitwagon with no crew. It drives to a grid reference, opens up and swaps packs on its own. It works in trials, although in its one live test it was the first thing destroyed.

nodes.t: “Iron Thunder”: tracked 152 mm howitzer
nodes.x: The backbone of Pact massed artillery. Before mechs, batteries of these decided battles.

nodes.t: Indirect fire; shoot and move
nodes.x: Order 5's kneeling lines took over direct fire, but indirect fire still needed tubes. The TL-90 added an autoloader and shoot-and-move drills, because mech raids could now reach the gun lines.

nodes.t: Rocket artillery behind the fortress belt
nodes.x: Tracked rocket launchers alongside the tube guns: cheaper, quicker to move, and enough to break up an assault on a fortress belt before it reaches the kneeling lines.

nodes.t: “Watchtower”: radar and fire control for the Air Umbrella
nodes.x: A Leiting chassis carrying a folding radar and the fire-control link on which Order 19 depends. It cues hundreds of Tiebi rocket racks onto a Kestrel flight's landing approach at once, and it holds a higher protection priority than any other Pact vehicle, the mechs included. That link was also the first occasion on which Tianshu aimed weapons rather than trains.

nodes.t: Tank transporter trucks and rail flats
nodes.x: Tanks wear out their tracks on long drives, so armies moved them by truck and rail. Mechs turned out to wear out their knees even faster.

nodes.t: Low-loader for a Garrison lying on its back
nodes.x: A Garrison walks at 30 km/h and needs new knee bearings every few hundred kilometres, so the US Army moves its frames by road, lying flat on these low-loaders. Every American frame built since has had lift points for one.

nodes.t: Tracked, armoured carrier for a kneeling Tieshan
nodes.x: The M1100 idea, rebuilt on armoured TL-92 running gear. A Tieshan kneels on the back and rides to the line, saving its legs for the fight; at the line the company steps off and is firing within a minute, as the drill requires.

nodes.t: Follows Koschei on tracks, feeding it by cable
nodes.x: Frame-carrier running gear scaled up until it could carry a micro-reactor and an MTU-7 generator stack, following Koschei on its own tracks. The cable between the two is the weak point, and Department Zero has accepted that it can't be armoured.

nodes.t: An ice-road hauler that carries a frame
nodes.x: Boreal built ice-road haulers before it built frames, so its first frame carrier was naturally a hauler: a tracked over-snow tractor with a heated deck for a Tundra lying down, and a cab that can keep two drivers alive if the road gives way. Norway placed its order before Ottawa did.

nodes.t: A scout car that runs as cold as the snow
nodes.x: The Wolverine's companion: a low, insulated scout car that lies up for days on a reformer-stack trickle with nothing switched on but its passive sensors. It finds the enemy, and the Wolverines decide what to do about it.

nodes.t: An open-drawing scout car from Tempelhof
nodes.x: Funkenwerk's second product, and the first it sold in any numbers: a light scout car on a modular cell stack, built to keep pace with a Läufer screen and to be repaired with whatever fits. The drawings are public, so the Dutch contingent built forty of its own, and Funkenwerk, true to form, put that on a poster as well.

nodes.t: “Foal”: the supply mule that follows the wind riders
nodes.x: A tracked mule from the Darkhan sheds that follows a Bürged across the steppe with fuel, ammunition and a felt tent aboard. It runs on a tractor's multi-fuel diesel, steers itself between waypoints and can be repaired by any herder's mechanic, which is why the wind riders seldom have to wait for a depot.

nodes.t: Ex-mining trucks, painted white
nodes.x: The UN has no vehicle maker, so the white convoys ran on whatever members gave: ex-mining haul trucks with welded-on armour, and surplus Drovers and Kafilas bought second-hand, all stripped of markings and painted white. The drill, as Efua Mensah wrote it, is that a white convoy stops for any convoy that asks, whoever owns it.

nodes.t: Beamed power, delivered by truck
nodes.x: Shackleton Works' ground station for the Relay Rectenna is a tracked mast that catches the Republic's beam and passes it to the white squads' frames within a few kilometres. It is deployed with UN operations, and the Republic parks a relay satellite over it for as long as Geneva asks.

nodes.t: An ace's transporter and racing pit
nodes.x: Castellani delivers each frame as an Italian team would deliver a racing car, in a red-and-gold transporter with a workshop inside, a crane, spare Stack-R cells and the engineers who tuned them. A Falco rarely fights far from its Bisarca, and the Union's enemies have learned to look for the transporter first.

nodes.t: A chariot for a sworn pair
nodes.x: Nashik's carrier for an Ashvin pair: two frame cradles side by side, a shared cab for both pilots on the road, and the unit store where their augmentation rigs are kept between sorties, logged in and logged out under the Oath. Built on licensed TL-12 running gear, cooled for the plains.

nodes.t: A particle cannon on tracks, cable and all
nodes.x: The Iskra can't move while it fires, so OKB-7 gave it a carriage: a tracked mount for the cannon, coupled by cable to an MTU-7 generator truck a few hundred metres back. The pair is slow, loud and visible from orbit, and that is the price of the hardest-hitting weapon on the battlefield.

nodes.t: A coilgun battery on a coastal truck
nodes.x: Japan's coastal defence moved its newest capacitor onto wheels: a Type-11 chassis carrying a Mk.III core and a long coilgun, able to fire from a beach and leave before anything answers. Beijing's customs seizures began a month after its first trials.

nodes.t: A tank with no crew and a reactor no human runs
nodes.x: Beijing's first uncrewed tank is a Tiejia-IV hull with a Salt Core, a Drum Rifle and no hatches at all. Tianshu drives it, aims it and runs its reactor, while a Tianyan pilot approves what it does, and six of them walk beside each trial squad. In Moscow it is generally described as a train with a gun.

nodes.t: “Crescent”: an armoured ambulance and water carrier
nodes.x: Protect First on tracks: a Kafila hull rebuilt as an armoured ambulance, with a water plant, a surgical bay and room for twelve stretchers. It follows the Harmattans into towns they have come to shelter. The Gulf associates asked what it was armed with, and Khartoum said water.

nodes.t: The Union's main battle tank
nodes.x: A fast, autoloaded tank built for the cavalry tradition: lighter than a Marshal, quicker across country, and fitted with the best fire control in Europe.

nodes.t: A sensor mast and a place behind the screen
nodes.x: After the Maghreb Depot Strikes the Union stopped sending tanks in first. The Hussard-B waits hull-down behind the Écuyer screen, its mast up, and fires at whatever the screen finds.

nodes.t: A tank that jams before it shoots
nodes.x: The first Union tank designed for Directive 5, with a Störer pod on the turret, Fenrir missiles in the bustle and a quiet fuel-cell drive for the last kilometre. In the doctrine, and in the way its crews talk about it, the main gun is the second weapon.

nodes.t: A coilgun on tracks, buffered by a licensed core
nodes.x: A Cuirassier rebuilt around the Spiegel coilgun, with a Licensed Core that recharges it faster than the Pavise can manage. It fights beside the hunter-killer lances and kills what they blind. Funkenwerk's view, offered fairly often, is that the Union has bought its own idea back.

nodes.t: The ethics panel's first tank
nodes.x: A prototype that the ethics panel had to approve line by line: a coilgun, a jammer mast, and a crew of two who can override every automated system aboard. It is slower to fight than anything Beijing builds, and deliberately so. Its crews call it the committee, after the process that produced it, and Strasbourg's own papers describe it, in much the same spirit, as accountable.

nodes.t: “Knight”: Russia's heavy tank
nodes.x: A heavy, low tank with a 152 mm gun and an autoloader, built to break through prepared defences in the deep-battle tradition. It is slower than a Marshal and harder to stop.

nodes.t: Roof armour and rockets for the Caspian
nodes.x: The Vityaz after Talysh, where Merlins killed tanks from above: reactive roof armour, a Type-03 rocket rack for walking targets, and orders to stay close to the Tieniu.

nodes.t: “Ram”: the second wave's tank
nodes.x: Built to arrive with the second wave of an echeloned assault, when the Grad-M batteries have emptied and the defenders are reloading. Twin diesels, a 152 mm gun and a dozer blade for the craters the first wave left.

nodes.t: The Molot on tracks, ahead of the Mamonts
nodes.x: The breakthrough groups' tank: a Molot autoloading cannon in a turret, using the same OKB-7 autoloader as the other heavy frames. It goes into the gap first and the Mamonts widen it behind. At the Hari River more Taran-2s were lost than Mamonts, and that was the job they were built to do.

nodes.t: A siege tank for the Krepost's escort
nodes.x: Moscow's tank for a long war: a Taran-2 hull with city-breaking armour, a Molot and a mine plough, built to walk beside the Krepost and the siege trains into fortified towns. Every bloc's analysts have noticed where the plough is aimed.

nodes.t: A truck, a gun and a crew who know the ground
nodes.x: The vehicle of every irregular war before mechs: a commercial pickup with a machine gun or recoilless rifle bolted to the bed. Cheap, fast and everywhere.

nodes.t: A pickup that can kill a frame
nodes.x: The great equaliser of the Convoy Raids: a desert pickup carrying a bootleg Hornet pod or a pair of salvaged ATGM tubes, kept under a tarpaulin until a frame walks past. No factory makes them, though a great many dealers sell them. Qadira's crews learned their trade on them, as did about half of Grey Lantern's.

nodes.t: A mine-proof truck sold to anyone
nodes.x: A V-hulled armoured truck built under licence in a dozen countries and sold to all of them: mine-resistant, easy to fix and big enough for a squad or a load of frame parts. The League rode in them, the white convoys painted them, and Grey Lantern buys them by the shipload under whatever flag it is using that year.

nodes.t: Same truck, now with a pod and a jammer
nodes.x: The Kopje after twenty years of frame wars: a Hornet-pattern pod on a ring mount, a cheap jammer copied from the Störer, and a winch for dragging a downed frame out of a fire zone. It is the most common armoured vehicle in Africa.

nodes.t: A recovery truck that can lift a frame
nodes.x: A six-wheeled crane truck with a winch, a frame cradle and a workshop in the back, built in Turkey, Brazil and South Africa from whichever parts were cheapest that year. It doesn't appear in anyone's doctrine, but most armies without a Pitwagon run on it.

nodes.t: A recovery truck that can also refuel a frame
nodes.x: The Mule with a Q-Mix generator and a battery bank, so it can recharge a hybrid frame or a Kopje as well as lift one. The Charter's armies take them everywhere, and Grey Lantern rents them by the week.

nodes.t: Loitering munitions and spotter drones
nodes.x: The drone war that came before mechs: cheap quadcopters, loitering munitions and long-range spotters, contested by jammers on both sides. Mechs did not end it, and for the most part gave it larger targets.

nodes.t: “Dragonfly”: a jammer you can throw away
nodes.x: Directive 5's cheapest weapon is a small jammer drone that a Haubert lance launches by the dozen before contact. Each one screams on a different band until it is shot down, and the doctrine counts every one shot down as a shot that was not fired at a frame.

nodes.t: Desert drones built from hobby parts
nodes.x: The raid bands' eyes in the Convoy Raids were hobby airframes with phone cameras and a grenade under the wing, launched from a pickup and flown off a laptop. People still say they found convoys for Abu Ghubar a day before the convoys found him, and every bloc learned from them to watch the sky over the dunes.

nodes.t: The network's eyes along the belt
nodes.x: Thousands of small spotter drones circle the Fortress Belt and report everything they see to Tianshu, which decides what matters. They cue the Air Umbrella's racks and the Wanglou radars. No one flies them in the ordinary sense; the network does.

nodes.t: Drones that keep the link alive
nodes.x: Beijing's quiet answer to the question the Tianyan trials have avoided, which is what happens when the link is jammed. A ring of relay drones flies above each squad and re-routes the link around any jammer it finds. In trials the Union's Libelles grounded half of them within a minute.

nodes.t: A drone that waits, then dives
nodes.x: Mass-produced loitering munitions sold in crates of twenty, each one circling until it finds a hot engine or a frame's knee and diving on it. They are the cheapest anti-frame weapon ever built, and every bloc's jammers exist partly because of them.

nodes.t: Halcyon's strike fighter
nodes.x: The fighter whose wing binders, avionics and flight-control software every Halcyon frame inherited. It ruled the air in the decade before mechs.

nodes.t: Escort for the first variable frames
nodes.x: Built on the same line as the Merlin. The Merlin could fly but couldn't dogfight, so Gyrfalcon IIs escorted every Merlin flight, dealing with interceptors while the frames transformed and landed, and from then on escorting frames was the American fighter's main job.

nodes.t: Escort for drop-and-strike
nodes.x: Designed around a Kestrel's two worst moments: landing and take-off. Lanners hold the air over a landing zone for forty minutes, then cover the climb-out. In the Forty-Minute War they kept Kestrel losses low, until the Pact's advisers switched to hitting the swap pits.

nodes.t: Laser defence on a capacitor bank
nodes.x: After the Sapsan, escort fighters had to survive rocket salvos as well. The Saker carries a PL-2-derived laser and a Mitsurugi capacitor buffer charged by its engines, which makes it the first fighter to run on mech power technology, and its pilots train alongside the Harriers they escort.

nodes.t: Armoured ground-attack jet
nodes.x: A slow, armoured jet built around a rotary cannon for killing tanks, with hours of loiter time.

nodes.t: Learned to hunt walking targets
nodes.x: A mech is the tallest thing on the battlefield and can't hide in a fold of ground. Shrikes were rearmed with heavier cannon rounds and top-attack bombs aimed at hip and knee actuators, and flew low enough to stay under early mechs' sensors.

nodes.t: Hours of support a Kestrel can't give
nodes.x: Where Kestrels raid, Shrikes stay. With hours of fuel against a Kestrel's forty minutes, the Shrike II flies the long support missions, firing glide munitions from beyond Hornet range. The Army asks for Shrikes by name, which the Air Force pretends not to notice.

nodes.t: “Swift”: OKB-7's high-speed interceptor
nodes.x: Before it built mechs, Kirov-Mikoyan OKB-7 was a fighter bureau. The Strizh was built to catch US bombers, and the bureau's heavy, aggressive engineering carried straight into the Medved.

nodes.t: Look-down radar for walking targets
nodes.x: Re-radared to find mechs moving through broken ground. At the Talysh Mountains it found the Merlins too late, after they had already transformed and gone.

nodes.t: “Peregrine”: built to catch Kestrels mid-transformation
nodes.x: Designed after the Forty-Minute War around one number: the two seconds a Kestrel spends half-folded, too slow to fly and too high to fight. Sapsans circle over landing zones and dive into that window with short-range missiles. With the Air Umbrella, they're why the Harrier carries a point-defence laser.

nodes.t: Rocket salvos too big for one laser
nodes.x: OKB-7's answer to the Harrier: rocket salvos too large for one PL-2 to stop, and a dive that clears the landing zone before the Harriers' wingmen can reply.

nodes.t: “Swallow”: the Union's multirole fighter
nodes.x: A good, expensive European fighter, bought in small numbers by every Union member.

nodes.t: Lost the Maghreb air battle, changed jobs
nodes.x: In the Maghreb Depot Strikes US pilots out-flew the Hirondelles and destroyed the Union's hydrogen depots in two weeks. The Union concluded that it would not beat the Americans fighter for fighter, and rebuilt the Hirondelle around jamming rather than dogfighting.

nodes.t: The fast end of Directive 5
nodes.x: A two-seat electronic-attack fighter, with jammers in place of half its missiles and a back-seater whose task is to blind enemy radar before the Haubert lances move. It scores fewer kills than the old Hirondelle did, and has a great deal more influence on how a fight goes.

nodes.t: Interceptor for the hunter-killer lance
nodes.x: The air half of Directive 8. Martinets wait over a Kestrel flight's predicted landing zone, cued by Pavise jammers on the ground, and attack the Kestrels on approach. The Spiegels take the ones that make it down.

nodes.t: “Swan”: swing-wing strategic bomber
nodes.x: OKB-7's intercontinental cruise-missile carrier.

nodes.t: Standoff missiles for swap pits and carriers
nodes.x: The Forty-Minute War showed the Pact where the United States is weakest: the swap pits and the carriers that feed its Kestrels. The Lebed-M fires long-range missiles at both from far outside US fighter cover.

nodes.t: Airborne radar and jamming aircraft
nodes.x: A converted airliner with a rotating radar dome and jamming pods: the eyes of Union air defence.

nodes.t: Rebuilt as a flying jammer after Maghreb
nodes.x: After the Maghreb strikes the Argus fleet was rebuilt for electronic attack, with fewer radars and far more jammers. It flew the first Directive 5 engagements, blinding enemy sensors before the Écuyers moved.

nodes.t: Command jammer for VEK lances
nodes.x: It carries data links to every Haubert lance and enough jamming power to blind a division. It was also the biggest and slowest target over any battlefield, as the Air Umbrella demonstrated.

nodes.t: Pulled back, still in charge
nodes.x: Once Pavises could jam from the ground, the Argus withdrew to high altitude well behind the line. It no longer jams the enemy; instead it ties every lance, Pavise and Martinet into one picture, which has proved a harder job to replace.

nodes.t: Strategic jet airlifter
nodes.x: Halcyon's four-engine transport, built to carry tanks to wars across an ocean.

nodes.t: One Garrison, lying down
nodes.x: A strengthened floor and a longer ramp let it carry one Garrison or Sparrowhawk across an ocean, and America's whole expeditionary model rested on them.

nodes.t: Frame airlifter: three Kestrels or two Teamsters
nodes.x: The first airlifter designed around mechs, with a nose and a tail that both open so frames can walk straight through, and rough-strip landing gear that puts it down close enough to the front to matter. It exists because the Heron Heavy proved that frames slung under rotors get shot down.

nodes.t: A swap pit that flies in
nodes.x: A Condor that lands on a road, lowers both ramps and becomes a swap pit, with forty QX-3 packs, two cranes and an Osprey aboard. It is gone again within the hour, and Sapsan pilots hunt Condor Pits as hard as they hunt Kestrels.

nodes.t: Re-beams orbital power to Kestrels under the clouds
nodes.x: A Condor airframe with a rectenna on top and a transmitter underneath. It catches power from the ring's microwave relay above the weather and passes it down to SKYLINE Harriers. If it works, the forty-minute clock lasts as long as the relay stays up.

nodes.t: A fighter that never has to land to recharge
nodes.x: The Saker rebuilt around SKYLINE: a rectenna in the spine draws beamed power from the relay above the clouds and feeds a Mk.III-buffered laser that can now hurt more than missiles. Under the relay it escorts Kestrels for as long as the beam holds. Away from it, it does about what a Saker does, at a good deal more cost.

nodes.t: An electrothermal gun with wings
nodes.x: The Shrike line's answer to frames that shrug off 30 mm: the Regulator's electrothermal gun along the belly and armour that takes a Drum Rifle burst. It loiters for hours over a fire team, which is the one thing a Kestrel still can't do.

nodes.t: “Golden Eagle”: a rail gun in the spine
nodes.x: Moscow's heavy interceptor, built once Harriers had learned to shrug off rocket salvos: a Type-12 rail gun along the spine, fed by a Copied Core, to kill a Harrier beyond the reach of its laser. It needs a long runway and a longer budget, and Beijing was not offered one.

nodes.t: “Kite”: the lance's own fighter
nodes.x: The Martinet grown into an electronic-warfare fighter that flies with a Pavise lance rather than above it, with a Störer pod under each wing, two dozen Libelles in the bay and Fenrir missiles for anything that switches on a jammer of its own. The ethics panel made a pilot a condition of approval, and the pilots, consulted in their turn, asked for two.

nodes.t: An uncrewed strike jet flown by the network
nodes.x: Beijing's first combat aircraft in a generation, because it waited until it didn't need pilots. Tianshu flies the Kunpeng in flocks of twelve, cueing strikes from the Spotters' picture and handing targets to the Air Umbrella. It has no cockpit, so it turns harder than anything with a person inside. It is named for the fish of the old story that became a bird so large its wings hid the sky.

nodes.t: A turboprop attack plane any air force can afford
nodes.x: A light turboprop that flies off dirt strips with guns and rockets under the wings, sold to every air force without a fighter budget. It couldn't survive a Sapsan, but in the wars it actually flies in it has very seldom had to.

nodes.t: A turboprop that hunts frames
nodes.x: The Hornbill with a mast sight, a Hornet pod and armour around the engine. League squadrons fly them, Grey Lantern leases them with pilots, and the white squads borrowed two for Mong Hsat.

nodes.t: Old airliners that carry one frame, lying down
nodes.x: Retired wide-body airliners with the floor reinforced and the nose cut to open, bought second-hand and flown by crews who don't ask what's in the hold. Each carries one frame on its back. Grey Lantern's airline has never had the same name twice.

nodes.t: Tank-hunting attack helicopter
nodes.x: Halcyon's attack helicopter. It hid behind ridges, popped up to fire missiles, and dropped back down.

nodes.t: A mast sight above the ridge, the rest below it
nodes.x: A mech's sensor head sees over the ridges Kites used to hide behind. The HH-52's answer was a mast-mounted sight, so only a ball the size of a football shows above the crest while the airframe stays hidden. After that, Kites found Tieniu more often than Tieniu found Kites.

nodes.t: Fire-and-forget missiles aimed at the knees
nodes.x: Kite IIIs escort Brannock fire teams and hunt enemy frames from behind, aiming at knee and hip actuators to leave a frame stranded rather than destroyed. Hornet anti-air pods keep them low and careful, but they're still the fastest anti-mech weapon a commander can call in.

nodes.t: Quiet hybrid drive and a point-defence laser
nodes.x: The first gunship built with mech technology: an HT-12-style hybrid drive that lets it hover on batteries with the turbines throttled back, and a small PL-2-derived laser to shoot down anti-air rockets. It's the only rotorcraft with a chance under the Air Umbrella.

nodes.t: Tiltrotor assault transport
nodes.x: Halcyon's tiltrotor, carrying airborne infantry with a Ranger light tank slung underneath.

nodes.t: Flew the Sparrowhawk drops
nodes.x: A heavy-lift Heron built to sling a stripped-down Sparrowhawk. In the Tiltrotor Drops at the end of Iron Gate the frames did well and the Herons did not, with nine shot down in a month, and Halcyon's answer was a mech that could fly itself in. The airframe stayed in service, though not in that role.
nodes.z: 2166 · frame drops end; the Merlin flies itself in

nodes.t: Flies battery packs to the swap pits
nodes.x: Herons stopped carrying frames and started carrying what frames need. A Pit Runner slings four QX packs or a load of LR-3 magazines to a forward swap pit, and leaves before anyone starts shooting at the pit.

nodes.t: “Truck”: the world's biggest helicopter
nodes.x: Big enough to lift a light tank, though a 72-tonne Tieniu was well beyond it.

nodes.t: Spare limbs and shell reloads
nodes.x: It can't lift a frame, so it lifts everything else: replacement legs, Type-01 shells and rocket racks, flown straight to kneeling lines the trucks can't reach.

nodes.t: Grad-M reloads within the hour
nodes.x: Bigger rotors and an underslung cradle for Grad-M batteries, so a wave's first salvo can be reloaded within the hour. Pact crews call it the second salvo.

nodes.t: Light scout helicopter
nodes.x: A small, quiet scout helicopter that spotted for Union armoured cavalry.

nodes.t: Spotter for the Écuyer screen
nodes.x: The Colibri flies below the treeline behind the Écuyers and lifts a mast sight over the trees to look where they're looking. It's smaller and quieter than any frame, and it sees what a mech's own height gives away.

nodes.t: Light jammer helicopter
nodes.x: A Colibri with a jamming pod, flying low over a Union lance to extend its electronic attack. It is cheap enough to lose, and the planning assumes that it will be.

nodes.t: “Bumblebee”: armoured assault helicopter
nodes.x: OKB-7's heavy assault helicopter: armoured, rocket-armed, and able to carry a squad in the back.

nodes.t: “Orca”: gunship for the mech waves
nodes.x: OKB-7's answer to the Kite: a heavily armoured gunship that flies just behind Order 11 waves, firing rockets into whatever the kneeling lines flush out. It trusts its armour more than its sights, which suits Pact crews.

nodes.t: Flies inside the Air Umbrella
nodes.x: Built to fly under the Pact's own rocket umbrella, with identification gear the Wanglou trusts. It hunts Kestrels in the few seconds after they land, when they're down but not yet ready to fight.

nodes.t: A gunship with two uncrewed wingmen
nodes.x: The Kite IV given a second job: it flies with two uncrewed Kites that carry the missiles while the crewed aircraft stays below the ridge. Washington's position is that a person always pulls the trigger, and under Unaltered Crews it takes some care over which person that is.

nodes.t: A utility helicopter for everyone
nodes.x: A medium twin-engine helicopter built for oil rigs, forestry and mining, and bought by every army that couldn't afford a Heron. It carries a squad, a load of frame parts slung underneath, or a casualty out of somewhere bad.

nodes.t: Door guns and a rocket pod
nodes.x: The Ibis with armour on the floor, door guns and a rocket pod on each side. It isn't a gunship, though it is the gunship most of the world's armies actually have. The keepers fly one, painted white, to carry the Jinn's patients to Khartoum.

nodes.t: The Regulator on an American capacitor
nodes.x: When Japan goes into China's sphere the Regulator loses the Mitsurugi capacitor its gun was built around. Brannock-Hale refits it with the Liberty Core in a year, accepts a slower rate of fire, and sends it north to Canada and south to the Isthmus by the thousand.

nodes.t: Built faster than it could be painted
nodes.x: The crewless Tiejia enters mass production for the Pact Civil War, still on a salt core no human runs. Beijing builds them on the same lines as the Tieshan-Zhan, and Tianshu fights them in companies of forty.

nodes.t: “Mirage”: an ambulance column that never stops
nodes.x: The Hilal grows into a whole column, with ambulance, water carrier, surgery and spares on one Simoom hull, built to keep moving behind the North African Front and to carry the Grafted Battalions' wounded all the way to the Hospital Safinas.

nodes.t: “Portcullis”: a tank that blinds the enemy's power
nodes.x: Directive 12 makes the enemy's power supply the first target. The Herse is the Dragon rebuilt to jam relays and spoof beamed power, and it runs on a field reformer that makes hydrogen from whatever fuel the column captures.

nodes.t: A siege tank that never stops for fuel
nodes.x: The siege trains turn west with a fission core in every escort tank. The Taran-F is fast to build, hard to stop and slowly poisonous to its own crews, who are rotated out on a schedule the doctors set and the generals ignore.

nodes.t: Ice-road haulers for both sides
nodes.x: Boreal's haulers serve both armies of the Winter War, built in the same sheds and painted at the gate. When the front breaks, some of them carry refugees north onto the ice instead of frames south.

nodes.t: The only convoys both sides let through
nodes.x: The Open Cities need food and medicine from outside, and the UN's white convoys bring it in under a flag both sides have agreed not to shoot at. The trucks are old mining haulers and the drivers are volunteers, and the register of those who did not come back is a long one.

nodes.t: A tank for holding ground, not taking it
nodes.x: Permanent presence needs tanks that can sit in a town for years. The Provost is lighter than the Regulator, burns cheap fuel from the Belt, and carries a loudspeaker and a medical bay as standard. It holds the Andean border through the Federation's collapse.

nodes.t: Back on diesel, and still crewless
nodes.x: The Mandate takes the salt core out of the Tiejia, since no reactor may fight on Earth. China keeps the tank crewless and puts a diesel where the core was, and the network that drives it registers no difference worth reporting.

nodes.t: The Desert Turbine on six wheels
nodes.x: The Commonwealth sells a truck with every frame: a six-wheeled carrier on the Desert Turbine that runs on anything and can be fixed with anything. Half of Earth's reconstruction rides in one, by Khartoum's reckoning.

nodes.t: Integration duty on tracks
nodes.x: The Union's peace tank carries as many interpreters as gunners. It runs on Quebec hydrogen and is sent wherever the Union's members are pulling apart, which is most of the time.

nodes.t: Russia's heavy tank, back on diesel
nodes.x: With fission banned from Earth's battlefields, the Ascendancy goes back to the name of its first heavy tank and the engine of its siege trains. Its crews are oath-sworn like its pilots, and its augmented gunners are listed as equipment owed to the unit.

nodes.t: A truck the UNEL can switch off
nodes.x: The white squads' trucks draw beamed power from the UNEL's relay, and so never need fuel. Every driver is briefed on the other half of the arrangement, which is that the same relay can stop the truck in the road.

nodes.t: Tanks from three armies, welded into one
nodes.x: When the Andean Federation fails, its warlords rebuild whatever the war left in the mountains, putting American hulls, Pact turrets and Commonwealth turbines on the same chassis. Those who trade in them say no two are alike, and all of them run on cheap fuel shipped down from space.

nodes.t: Carries a rescue frame to the rubble
nodes.x: Under Beijing's protection, Mitsurugi builds rescue vehicles again: a tracked carrier that brings a Kizuna-Go to a collapsed building and powers it while it digs. Rescue work is the one activity in Kansai that no one has the standing to order stopped.

nodes.t: Haulers for the Quebec hydrogen fields
nodes.x: Boreal East builds its ice-road hauler for the Union's hydrogen fields, while Boreal West sells the same design to Washington. The two companies still share a parts catalogue, an arrangement neither has ever formally acknowledged.

nodes.t: A mech hunter for thin air
nodes.x: Brannock-Hale Monterrey revives the Hound for the Bolivian Annexation: a light hunter with a turbocharged engine for the altiplano and missiles that still work at four thousand metres. It is the first new American ground vehicle in a generation.

nodes.t: “Linked Hearts”: an aid convoy with its own power
nodes.x: China's aid arrives as a convoy that powers the town it stops in. During the Cordoba Blackout the Lianxin trucks light hospitals the local grid can't, and the network logs every one of them.

nodes.t: “Mercy”: a refugee bus that is also a clinic
nodes.x: The Commonwealth's carrier for a crowded world has forty seats, a clinic, a water plant and a turbine that runs on anything. It is sold alongside the Gharbi, and given away when the buyer can't pay.

nodes.t: A low-loader for the heaviest frame of 2327
nodes.x: The Keystone is too heavy for any carrier Brannock-Hale already builds, so the company goes back to the oldest line in its catalogue: the frame hauler. The new one has twelve axles and a crane, and it is the same idea as the 2163 original.

nodes.t: Off the relay, back on fuel
nodes.x: The Relay War makes beamed power a liability: a fighter that drinks from a relay can be starved or spoofed. Halcyon gives the Goshawk fuel tanks again and keeps the receiver only for stealing the enemy's power.

nodes.t: The rail-gun fighter over the Bering Strait
nodes.x: Moscow's Alaska advance is covered by Berkuts flying from Chukotka, with their spine rail guns now fed by field reactors on the ground between sorties.

nodes.t: Hunts relays, not fighters
nodes.x: The Union's lance fighter is rebuilt to find and kill the enemy's beamed-power relays, carrying Fenrir swarms that split to hit a whole relay field at once.

nodes.t: The network's strike jet, in thousands
nodes.x: Beijing builds its uncrewed strike jet faster than Moscow can shoot it down, and flies it from the Spratlys to Australia.

nodes.t: Flying the reconstruction in
nodes.x: The Condor comes back as a civil airlifter, carrying bridge sections, water plants and Steward frames into places with no roads left. It burns cheap fuel from the Belt, and there is plenty of it.

nodes.t: Water bombers for a planet still burning
nodes.x: The biosphere is still burning in places, a century after the war. Converted freighters from the Lunar yards drop water and retardant ahead of the Albedo II frames that cut the firebreaks.

nodes.t: Still the plane any air force can afford
nodes.x: The turboprop that hunted frames in the 2180s is still being built in Tangier a century later, now with a turbine that burns anything. Every warlord in the Andes has a few.

nodes.t: Flies escort for the Gyrfalcon
nodes.x: Halcyon's first new fighter in a century, built to fly beside the Gyrfalcon frame from runways and anchorages alike. Washington orders it after watching what a colony could do in 2312.

nodes.t: A strike jet that never runs dry
nodes.x: The network's jet a century on, flown in relays so that some are always overhead. China treats it as a rehearsal for a doctrine in which power no longer limits anything.

nodes.t: Gunships for the South American Front
nodes.x: The Kite and its uncrewed wingmen fight Brazil's push for Africa from the river valleys, low under the crest line where the Brazilian frames can't follow.

nodes.t: Gunships for the siege trains
nodes.x: The Kosatka flies ahead of every siege train, marking targets for the Taran-Fs and refuelling from the train itself.

nodes.t: Rescue tiltrotor for the reconstruction
nodes.x: Halcyon's civil tiltrotor carries an Osprey-C rescue frame slung underneath and drops it beside a flood or a collapse. It is the descendant of the Heron Pit Runner, flying medics where it once flew batteries.

nodes.t: The Ibis again, painted white
nodes.x: The cheapest helicopter in the world is still in production. Most of the new ones go to relief agencies, and the rest go to the Andes.

nodes.t: Gunships over the altiplano
nodes.x: Rebuilt for the thin air of the Bolivian Annexation, with bigger rotors and a turbocharged engine. The Kite line has now been in service for a hundred and sixty years.

nodes.t: Drones by the hundred thousand
nodes.x: Network War means drones in numbers no human could direct: spotters, relays and suicide drones flown as one swarm by Tianshu.

nodes.t: A throwaway jammer for relay fields
nodes.x: The Libelle rebuilt to sit beside an enemy relay and jam it until someone finds it and shoots it.

nodes.t: Sold by the crate in the Andes
nodes.x: The loitering drone is now a commodity, sold by the crate to anyone with a border and assembled from Belt lithium and Earth plastics.

nodes.t: Drones that never land
nodes.x: China's newest swarm recharges in the air from tanker drones, so the network's eyes never close.

nodes.t: Infantry carriers with air in the back
nodes.x: Colony One's first vehicles are American Drover IIs, sealed at Phobos and shipped down. Pressure cabins where the troops sat. Filters that clog in a week. The colony's Red Roster learns to drive them in the war years.

nodes.t: Funkenwerk scout cars with pressure cabins
nodes.x: The Union's Mars station gets Funkenwerk's open-drawing scout cars, rebuilt with pressure cabins. When Strasbourg cuts the station off, its scientists keep them running with spares bought from Colony One.

nodes.t: A crawler you can fix in a tunnel
nodes.x: Dustline's first design. A crawler built from Drover parts, cold cells and whatever else survives the dust. Low enough for the lava tubes, simple enough to rebuild underground.

nodes.t: Measures twice, drives once
nodes.x: Vesta Works' rover for the south is slow, careful and covered in instruments. It charges from the areothermal grid, and its crews log every trip, in full, for the panels.

nodes.t: Pushes rocks, tows ships, gets paid for both
nodes.x: The caravans' workhorse, and a reliable earner: a tug that can push a small asteroid, tow a crippled ship or haul a hold of ice, and that saves on running costs by splitting its fuel and air from the rock it works. Skycut builds them on the old militia tugs' pattern.

nodes.t: Legs for rocks too small to drive on
nodes.x: On an asteroid with almost no gravity, wheels lose grip and tracks float. The cargo walker grips with its feet instead, running on cheap Arsia lithium, and carries a hold's worth of crates across a rock in one trip.

nodes.t: A heated hall on tracks
nodes.x: The Communion's crawlers descend from the Canadian ice-road haulers that carried refugees north in the war. Out in the far dark they are towns on tracks, each with a hall, a hearth, a drive running a century past its rating, and room for everyone.

nodes.t: A transport that is fed, not fuelled
nodes.x: Umoja's transport is partly grown, muscle and grown cells on a salvaged frame, and it is fed rather than fuelled, on ammonia from Ganymede's ice. It descends from the League's ambulance columns and, as the keepers would expect of anything they grow, it still carries the wounded first.

nodes.t: The sworn pair's chariot, rebuilt for Io
nodes.x: The Nashik Rath once carried a sworn pair to the fight. At Europa the Ashva rebuild it for Io's sulphur plains as a shielded rescue rover, big enough for two frames and for the people they pull out of a broken habitat.

nodes.t: An airship that never lands
nodes.x: The Ascendancy's cloud stations at Venus are linked by skiffs that float in the habitable layer and never come down. They run on sunlight above the clouds and carry the sealed Volk-V frames between stations.

nodes.t: Moves a battery along the Red Wall overnight
nodes.x: The MRD's batteries are only as useful as their positions, so Vesta builds a tractor that can move a Hammer of Mars gun along the Red Wall in a single night. Colony One's spotters have not, so far as anyone can tell, found the same battery twice.

nodes.t: An air-droppable rover for Mars
nodes.x: The Rapid Defence Force's light vehicle, dropped from Phobos with the Dropguards. It descends from the Ranger, the air-droppable tank of the 2160s.

nodes.t: Takes a sworn pair to the monster
nodes.x: The Rath-E rebuilt to carry a pair of Nakulas into Jupiter's radiation belts and bring them back.

nodes.t: Small enough for a lava tube, quiet enough to stay there
nodes.x: After the fleet falls, Colony One's partisans drive carts built to disappear: small, cold and slow, carrying tunnel charges and the people who set them.

nodes.t: Armoured cars for a city that hates its garrison
nodes.x: The garrison of the Colony One Bastion drives sealed armoured cars in pairs, never one alone. The First City's people call them the landlords.
