nodes.t: An IFV with Washington's seal on the ignition
nodes.x: The New Philadelphia Arsenal's carrier is American in everything except one part, an ignition lock that opens only with Washington's code. Its crews accept the lock in good faith, as the price of the charter.

nodes.t: Lined with mats that eat the radiation
nodes.x: The Kin Carrier grown once more, this time lined with radiotroph mats that feed on Jupiter's radiation and, in feeding, shield the people inside.

nodes.t: Carries kilometre mirrors across the ice
nodes.x: The Long Mirrors must be carried out in folded sections and raised on the ice, a work that takes a season. The sledges that bear them are the largest vehicles the Communion builds.

nodes.t: A crawler for the catalysed cell's trials
nodes.x: The MRD tests its catalysed fusion cell in the field rather than in a bunker, and publishes every run. The field laboratory carries the cell, its instruments and a crew of six, all of them volunteers.

fleets.label: Fleets & Carriers
fleets.intro: How mechs get to the fight, and the navies that fight beside them, from converted amphibious ships to the orbital lines built after the Lunar Mandate. Where the briefs or the 2312 game give stats, the card shows them: C for combat, F for fighters (frames and fighter craft together) and T for troops.
turns: A reactor is a battery charger
Merlins proved variable frames could land on a carrier deck. The Navy noticed that one carrier reactor could recharge a whole squadron's batteries at once.
Every bloc carries frames its own way
The United States goes by sea, the Pact by rail and ground-effect craft, and the League by mining crawler and old car ferry.
Warships before anyone can use them
The lunar yard builds catapult cruisers for every bloc. Nobody has fought ship to ship yet.
Yernon, and warships in the sky

A single British dreadnought breaks the Russian inner fleet, and every navy spends the next century building dreadnoughts. In the air, the Aerie and the Tsitadel are the first ships built to fight there, and the last: the Lunar Mandate bans them. In orbit, carriers learn to launch fighter craft beside their frames, as every carrier in 2327 still does.
Every power builds its own yards
The Lunar Mandate keeps Luna's slipways for the UN, so the powers build yards in their own orbits, and their ships stop looking alike.
Carriers come back down to the sea

The Mandate bans reactor-lifted ships from Earth's sky and closes the drop lanes, so frames on Earth travel by sea, by rail, by ground-effect craft and by airship again. What goes up goes on licensed rockets, the elevators, or China's accelerator.
Colonies start out with their sponsors' old hulls: American ships on northern Mars, Union ships in the south, Chinese ships in the Belt. Their own designs replace them one class at a time.

In 2312 Colony One fires on the Americans from American hulls, and the MRD breaks it with Union hulls running its own code beside its first Axioms. The Syndicate launches its first carrier the same year.

Colony One's remnant builds where nobody can see it, and the Constitutionalists commission their first hulls. The Earth powers build against the colonies: American frigates to hunt cold hulls, a battleship no cyberweapon can reach, and Chinese torch-hunters for ships that fly without Beijing's licence.

After 2312 the next wars will be fought on Mars and the moons of Jupiter, not between fleets. Carriers learn to land frames: through Mars's thin air, onto airless moons, and down through Europa's ice. Many of them borrow from Earth's sea carriers and from each other.
Every navy is built for what it protects

The Commonwealth sends its Meroë dreadnoughts only when protecting someone means facing a fleet. Umoja's carriers land and grow fortresses, the Syndicate's newest is a debt collector, and the Ascendancy's Sudarshana is built so that no single enemy ship can break its fleet again.
fams: Flight decks that became swap pits.
From cargo airships to the first warships of the sky.
Tenders and catapult ships first, then frames and fighter craft launched together.

profile.t: The Rapier, Ballista, Veyenda, Ironshield, Thunderbreak and Leviathan line on Hampton Roads plants, still the fleet in 2327; Colony One flew the same hulls until 2312. Since the crisis, ships built for the next colonial war: Marshal frigates to hunt cold hulls and the air-gapped Independence. Drop tenders over Phobos and the Bastion. On Earth: the Lexington, a supercarrier on fuel; the Monterrey amphibious ship; and the last helicarriers. For Mars: the Inchon, an assault carrier with the Monterrey's well deck.

A class from each subfaction, from the Dutch Fluyt to the British Dreadnought, on sealed plants from the Malapert docks; the Sovereign at the Trojans; Hanse anchorage ships that turn captured rocks into bases. The MRD still flies some of its old Fluyts and Caravelas. On Earth: the Mare Nostrum for the Union's inland sea, and icebreaker carriers for the Quebec fields. Ostia assault anchorages that bring their own beachhead.

Steppewinds and Windchasers for the outriders, Heixing logistics, and the Longchao, Shendao and Tianqi on network-run plants and Type-40 torches. Since the crisis, Jianwei torch-hunters for unlicensed ships and the Tianmen, a carrier for fusion frames. On Earth: Ciji hospital ships, Kansai's rescue tenders under its flag, and the railway and accelerator that throw cargo into orbit from Darkhan. Pojun assault carriers that throw frames at airless moons.

Bogatyr battleships, Strela pickets and Volga army transports on Kurchatov breeders through the long peace; a Kitezh at Mercury in 2312; Sokol frigates and the Sudarshana, its answer to Yernon, by 2327. On Earth: land fortresses turned into travelling towns, diesel ground-effect carriers, and the Samudra on the monsoon coast. Sadko assault carriers, copied from the Ashva's under-ice ships.

Khamsin escorts from the first relief convoys, then Kafila transports, Safina carriers and Hannibal battleships; Cherguis at Eros in 2312 and the Meroë by 2327. Umoja's ships grew from its hospital ships. On Earth: Bahari relief ferries and Shifa crawler hospitals.

Warden, Arbiter, Providence, Safeguard, Adjudicator and Pillar classes from the lunar yards, which declare a no-fly zone over Mars in 2312 that neither side inside it respects; Assessor cutters that board warships on Earth's approaches to fit the Second Seal. On Earth: the licensed lift shuttles that are the only way up, and Long Lifter airships for towns with no roads.

The Lifeline from its first years, American Rapiers, Ballistas and Veyendas beside its own Ironbounds and Dustwings; the fleet broken in 2312; Wayfinders and the Revenant built since in hidden docks on quiet reactors. Ghostlight landers for raids on Directorate ground.
Contractor-built hulls on American lines: the Liberty and Concordia first, after New Philadelphia, then Madisons, a Federalist and a Resolute built at Hampton Roads and handed over through the 2320s.

Survey cutters first, then inherited Union carriers reworked on Deimos and its own Axioms before the crisis; Redlines, Vanguards and Union hulls on its own code in 2312; the Data-Wing prototype by 2327. Gradient entry tenders to hunt the remnant on Mars.

Chinese hulls on lease, then Skyblades, the Fortune and the Ledger by 2312, the first Goldpurse launched at Ceres that year, and the Plutonian Krillmask. No new battle line since: the caravans spend on exchanges, not hulls, and build only Strongbox carriers for claim enforcement.

Ganymede biocarriers grown from the Hospital Safina's vats and Seedshield pickets before the crisis; Baobab ecologies and Greenwall battleships by 2312; Rainmakers and Harvesters after it, and the Lifetide by 2327. Mbegu seeding carriers that land and grow fortresses on Ganymede and Callisto.

Radiation cutters from the first years at Jupiter, then the Hakobune and Ashva corvettes; Sentinel carriers and Bastion evacuation ships by 2312; Vajra frigates and Kurukshetra battleships after it, and the Perun by 2327, all on exile torches. Antardhara under-ice carriers for Europa's ocean.
Habitat-ships, Reliquaries and Candle couriers on fission drives a century past their rating; the Hearth carrier after the crisis, then Pilgrims and the rare Testament.

nodes.t: Catapults, arresting wires and ninety jets
nodes.x: America's fleet carriers, nuclear-powered and catapult-launched, were built around Halcyon's Gyrfalcons. In the end it was their reactors, more than their flight decks, that shaped what the Navy did with them next.

nodes.t: Variable frames on a carrier deck
nodes.x: Halcyon landed Merlins on a supercarrier to prove they could operate at sea, and they could. The more useful result came from below deck, where one carrier reactor turned out to recharge every battery spine in a squadron at once; a shore base needed hours to do the same.

nodes.t: Supercarrier rebuilt as a floating swap pit
nodes.x: Kestrels don't need catapults, but they do need batteries. The United States rebuilt its supercarriers with swap bays where the catapults had been, charged straight off the reactor, and one carrier can turn around forty Kestrels an hour without a single swap pit ashore.

nodes.t: Reactor-fed point-defence lasers
nodes.x: After Svalbard the Kestrel carriers were refitted for Harriers and given point-defence lasers fed straight from the reactor. Because the power comes off the ship's own plant, the lasers can keep firing for as long as the ship has steam.

nodes.t: Beams reactor power to Harriers overhead
nodes.x: A Harrier carrier with a SKYLINE transmitter on its island, beaming reactor power to any Harrier in line of sight. It does what the ring's relay does, without needing the Republic's permission. The Navy's carriers end up in orbit, but they keep the shape: the Ironshield of 2327 still has a supercarrier's flat deck and point defence fed straight off the reactor, and American doctrine still calls carriers flying citadels.

nodes.t: Well decks, tiltrotors and landing craft
nodes.x: Big-deck amphibious ships carrying marines, tiltrotors and landing craft, with a floodable well deck in the stern.

nodes.t: Garrisons standing in the well deck
nodes.x: Amphibious ships were given raised hangars and a rebuilt well deck so that Garrisons could stand upright. A Garrison can't swim, so landing craft carried them ashore two at a time. Each ship took six frames, and the crew slept in what had been the vehicle deck.

nodes.t: The first ship designed around mechs
nodes.x: Tall hangars, frame-sized lifts, and a well deck Teamsters can wade out of in four metres of water. It lands a full fire-team company with its Drover IIs, then stays offshore as their workshop.

nodes.t: Flat-deck ships Japan won't call carriers
nodes.x: Flat-deck “destroyers” that are carriers in all but name, kept small and defensive by law.

nodes.t: Rescue frames delivered by sea
nodes.x: A helicopter destroyer refitted to carry Kizuna rescue frames to earthquake and tsunami zones. The Japanese public watched mechs walk off a ship on live television and start digging people out of rubble.

nodes.t: Island defence from the sea
nodes.x: A fast landing ship for Japan's outlying islands, with a stern ramp and a frame deck. It put the Hayates into the surf at Yonaguni during the Yaeyama Incidents.

nodes.t: Union amphibious ships for the Mediterranean
nodes.x: Union member navies' helicopter carriers and dock ships, built for evacuations and peacekeeping around the Mediterranean.

nodes.t: Fast ship for a modular task group
nodes.x: A fast roll-on, roll-off hull carrying three lances and every hardpoint module they might need, so that crews can refit the frames during the crossing and the task group arrives already set up for its mission. Union carriers still work this way in 2327: the Luftkogge runs a multinational task group from its bridge, and the Martian Research Directorate's Vanguard refits its fighters between missions.

nodes.t: Icebreaker hull for the Arctic lances
nodes.x: Built for the Arctic seabed dispute, with an icebreaker hull, heated hangars and a reformer plant that refuels BZ-6 stacks from the ship's own diesel, the Polar Carrier was the ship that carried the lance which fought at Svalbard.

nodes.t: A Polar Carrier frozen in for the refugees
nodes.x: When the Canadian Front breaks, the Canadian crew of one Polar Carrier take refugees north rather than home, and let the ice close around the hull in a fjord on Ellesmere Island. The reformer plant and the heated hangars, built to keep a lance warm, keep a town alive instead, winter after winter, on whatever diesel can be found. The survivors call the ship the Hearth, and when their descendants go out into the dark, they carry the name with them and give it to their carriers. (Gen 5, the war's first years.)
nodes.z: Frozen in · its people carry the name into the dark

nodes.t: Bow-ramp ships for the Caspian and Pacific coasts
nodes.x: Pact landing ships: bow ramps, short range, built in numbers.

nodes.t: Tieniu over the beach in Azerbaijan
nodes.x: Landing ships with reinforced decks for kneeling Tieniu, used to put frames on the Caspian coast during the crisis. A Tieniu lying on a ramp can't fire back, and the Merlins took advantage. The losses on the ramps are why the Pact moved its frames another way afterwards.
nodes.z: 2174 · the Pact moves frames by rail and ground-effect instead

nodes.t: Commercial vehicle shipping
nodes.x: Civilian roll-on, roll-off ferries and container ships. Every navy quietly counted them as reserve sealift.

nodes.t: Old car ferries with frames on the car decks
nodes.x: League states buy retired vehicle ferries and carry frames in them along the Red Sea and Gulf coasts, the frames lying down on the car decks between ports. The ferries are cheap and deniable, though there is nothing on them in the way of armour.

nodes.t: A container ship that is secretly a mech base
nodes.x: Grey Lantern's floating base looks like any container ship in any port. Some of its containers are workshops, some are hangars, and two open into a launch rail for Lantern Customs. It's registered under a different flag every year.

nodes.t: Rail-mounted guns and troops
nodes.x: Armoured trains are an old Eurasian habit, kept up because they guard borders across distances no road network covers.

nodes.t: Kneeling Tieniu on armoured flatcars
nodes.x: Tieniu walk slowly and break down often, so the Pact moved them by rail, kneeling on braced flatcars from which they could fire their shoulder cannons straight off the train. The timetables came from Tianshu, a Tianlong logistics program, and this was the first time the Pact let software decide where its frames went.

nodes.t: Trains that feed the fortress belt
nodes.x: A railway behind the fortress belt carries Tieshans, Tiebis and ammunition to whichever sector is under attack. The belt only works because the trains move reserves faster than an enemy can walk, and Tianshu, which writes the timetables, reroutes them faster than any staff officer could.

nodes.t: The flatcars under the tarpaulins
nodes.x: Wide-gauge trains bringing Kalibr-305s, Iskras, MTU-7s and Tsars up to the border. It is the train in the Siege Question's satellite photos, with a 50 m shape under the tarpaulins.

nodes.t: Fission-powered crawler, prototype
nodes.x: A crawler the size of a city block, with a Pamir reactor, two Iskra turrets and a hangar of Mamonts. It has never moved more than a kilometre under its own power, and every bloc's satellites watch it try.

nodes.t: The first that can cross a border
nodes.x: A working Krepost, built for Moscow's push west into Europe. It is slow, close to unstoppable and able to run its Iskras continuously off the reactor, but it can't cross a river until engineers have built it a bridge, and the bridging work tells its enemies exactly where it is going. (Gen 5, the war's first years.)

nodes.t: Where the Grafted Battalions were kept alive
nodes.x: On the North African Front the Safinas stop carrying Haboobs and start carrying the wounded. Their water plants and refineries are given over to culture vats, and the grafts grown from the stolen cultures are fitted in their hangars, well behind the line. Each crawler becomes a sealed little world, keeping its people alive on its own water and its own grown tissue, and every ship Umoja builds afterwards is made to the same pattern. The Commonwealth keeps the name Safina for its carriers, though it rarely mentions what the crawlers grew. (Gen 5, the war's first years.)

nodes.t: Beijing's trains on lines Moscow never mapped
nodes.x: When the Pact splits, the Fortress Belt Railway turns to face west. Steppe outriders guide the trains along lines Moscow's planners never mapped, Tianshu reroutes them faster than the siege trains can follow, and Tieshan companies arrive at fights the Russians thought were days away. Beijing never stops building on the idea, and with the Tian Shan Rail wrecked in the war, it builds the next one where Steppe crews can guard it. In 2327 the line across Mongolia is the Ground to Orbit Accelerator, still run by Steppe crews, and it launches straight to orbit. (Gen 5, the war's first years.)

nodes.t: Bucket-wheel excavators and dragline rigs
nodes.x: Open-cast mining machines weighing thousands of tonnes, crawling a few hundred metres an hour. The largest land machines ever built.

nodes.t: Mining rigs as mobile frame depots
nodes.x: League mining companies parked old crawlers out in the desert and used them as workshops for the militia frames, and the Type-01Q's recoil dampers came out of those workshops.

nodes.t: A mining crawler that carries a battalion
nodes.x: Qadira rebuilt a bucket-wheel crawler as a mobile base, with a hangar for eight Haboobs, a workshop, a water plant and a small refinery. It moves at 3 km/h and hides inside sandstorms, and the League's people come to speak of the Safinas as their capital ships.

nodes.t: Tracked rocket transporters
nodes.x: Huge, slow tracked platforms that carried rockets to the pad, and later carried cargo to the elevator anchors.

nodes.t: A swap point that drives itself
nodes.x: Bulwarks spend their lives seizing swap points, so the Army built one that brings itself: a launch-crawler chassis with Pitwagon bays, a turbine plant, and a Bulwark platoon riding on the roof. It's slow and impossible to hide, so it moves at night.

nodes.t: Lifting-body airships for remote freight
nodes.x: Helium hybrid airships that hauled mining gear to places with no roads. Slow and huge, they could set down on any flat ground.

nodes.t: An airship hangar for four Kestrels
nodes.x: America's first airborne carrier: a hybrid airship with a hangar gondola, swap bays, and turbine-driven fans to hold station. Kestrels launch by dropping out of the hangar and transforming. It's far too slow to survive anti-air fire, so it only works over the sea and empty desert.

nodes.t: The first helicarrier
nodes.x: Four ducted lift fans, turbines that burn fuel at a rate the Navy won't publish, and nine hours aloft. It carries eight Harriers and swaps their packs in the air, but it is a carrier rather than a warship, lightly armed and kept well out of range of any fight. The Navy has built only one.

nodes.t: Lift fans on beamed power
nodes.x: The Rookery refitted with a dorsal rectenna to run its lift fans on SKYLINE power. Under the relay it has stayed up for thirty hours. Outside the beam it has about forty minutes, the same limit the Kestrels it carries have always lived with.

nodes.t: Helicarriers in squadron service
nodes.x: Production helicarriers on HT-20 turbine-capacitor plants, topped up by SKYLINE wherever the relay reaches. Still carriers, not warships: any commander who takes one within range of a Mamont is relieved of command. (Gen 5, the war's first years.)

nodes.t: The first production warship built to fight in the air
nodes.x: A Rookery-class hull with an orbital warship's armour and catapults, lifted and powered by a fusion plant small enough to fly. The United States has never said where the reactor came from, and the procurement file names the supplier only as ██████ ████████ █████. Unlike the Rookeries, it is built to fight: it carries a mass driver and laser batteries, and launches frames straight off its catapults. (Gen 5, the war's last years.)
nodes.z: War's end · the Lunar Mandate bans reactor-lifted ships from Earth's sky

nodes.t: Surplus cargo airships moving Gen 1 frames
nodes.x: League militias bought second-hand cargo airships to move frames across deserts with no roads, and for a while it worked well. The old hands say the trouble started the moment people began shooting at them, and in the Convoy Raids that happened almost at once.
nodes.z: 2176 · too easy to shoot down in the Convoy Raids

nodes.t: Radar balloons over bases and borders
nodes.x: Tethered balloons that lift radars and radio relays high above bases, for far less than any aircraft costs.

nodes.t: OKB-7's Caspian sea-skimmers
nodes.x: Wing-in-ground-effect giants that fly a few metres above the Caspian at 500 km/h, and which are classed with some difficulty, being too low for aircraft and too strange for ships.

nodes.t: Flew Tieniu across the Caspian
nodes.x: A ground-effect craft with a nose door and a reinforced deck for two kneeling Tieniu. In the Caspian Crisis it landed frames on beaches in hours, where the landing ships needed days.

nodes.t: Ground-effect carrier for a Tieshan company
nodes.x: Bigger and faster than the Kaspiy, and armed with rocket racks, a Kaspiy-II can land a Tieshan company on any shore of an inland sea within the hour. It can't climb, though, so it can't cross land, and its war stays on the water.

nodes.t: Fission-powered ground-effect cruiser
nodes.x: A Kaspiy hull with a Pamir reactor driving its fans. With unlimited power it can climb out of ground effect for minutes at a time, Moscow's first craft to fly with frames aboard instead of skimming. Every bloc worries about what happens if one comes down over a city.

nodes.t: Moscow's flying fortress
nodes.x: Kaspiy-Atom lift under a Krepost's armour and Iskra turrets. It flies low and slow, it's very hard to bring down, and it carries a full breakthrough group of Mamonts. If one is ever shot down, a reactor comes down with it. (Gen 5, the war's last years.)
nodes.z: War's end · the Lunar Mandate bans reactor-lifted ships from Earth's sky

nodes.t: “Ark”: a fusion-lifted rescue carrier
nodes.x: The Amaterasu reactor was too big for any normal frame, so Japan built a ship around it. Officially the Hakobune is an unarmed disaster-response ship, with a hospital deck, lift fans and eight rescue frames, though its hangar is also exactly the right size for Takemikazuchi. Its first flight is the one that convinced the other blocs that fusion could fly. (Gen 5, the war's first years.)

nodes.t: The Ark goes north to Vladivostok
nodes.x: When Japan falls into China's sphere, the Hakobune's crew fly it north before Beijing can claim it, with Mitsurugi engineers packed into the hospital deck, and set it down at the company's Vladivostok subsidiary. Moscow wants the reactor. The Nashik pilots want the ship, and in the end Moscow and Delhi let them have it. Under their Oath it stays what it was built to be: unarmed, and sent wherever people need digging out. The Mandate grounds it with every other reactor-lifted ship, so after the war it goes up instead, with the Nashik pilots and the Mitsurugi exiles, to Europa and Io. The Ashva Compact's Sentinel-class carriers are built around its hangar. (Gen 5, the war's last years.)

nodes.t: Tugs and supply craft at the elevators
nodes.x: Small orbital tugs that moved cargo between the elevator tops and the early stations.

nodes.t: Tugs that carry Lifters to the job
nodes.x: Tenders with open cradles for Lifter frames, taking work crews out to new station segments. In the Rivet Strike they became the workers' fleet.

nodes.t: Long-haul carriers for Rigger crews
nodes.x: Larger tenders that take Rigger crews out for weeks on salvage contracts, with a winch bay and crew quarters. The Tether Incident was fought from two of them.

nodes.t: The first warships in orbit
nodes.x: The first dedicated warships, with a mass driver along the spine and catapults for Marlinspike frames. None of them has yet been used in a fight.

nodes.t: Carries frames down, can't climb back
nodes.x: Carries frames down through re-entry, lets them go in the upper atmosphere, and can't get back to orbit on its own. Every atmospheric warship after it copies its armour and catapults. (Gen 5, the war's first years.)
nodes.z: War's end · the Mandate closes the lanes down to Earth

nodes.t: Frames for boarding, fighter craft for the long reach
nodes.x: By the war's last years every orbital fleet has learned the same thing: frames win boarding actions and close fights around stations, but they are too slow for open space. The lunar yards' answer launches both. Marlinspike descendants go off the catapults, small fighter craft off a second deck, and every carrier in 2327 still does the same and counts both as its fighters. After the Lunar Mandate the yards go on building it for the UN, and UNEL's Safeguard is its direct heir. No other power will build in a slipway the UN controls. Each goes back to the yards it started before the war, and within a generation each has carriers of its own: the Ironshield, the Longchao, the Luftkogge and the rest. (Gen 5, the war's last years.)

nodes.t: Armed tenders from the Rivet Strike
nodes.x: After the Rivet Strike the station militias kept their frames, and their tugs and tenders too, with cutting gear and rivet guns bolted on. They were bought for hauling rather than fighting, but they are the nearest thing to an escort in orbit.

nodes.t: Hull sections thrown up the Tian Shan
nodes.x: The Pact's first hulls of its own are built on the ground in sections small enough for the Tian Shan Rail, launched one at a time and bolted together in orbit. They are small, cramped and very cheap per tonne, which is most of their appeal, and both halves of the Pact go on building them through the war until the rail is wrecked.
nodes.z: The war · the rail is wrecked on the Central Asian front, and relaid under inspection after the Mandate

nodes.t: The Union's docks inside the Republic
nodes.x: Through the war the Union's leased docks on Malapert Mountain build frigates to the Union's own designs, under the Lunar Guard's eye. The same docks build the dreadnought that wins at Yernon, and after the Mandate they are the only bloc docks inside UN jurisdiction.

nodes.t: Interceptor and scout, Latin subfaction
nodes.x: A very fast corvette with two light coilguns and missile rails, at its best hunting in wolf packs: screening convoys, marking targets and chasing raiders down. Its Latin-heritage crews paint their hulls, choose dramatic call-signs and fly with more risk than the manuals allow. Colony One never had corvettes of its own, and until 2312 every Rapier it flew was an American hull.

nodes.t: Clandestine rebuild
nodes.x: The first class Colony One's remnant builds in its hidden docks beyond the main lanes. It is a Rapier, rebuilt from memory and from the few that escaped in 2312. None has been deployed openly. The docks are hidden for the same reason: the remnant doesn't want Washington knowing it has a navy again.

nodes.t: Escorts paid for by the megacorporations
nodes.x: The American corporations that kept the war effort supplied buy escorts of their own to guard their shipping. They want hulls that are cheap to run and easy to trust, which is still what the Ballista is.

nodes.t: Dependable escort, Latin subfaction
nodes.x: Three or four medium coilguns, a point-defence grid, and very little that breaks. Corporate fleets ran them through the war because they were cheap to keep, and they are still easy to maintain and easy to trust, if not as tough as Chinese or Union frigates.

nodes.t: Sleek, standardised, corporate-built
nodes.x: The Constitutionalists' first hull, commissioned after New Philadelphia: American-derived, contractor-built, and wired to fight alongside US forces rather than alone.

nodes.t: Raiders under a new flag every voyage
nodes.x: Grey Lantern sells the war a navy of privateers, fast and disguised raiders that hunt anyone's freighters for anyone's fee. The company doesn't last, but its methods do: false transponders, hidden guns and ships that look like something else turn up in half the navies of 2327.

nodes.t: Reactor-fed lasers on a picket hull
nodes.x: The Navy tries pickets armed only with the reactor-fed lasers that once guarded its Harrier carriers. In vacuum they shed heat so slowly that they can fire for minutes, not hours.
nodes.z: Retired · once coilguns got cheap, few navies wanted a ship that had to wait to cool

nodes.t: Deterrence and local defence
nodes.x: A US Navy frigate class built at Hampton Roads and handed over to New Philadelphia hull by hull through the 2320s, refitted for local defence and showing the flag. Like the rest of the Constitutional fleet, it can't be sent to war without Washington's approval.

nodes.t: The Ballista's replacement, built for brickwork repairs
nodes.x: Thick armour that takes patching well, three or four medium coilguns, and a hull built for the fast, ugly fixes Martian yards are good at. Martian crews swear by them. Earth engineers find them alarming. The remnant still builds them in secret.

nodes.t: The Mongolian outriders go up
nodes.x: The Steppe crews who guided Beijing's trains in the Pact Civil War go up through the Ground to Orbit Accelerator. Their light, fast craft scout ahead of China's expeditions into the Belt.

nodes.t: Outrider and scout, Steppe subfaction
nodes.x: Light, very fast and agile, with vectoring built for swarming. It is weaker than American or Union corvettes but better at not being hit, and many have been sold into the Belt, where they work as couriers and are slowly being traded out for Skyblades.

nodes.t: The backbone of the caravan escorts
nodes.x: Two coilguns and a modular rack on a very fast, nimble hull, kept polished like a racehorse. Skyblades guard convoys, hunt pirates and are replacing the Belt's old Steppewinds.

nodes.t: The Belt houses arm their tenders
nodes.x: The Belt's prospecting families bolt guns onto their tenders to stop claim-jumpers, then build faster hulls for nothing else. Every Skyblade crew can name the cutter its house started with.

nodes.t: The most dangerous frigate in the system
nodes.x: Four or five medium coilguns, two micro-fighters or drones, and the speed to flank, strike and leave. Steppe crews treat them like living horses, and the Belt caravans pay well over the odds for any they can buy.

nodes.t: Built to treaty, crewed by many nations
nodes.x: The refounded Union builds escorts that comply with every treaty it signs: low emissions, careful fire control and room for inspectors.

nodes.t: Patrol and picket, Dutch subfaction
nodes.x: Low-emission and careful, with excellent sensor discipline. Fluyts are built to avoid trouble rather than start it. The Union handed some down to the Martian Research Directorate, which keeps them for courier work until its own corvettes are ready. In 2312 the Directorate's Cyclonian group still flies two, one with its Dutch crew.

nodes.t: Long-range scout frigate, Portuguese subfaction
nodes.x: Four medium coilguns and very good navigation. It is less deadly than a Windchaser, but steadier and more economical with fuel, and the Martian Research Directorate uses the Caravelas the Union handed down to fill out its screens until there are enough Redlines.

nodes.t: Patrol beyond the Moon, with a stateroom for an envoy
nodes.x: Paris's frigate for the anchorages beyond the Moon: four coilguns, a long sensor mast and a stateroom for whichever envoy it is carrying. Its officers dine in full dress every night of a six-month patrol. Near Mars the Directorate's ships shadow it, politely, and log everything.

nodes.t: Calculation-first skirmisher
nodes.x: The Directorate's own frigate: fast, cold-running, and built around predictive fire control that improves the longer it watches a target. Its captains tend to come from orbital mechanics and prefer simulated duels to live drills. The first Redlines of 2312 have a sensor-integration fault that leaves their armour unreliable; the Vesta analysis sectors refit the class that year, and the Zephyria yard turns from mining hulls to build another.

nodes.t: Armed tugs on the Orbital Front
nodes.x: In the war every fleet needs ships cheaper than a cruiser to watch the lanes, chase raiders and screen convoys. The lunar yards build armed pickets by the hundred, and most escort classes still in service in 2327 descend from them.

nodes.t: The lunar crews' pickets, under the UN
nodes.x: After the Lunar Mandate the lunar crews' pickets become the UN's patrol fleet. They enforce exclusion zones and escort relief convoys between Earth and Luna.

nodes.t: Orbital patrol, Earth subfaction
nodes.x: The backbone of UNEL's patrols, built to intercept unsafe traffic and to stop other people's fights from spreading. Its crews are drawn for the most part from civil-service families.

nodes.t: Exclusion-zone enforcer, Luna subfaction
nodes.x: Three precision coilguns, ablative plating and a thermal damping suite for working in lunar shadow. Arbiters are built to end fights, not chase them. In 2312 Arbiters hold station at the edge of the no-fly zone the UNEL declares over Mars, which is recorded as being largely disregarded by both sides fighting inside it.

nodes.t: Escort for relief convoys
nodes.x: A fast escort for relief convoys and evacuation lanes, named, like the Tunis Works frames, for a desert wind.

nodes.t: Patrol frigate with a hospital bay
nodes.x: The Chergui guards shipping lanes and outlying settlements, and carries the kind of hospital bay most navies would give to a transport. In 2312 the Commonwealth battlegroup sent to watch the Union at Eros is screened by Cherguis.

nodes.t: Picket and courier
nodes.x: Fast and lightly armed, sent ahead of every Ascendancy formation.

nodes.t: The first ships built for Jupiter
nodes.x: The Nashik exiles' first warships at Europa and Io are cutters, armoured against Jupiter's radiation more than against any weapon. In those first years they pull crews out of failing habitats far more often than they fight.

nodes.t: Raider-hunter
nodes.x: Escorts convoys along the Ascendancy's extraction routes and hunts the raiders who prey on them.

nodes.t: Habitat picket
nodes.x: A small picket that guards Umoja's habitats and seed shipments, and tends its own damage: its hull composites heal the way its crews do.

nodes.t: Biological security patrol
nodes.x: Umoja's patrol frigate, with sealed life-support and quarantine bays. Its first job is keeping anything alive and uninvited away from Ganymede.

nodes.t: Route patrol, named for the sworn pilots
nodes.x: Armoured for radiation and debris, and sent to anyone in trouble on the Jovian routes. The class takes its name from the Nashik pilots' oath name for themselves.

nodes.t: Convoy defence
nodes.x: A heavy frigate for convoy defence and route control, built with the endurance to stay on station through Jupiter's radiation for as long as a convoy needs it there.

nodes.t: Stealthy courier
nodes.x: A cold-running courier that carries messages and pilgrims between the Communion's scattered habitats, passing through the dark without being seen.

nodes.t: Insulated long-range escort
nodes.x: A sparse, cold-hardened frigate built for very long voyages, far from any dock and far from any light. Pilgrims rarely travel together, and few captains outside the Communion have seen more than one at a time.

nodes.t: Cargo between the elevator tops, the Moon and Mars
nodes.x: Ascension's freighters, then the Republic's and the blocs', move cargo from the elevator tops to the stations and the Moon. One of them carried Colony One's settlers to Mars.

nodes.t: Keeping the Moon and Mars supplied
nodes.x: Through the war the lunar crews keep freighters running to Luna and to a colony on Mars that Earth has stopped paying attention to. Colony One grows up on what they bring.

nodes.t: Modular hauler, Latin subfaction
nodes.x: Found everywhere from Luna to the Belt, with deeply modular cargo, troop and science bays. Its name is a corruption of leyenda. Colony One fits its Veyendas out as homes.

nodes.t: Contractor-built logistics
nodes.x: The Constitutionalists' transport, among their first hulls, built and serviced by the American contractors who run most of their logistics.

nodes.t: The ships that put Colony One on Mars
nodes.x: Landers built in Ascension's last years set Colony One down in the north, and an unannounced camp in Melas Chasma months later. Colony One's own transports are still built around their life support.

nodes.t: The mother ship of Colony One's fleet
nodes.x: Long-duration life support and sealed biosystems tuned to Martian physiology, for moving troops and habitats and evacuating the wounded. Crews paint settlement murals on its walls.

nodes.t: Belt water, routed by Tianshu
nodes.x: Automated haulers bring Belt ice and ore inward on routes Tianshu plans years ahead. Their crews are few and their holds are huge, and when one wears out, someone always buys the hull.

nodes.t: “Black Star”: the backbone of Chinese logistics
nodes.x: Highly automated cargo and troop handling lets it run on a reduced crew. In the Belt it is the most common bulk hauler, carrying ore, migrants and whole clans in cramped quarters.

nodes.t: Aid and reconstruction, French subfaction
nodes.x: Built for habitability and crew welfare rather than for capacity, and often sailing with more inspectors aboard than soldiers, the Fusilier is a transport for aid and reconstruction work. The Martian Research Directorate uses the Fusiliers the Union handed down to run between its settlements.

nodes.t: An army moved at once
nodes.x: A bulk transport for troops, colonists and their machines. It inherits the siege trains' job of moving a whole army at once.

nodes.t: Reconstruction cargo for a damaged Earth
nodes.x: The UN's first new hulls after the Mandate carry reconstruction cargo, refugees and relief down to Earth's orbit. Their crews take to calling them arks.

nodes.t: UNEL's humanitarian flagship class
nodes.x: Carries troops, refugees, medical cargo or reconstruction modules, with the best environmental control in the system and almost no guns. Earth crews call Providences arks, after the relief ships before them.

nodes.t: Armoured evacuation ship
nodes.x: Heavily armoured for radiation and debris, and built to get a whole habitat's people out when something breaks. The first come off the slips at Europa in 2312, the year the Ascendancy and the Commonwealth open their joint anchorage there.

nodes.t: Water, feedstock, refugees, whole communities
nodes.x: Named for the League convoys that kept the Jinn supplied, as people on the routes are quick to remind newcomers. It moves water, feedstock, refugees and, when it has to, whole communities.

nodes.t: A sealed ecology that travels
nodes.x: A transport that carries its own biosphere, so colonists, crops and livestock arrive alive across Jovian distances.

nodes.t: Anything that will fly, leaving Earth
nodes.x: After the war, those who no longer trust any government on Earth leave it in whatever will reach orbit and keep them alive: old freighters, worn-out ice haulers, stripped transports. Among them go the descendants of the ice communities.

nodes.t: A wandering habitat-ship
nodes.x: Part transport and part settlement, the Reliquary can survive for years in the dark with no outside support. What it carries is often holy as well as useful.

nodes.t: The lunar crews' carriers, under the UN
nodes.x: After the Lunar Mandate the yards go on building the mixed-wing design for the UN alone, with interceptor bays and room for relief cargo.

nodes.t: Peacekeeping carrier, Luna subfaction
nodes.x: Modular bays for interceptors, aid drones and research craft. Less armoured than an Ironshield but far more efficient, and crewed by lunar flyers proud of precise flying and minimal waste.

nodes.t: The Navy's flat deck goes to orbit
nodes.x: Barred from Earth's sky and unwilling to rent Luna's slipways, the United States builds its carriers at Hampton Roads, the orbital dockyard it started before the war, and builds them to look like the supercarriers they replace.

nodes.t: Fortress carrier, core fleet
nodes.x: Built to survive everything except subtlety, with dense point defence and the largest fighter wing in the system. It deliberately echoes the old supercarriers: flat deck, rugged angles, industrial pride. In 2312 the Resolute Dawn leads the Eagle's Reach battlegroup to a messy draw with the Union at the Trojans.

nodes.t: Corporate-integrated carrier
nodes.x: An American carrier design built at Hampton Roads for New Philadelphia, with contractor-built support systems and command architecture for working alongside US forces. It is meant for deterrence and political signalling rather than a war it fights alone, and in 2327 the first is still working up.

nodes.t: Fighters run on beamed power
nodes.x: A carrier whose fighters fly on power beamed from orbital relays: the SKYLINE idea taken into space. It needs fewer fuel stores and far more trust in the relays.
nodes.z: Abandoned · a carrier that needs a relay can be switched off from somewhere else

nodes.t: Surplus war hulls refitted for Mars
nodes.x: Colony One's first carriers are worn-out war hulls the Americans no longer wanted, refitted at Phobos. They eat parts and crew. Colony One can't keep them forever, so it designs the Dustwing to replace them.

nodes.t: Half an Ironshield, built for Mars
nodes.x: A compact carrier with fewer crew, simpler repairs and room to double as a lab or a transport, built from Phobos Forgeworks frames. The remnant still builds them in secret. “We don't need to outgun Earth. We just need to outlast it.” In 2312 Colony One has two, and American analysts rate them well below their own carriers; the Pale Horizon is lost when the MRD fires into the colony's fleet from behind.

nodes.t: Tianshu-run decks
nodes.x: China's first carriers are built in sections on the ground, launched by rail and built around Tianshu: fewer crew, more drones, and rotation control the American ships never match.

nodes.t: “Dragon Nest”: balanced and crew-efficient
nodes.x: Less armoured than an Ironshield but more adaptable, with fourteen to sixteen fighters or strike drones and exceptional rotation control.

nodes.t: Carriers with no pilots aboard
nodes.x: Beijing's first answer to fighter craft is a tender full of Tianshu-flown drones. The drones perform well, but the tenders prove fragile, and their drone bays are moved into the Longchao, where strike drones still share the deck with piloted fighters.

nodes.t: Holds big enough to be hangars
nodes.x: Emptied of ore, a Belt carrier's hold can take a whole squadron, and the caravans were carrying their own fighters in them long before anyone thought to call the result a carrier.

nodes.t: Carriers as markets and courts
nodes.x: Chinese carriers traded into the Belt to settle debts become caravan flagships: mobile markets, arbitration courts and convoy commands in one hull. The houses value the hangar space rather more than the fighters.

nodes.t: A home away from home for Syndicate pilots
nodes.x: Huge hangars and room for a large marine complement, paid for with armour. The Goldpurse lets its money do the talking. The first launches at Ceres in 2312, paid for with the profits of the Syndicate's lithium inspections, and joins the Azure Coin caravan, although the Belt's real prestige carriers are still the old Longchaos.

nodes.t: Command ships first, carriers second
nodes.x: The refounded Union builds carriers to run multinational task groups, the way its Lance Transports once ran a lance. Each one carries a fleet staff before it carries fighters.

nodes.t: Mid-weight carrier, German subfaction
nodes.x: Reliable, sometimes over-engineered, and fitted with a strong defensive grid, the Luftkogge is treated by Union doctrine as a command centre first and a weapons platform second, which is how the Union has preferred to run its task groups since the Lance Transports.

nodes.t: A command carrier that is also a court
nodes.x: Berlin's flagship class, named for the palaces medieval emperors moved between: a Luftkogge's command architecture grown to a size that needs a protocol office. Its fighters are excellent and its receptions are better. Each carries a German admiral's whole household, and every other nation's officers measure their standing by where they are seated at dinner.

nodes.t: Handed-down Luftkogges, reworked on Deimos
nodes.x: As the Union builds new carriers it hands its colony the old ones, and the Martian Research Directorate spends decades learning what it would change: the hangars, the refit system and the command architecture.

nodes.t: The thinking carrier
nodes.x: Adaptive hangars reconfigure its fighters between missions, and layered energy shielding stands in for armour. Its decks feel halfway between a warship and a research lab.

nodes.t: Prototype
nodes.x: The Martian Research Directorate's next carrier, still in prototype. The Directorate's remaining Luftkogges are to be phased out in its favour.

nodes.t: Lunar hulls refitted for evacuation
nodes.x: The Commonwealth's first carriers are bought from the lunar yards and refitted with hospital decks and water plants, much as the Safina crawlers were refitted before them.

nodes.t: Named for the League's capital ships
nodes.x: Built like the mining crawlers it is named for, with hangars, workshops, a water plant and a hospital deck. Its fighters fly cover for evacuations as often as they fight.

nodes.t: Grown as much as built
nodes.x: Umoja's first carriers grow out of the Commonwealth's relief carriers and out of the grafting knowledge that went to Jupiter, and their hulls mend themselves.

nodes.t: A carrier that feels like an organism
nodes.x: Self-repair systems, biotech composites and sealed ecological architecture. Its doctrine is habitat defence, but its hangars hold units other powers find hard to look at.

nodes.t: The Tsitadel's doctrine, in orbit
nodes.x: Grounded by the Mandate, Moscow's fortress idea goes up: a carrier that keeps its fighters inside its armour.

nodes.t: A fortress that carries its fighters inside
nodes.x: Named for the legendary city that sank beneath a lake rather than be taken, and built on the assumption that it might have to do the same, with an escape craft for every crew member. In 2312 a Kitezh leads the Eurasian battlegroup that destroys the abandoned Indian station at Mercury.

nodes.t: The Ark that went up
nodes.x: The Hakobune never flies in Earth's sky again after the Mandate, but it reaches Europa with the Nashik pilots and the Mitsurugi exiles. Its hangar is still the Compact's model for a carrier.

nodes.t: Built around the Hakobune's hangar
nodes.x: A carrier for rescue, convoy defence and habitat security, armoured for Jupiter's radiation. When one arrives, people believe someone might hold the line.

nodes.t: Whole communities in the dark
nodes.x: The ice communities' descendants leave in habitat-ships that carry everything they need, and go a long way from anyone else. Their first carriers are simply habitat-ships with hangars added.

nodes.t: Named for the carrier frozen in at Ellesmere
nodes.x: A long-range habitat-carrier for the coldest places in the system. The Communion names it after the Polar Carrier that kept its ancestors alive through the winters at Ellesmere.

nodes.t: Mass-driver battleships for whoever is buying
nodes.x: The lunar yards stretch the catapult cruisers into line ships with heavier mass drivers and sell them to any side that can pay. It is a good trade while it lasts, though by the second year of the war every great power is building its own.

nodes.t: Guns over boarding strength
nodes.x: The first battleships from America's own yards: heavy coilguns, heavy armour and small troop decks.

nodes.t: America's line-of-battle workhorse
nodes.x: Six to eight heavy coilguns, extreme durability, and a smaller troop deck than the Martian Research Directorate's or the Union's ships. Unofficial motto: “Steel over silicone. Fire over finesse.” Colony One flew a few as escorts until 2312, when the colony turned them on the Falcon Meridian battlegroup, led by the Thunderbreak Red Meridian.

nodes.t: The Constitutional capital ship
nodes.x: A modernised American battleship design, laid down at Hampton Roads for New Philadelphia and built for deterrence and interoperability with US forces. By 2327 only the first has been handed over.

nodes.t: The remnant's hidden capital ship
nodes.x: Rebuilt in the Black Docks on the hull of the war wreck Silas Vane claimed in the Belt in 2312, which is the only way the remnant could have afforded a capital ship. It is kept in the docks, and the remnant has never risked bringing it into the open.

nodes.t: Precision over weight
nodes.x: Beijing's battleships trade weight of fire for Tianshu-coordinated precision and good frigate screens.

nodes.t: “Divine Blade”: the finesse battleship
nodes.x: Six heavy coilguns and a precision-targeting suite. It hits softer than other battleships, and Chinese doctrine makes up the difference with AI-coordinated fire and better frigates. Wealthy Belt clans keep a few as prestige ships.

nodes.t: The Syndicate's first true capital ship
nodes.x: Strong enough to deter raids, cheap enough for a rich caravan, and modular enough to refit for trade war. Only the richest caravans can afford one, and they make sure everyone knows it.

nodes.t: Guns hidden in the cargo holds
nodes.x: Caravans tired of raiders fit heavy guns inside ordinary freighters and wait to be attacked. The Fortune's modular trade-war refits come from them.

nodes.t: Fleet cohesion over bravado
nodes.x: Balanced line ships with strong mid-range firepower, built to fight as part of a fleet.

nodes.t: Dependable line ship, Spanish subfaction
nodes.x: Thick forward plating and good endurance. It has less punch than a Thunderbreak but is easier to keep running, and the Martian Research Directorate uses the Galeóns the Union handed down for shows of force.

nodes.t: The most accurate battleship in the system
nodes.x: Built to set the geometry of a fight from stand-off range, with targeting that several Axioms can share in real time. Its captains are austere and almost devout about optimal solutions. The first Axioms are built at Zephyria and Deimos decades before the crisis, which is why the Directorate's captains know the class so well by 2312. That year the Directorate brings a second Axiom, the Spigen Halt, online with parts salvaged from a Third World War wreck and a thin crew from the Settled Equation, and both ships fight the civil war short-handed.

nodes.t: Presence, not fear
nodes.x: The UN's battleships exist to anchor negotiations and declare jurisdiction, and are built to last rather than to trade blows.

nodes.t: A mobile courtroom
nodes.x: Six heavy coilguns, very clean exhaust and systems built for long deployments. Its captains often come from diplomacy or civil government.

nodes.t: Armour forward, civilians behind
nodes.x: The Commonwealth's first battleships are built around a simple duty of care: hold a position while the civilians get clear behind them.

nodes.t: The Commonwealth's line of battle
nodes.x: The Hannibal carries its heaviest armour forward and is built to hold a position for as long as it takes the civilians behind it to get clear.

nodes.t: Habitat defence
nodes.x: Umoja's capital ship, built to stand between its habitats and anything that threatens their ecology.

nodes.t: Broken at Yernon
nodes.x: Moscow's line ships, assembled in orbit from sections thrown up the Tian Shan Rail, hold the inner lanes until the Battle of Yernon, where a single British dreadnought breaks them. The Ascendancy builds every battleship since with that day in mind.

nodes.t: America's first hulls from its own yard
nodes.x: The first American hulls from Hampton Roads come out in the war's last year, after Yernon has already been fought. Every American line ship and carrier since has come out of the same yard.

nodes.t: The Krepost idea, in orbit
nodes.x: After Yernon, Moscow's planners build the biggest guns they can on hulls that barely move: siege monitors to hold the lanes.
nodes.z: Scrapped · too slow to catch anything that could run

nodes.t: Slow, and very hard to kill
nodes.x: Named for the warrior heroes of Russian epic, the Bogatyr is heavily compartmented and slow, and from every station aboard there is a way out.

nodes.t: Named for the field of the great war
nodes.x: A heavily armoured battleship for decisive intervention on the Jovian routes, named for the battlefield of the Mahabharata. Few are built: a compact of a few hundred thousand people can crew only so many.

nodes.t: The Communion's rare heavy ship
nodes.x: Cold-hardened and long-ranged, the Testament keeps to the Communion's own reaches and is seldom seen outside them.

nodes.t: The ship that won Yernon
nodes.x: A British dreadnought from the Union's Malapert docks arrives alone at the Battle of Yernon, with Berlin under siege, and breaks the Russian inner fleet. The Union, written off since the European Front, is a great power again, and every navy wants dreadnoughts of its own.

nodes.t: The Senior Service has no rival in the void
nodes.x: Ten to twelve heavy guns, long-range precision cannon and a dense point-defence grid. The British kept the name to remind humanity who invented the concept. The Martian Research Directorate keeps the Dreadnoughts the Union handed down indefinitely. In 2312 the Sovereign anchors the Rhine Shield taskforce, which shatters the Trojan pirates in one pass and fights the Americans to a draw at the Trojans.

nodes.t: London's answer to every other capital
nodes.x: Named for the dreadnought that anchored the Rhine Shield in 2312: twelve heavy guns, a spinal rail cannon and a flag deck panelled in wood that cost more than the guns. The British built it because Paris had begun a dreadnought of its own, and Paris finished its own because the British had. No first among equals, and two of everything.

nodes.t: Sent only when protecting someone means facing a fleet
nodes.x: Named for the ancient capital of Kush, downriver from Khartoum, and built only in small numbers.

nodes.t: Dreadnoughts built in a hurry
nodes.x: Within a decade of Yernon every navy has rushed out dreadnoughts of its own. The American ones are the biggest and the worst: heavy, unreliable and expensive to crew.
nodes.z: Scrapped · under UNEL arms reduction, which few navies minded by then

nodes.t: Sustained fire, fielded in numbers
nodes.x: Eight to ten ultra-heavy coilguns and a spinal rail cannon. Less monstrous than Union or Chinese dreadnoughts, but more versatile. Every crew member must be unmodified. Colony One runs its few sparingly.

nodes.t: “Heaven's Fury”: a monastic artillery temple
nodes.x: Ten to twelve ultra-heavy coilguns tuned with AI targeting harmonics. Its crews take cognitive optimisation to work with the targeting AI. Some have ended up in the Belt through debt settlements.

nodes.t: A bank vault and a courtroom
nodes.x: Built for long, lonely voyages as a trade-route anchor and neutral court. It has three bridges: one to fly the ship, one to count the money, and one to negotiate marriages.

nodes.t: Lunar guardians that never leave
nodes.x: The UN's first heavy ships are monitors parked over Luna's poles, watching the lanes from fixed stations. The Pillar is what they become once someone decides they should be able to move.

nodes.t: Slow, immovable, hard to overwhelm
nodes.x: Hardened lunar composites, a spinal coil projector and the Custodian Array, a long-duration monitoring suite named for the lunar yard's giant. Its crews are almost monastic.

nodes.t: The answer to Yernon
nodes.x: Named for Vishnu's discus, and built so that no single enemy ship can break an Ascendancy fleet again.

nodes.t: Umoja's largest living ship
nodes.x: Dense with self-repair systems and sealed ecological architecture. Few powers want to find out what its hangars hold.

nodes.t: The Compact's heaviest ship
nodes.x: Named for the Slavic thunder god, and built to hold the Jovian line when nothing smaller can. It is the largest thing the Compact has ever built, and there is only one.

nodes.t: American hulls that changed flags in July 2312
nodes.x: When Colony One turns on the United States, American ships with Martian crews go with it, and the South American crew of the Rapier Quick Ember stays with the colony. They join the colony's own Rapiers, all of them American-built. Almost all are lost when the MRD fires into the colony's fleet from behind; the few that get away carry the drawings the remnant builds from.
nodes.z: Lost · broken in the first engagement; the survivors run for the hidden docks

nodes.t: Fluyts, Caravelas and Fusiliers, rewritten in Vesta
nodes.x: The Directorate still flies the Union ships handed down to it, some with their Dutch and Portuguese crews. In 2312 Ana Lubov's Innovation Bureau rewrites their fire control and sensor software to MRD standards rather than rebuild them: cheaper than new hulls, and impossible for Brussels to reach into. The Cyclonian group fights the civil war in them.

nodes.t: The boarding party that fits the Second Seal, on Earth's approaches
nodes.x: After the Weapons Resolution, UNEL inspectors need to board warships whose crews would rather they didn't. The Assessor is a small, fast cutter with a docking collar, a team of seal engineers and an armed escort section, sent to fit the Second Seal to every licensed plant on the approaches to Earth and the Moon and to check it afterwards. Navies that signed let it dock there. Past lunar orbit it has no right to board anyone; when it asks, it is kept at a distance, and the Assessors log who refused.

nodes.t: The Rapid Defence Force's ride down
nodes.x: The Mandate closed the drop lanes to Earth, not to Mars. The Rapid Defence Force keeps a handful of small tenders that do one thing: put a lance of Dropguards down fast. In July 2312 they carry the Force onto Phobos in a single pass. After the war they hang over the Bastion, so the city never forgets how quickly the Americans can arrive.

nodes.t: A dock that turns a captured rock into a base
nodes.x: The Union's lesson from the Trojans is that, to act beyond Luna, it needs not a colony but somewhere to dock. The Hanse is a dock with engines, carrying its own air plant, repair shops and garrison, built to latch onto a captured asteroid and make an anchorage of it within a week. Two hold the Mars Trojans, and a third waits at Luna for whatever the Union decides to anchor next.

nodes.t: Black hulls from Pluto
nodes.x: Built at Pluto by the descendants of the Far Lift, out of what the first settlers brought and what they could mine, and armoured for a place where nobody would ever come to help. Only one is known in the inner system: the LL Krillmask, which arrives at Ceres in 2312 with a refugee crew and joins the Syndicate's Azure Coin caravan in exchange for a refit. Its crew have little combat experience, and the ship is very hard to kill.

nodes.t: The Directorate's first hulls of its own
nodes.x: Before it can afford warships, the Directorate builds survey cutters: small, cold-running hulls that map Mars from orbit and spend years watching the same patch of sky. They site the Deimos array, and they teach a generation of MRD crews to fight by measuring first. The Redline is what they become once the Directorate decides it needs guns.

nodes.t: Built to find ships nobody admits exist
nodes.x: Washington knows the remnant is building somewhere, and that the next colony it fights will have designs of its own. The Marshal is the Navy's answer: a frigate with long-baseline passive sensors for hunting cold, quiet hulls like the Wayfinder, and a crew drawn only from the mainland, in line with the Navy's post-2312 rule that keeps Martians off American warships.

nodes.t: Air-gapped against the next Hasta
nodes.x: The Navy watched Project Hasta switch off Colony One's guns in a morning. The Independence answers it: fire control wired by hand with nothing networked that a cyberweapon can reach, and enough armour and speed to close inside an Axiom's stand-off range rather than duel it there. It is slower to aim than a Thunderbreak and much harder to blind.

nodes.t: Torch-hunter
nodes.x: Beijing licenses its fusion torch to no one, and by the 2310s ships on unlicensed exile torches are flying beyond the Belt and Syndicate caravans are outrunning the Windchaser. The Jianwei is built to catch both: a long-legged frigate on twin Type-40 torches, with the Steppe crews' boarding decks. China still calls the Syndicate a partner, and builds the Jianwei regardless.

nodes.t: “Heaven's Gate”: a deck for fusion frames
nodes.x: The Goldpurse showed Beijing that its client could put more fighters in space than a Longchao. The Tianmen is China's reply, laid down to carry the first frames on Tianlong's fusion core: fewer of them, but frames that never run out of power. In 2327 it is on trials, and every navy is watching its hangar.

nodes.t: The Navy's flat deck without a reactor
nodes.x: The Mandate keeps reactors off Earth's battlefields, and the Navy decides the sea counts. Its first post-war supercarrier burns cheap fuel shipped down from the Belt, carries quiet Peregrine flyers instead of Harriers, and tops up from a tanker every ten days.

nodes.t: Amphibious ship for permanent presence, Latin subfaction
nodes.x: Brannock-Hale Monterrey's frame assault ship carries Vaqueros and a hospital deck to wherever Washington means to stay. Its crews are mostly Mexican and Central American, and its first long deployment is the Andean border.

nodes.t: Rescue ships under a protector's flag
nodes.x: Kansai builds rescue tenders again, flying Beijing's protection flag beside its own. Their Kizuna-Go frames dig out flood towns from Kyushu to the Philippines, and Beijing has so far raised no objection.

nodes.t: “Mercy”: a hospital ship with a flight deck
nodes.x: China takes Japan's rescue-tender idea and builds it at scale: hospital ships with a deck of Tieniu-Min frames and a hold of water plants, sent wherever a disaster opens a door. The aid is genuine, and the influence that arrives with it is planned for.

nodes.t: A carrier for the Union's inland sea
nodes.x: The Union's lance transport grows into a carrier for the Mediterranean, where most of the Union's members meet and most of its quarrels start. It carries Bastides, interpreters and a court-martial room.

nodes.t: Icebreaker carrier for the Quebec fields
nodes.x: The Polar Carrier line comes back after a century and a half: an icebreaker hull carrying the Narwhal ice-and-ocean frames that guard the Union's hydrogen fields in the Gulf of St Lawrence.

nodes.t: “Ocean”: a carrier for the monsoon coast
nodes.x: India's coast was raided for a decade before the war, and the Ascendancy does not forget it. The Samudra carries Gaja monsoon frames along the coast in the storm season, when nothing else can land.

nodes.t: Refugee ferries that can carry frames
nodes.x: The League's ferry carriers become the Commonwealth's relief fleet: car ferries with clinics on the car decks and a few frames below, so that when a ferry arrives there is something to dig people out with.

nodes.t: A land fortress turned into a travelling town
nodes.x: The Mandate takes the reactors out of the Krepost crawlers. Moscow strips their guns too and sends them east as towns on tracks, carrying schools, clinics and a garrison to settlements the war left without any.

nodes.t: “Healing”: a hospital that drives to the people
nodes.x: The Hospital Safina's heirs carry no grafts and no frames, only beds, surgeries and water. They drive the Commonwealth's influence across Africa one town at a time.

nodes.t: Trains that feed the Darkhan accelerator
nodes.x: The Steppe railheads become a freight line into Mongolia, carrying payloads, frames and fuel to the foot of the accelerator. The trains are crewless and the timetable is Tianshu's.

nodes.t: Lift fans on kerosene, and short legs
nodes.x: Beamed power belongs to the UNEL after the war, so the helicarrier loses its relay. The Rookery-F flies on fuel instead, carries half the frames, and stays up for a day at most. The Navy keeps a few for disaster work and never builds another.
nodes.z: Gen 6 · fuel can't keep a helicarrier up long enough to matter

nodes.t: An airship that carries a frame to a town with no roads
nodes.x: The reconstruction needs frames in places with no runway and no road left. The UNEL's airships carry one frame each, slung underneath, and set it down beside a broken dam or a burning forest.

nodes.t: The sea-skimmer, without the reactor
nodes.x: With the fission Kaspiy banned, OKB-7 goes back to diesel ground-effect carriers for the Caspian and the Black Sea. They are slower than the Atom, and they carry no reactor for anyone to worry about.

nodes.t: Chemical rockets again: the only way off Earth the Mandate allows
nodes.x: The Mandate closes the drop lanes and bans reactor-lifted ships from Earth's sky, so everything that leaves Earth goes up on chemical rockets or the elevators. Every launch needs a UNEL licence, and every frame aboard is listed on it.

nodes.t: Payloads thrown up a mountain
nodes.x: China's answer to the Mandate's launch licences is a mass accelerator up a Mongolian mountainside, powered by a salt grid no human runs. It throws sleds of cargo and folded frames into orbit by the thousand, each one licensed, and each one cheaper than any rocket.

nodes.t: Down through Mars's air to find what's hiding
nodes.x: The Directorate knows the Colony One remnant is building somewhere on Mars, so it needs a way to put frames down fast. The Gradient is a Vanguard's adaptive hangar on a blunt aeroshell. It drops through the thin air on its heat shield, lets its frames out on retro packs a few kilometres up, and climbs back to Deimos for the next drop. Its first crews learned entry on inherited Fusiliers.

nodes.t: Cold hulls that land, strike and are gone
nodes.x: The remnant can't fight the Directorate's fleet, so it strikes on the ground. Ghostlights are Dustwing hangars stripped down to a quiet reactor and a drop cradle, built in the same hidden docks as the Wayfinder. Each one sets a pair of frames down beside a Directorate relay or depot and lifts again before anyone in orbit has a firing solution.

nodes.t: “Undercurrent”: a sea carrier that melts its way into Europa
nodes.x: Europa's ocean lies under twenty kilometres of ice, and whoever holds the ocean holds the moon. The Antardhara lands on the ice and lets its torch's waste heat melt it down the shaft into the water, where it works as a submarine carrier for frames built to swim. Its hull is a Sentinel's radiation armour. Its hangar comes from Kansai's rescue tenders, and its shaft-and-keel design from the Union's old Polar Carrier, bought as drawings from a Quebec yard.

nodes.t: “Breaker of Armies”: frames thrown at airless moons
nodes.x: China learned at Darkhan that it is cheaper to throw a payload than to fly it. The Pojun carries a spinal accelerator that fires frames down at an airless moon or a Belt rock on a ballistic track, and each frame brakes on cold-gas packs before it lands. A Longchao's hangar keeps it fed, and Steppe boarding decks let it take a habitat after the frames take the ground around it.

nodes.t: The Monterrey's well deck, rebuilt for Mars
nodes.x: The Phobos tenders can land a lance; the Navy wants to land a regiment. The Inchon takes the Monterrey's amphibious layout off the sea and into orbit: a well deck of heat-shielded drop pods, a hospital deck, and the guns to keep a landing zone clear from orbit. Washington doesn't say out loud what it's for, though on Mars it hardly needs saying.

nodes.t: A fortress that goes down to the sea king
nodes.x: Named for the minstrel who went down to the sea king's hall and came back. At the joint anchorage at Europa the Ascendancy watched the Ashva's under-ice carriers and copied them. It added a Kitezh's armour and the Union's icebreaker bow, bought through a contractor at Quebec. The Sadko is built for assault, not rescue: it burns through the ice under fire and puts its frames into the ocean beneath someone else's habitat.

nodes.t: “Seed”: lands, then grows a fortress
nodes.x: Umoja doesn't hold ground by occupying it. It grows something there. The Mbegu lands on Ganymede or Callisto and unfolds into a crawler, like the Shifa hospitals that drive across Africa. Then it seeds the ice around it with radiotroph mats that grow into shelter, power and walls within a season. Its frames hold the perimeter while the fortress grows.

nodes.t: A dock that brings its own beachhead
nodes.x: Where the Hanse needs an empty rock to dock with, the Ostia brings its own beachhead, taking the Mare Nostrum's landing decks into space so that it can put a battalion of Bastides down on a defended moon or asteroid and then, once they have taken the ground, turn itself into a dock. It is named for Rome's port, which began as a fort.

nodes.t: A Goldpurse with its money spent on landing craft
nodes.x: Syndicate houses do their own claim enforcement. The Strongbox is a Goldpurse with half its fighter hangar given over to marines' landers and ore-hauler drop cradles. It is Belt-built and Belt-crewed, and it serves as the debt collector for a house that wants a rock back.

orgs.label: Organisations
orgs.intro: The companies, laboratories and institutions behind everything else in the atlas, placed in the era where each first matters. After the war each power runs its outward business through a pair of institutions, one that talks and one that fights.
turns: Every mech maker began as something else: Halcyon built jets, Brannock-Hale tanks, Tianlong excavators, OKB-7 interceptors, Mitsurugi rescue robots. Their old products still show in every frame they build.

The Partnership Act let Brannock-Hale and Halcyon design, build, crew and maintain their own frames. It was meant to be temporary, and has been renewed ever since, mostly on terms the two companies' lobbyists drafted.
Halden, Department Zero, Tsukuyomi Lab and Vireo all begin their work in the same decade, and none of them answers to a parliament.

Neither Brannock-Hale nor Halcyon could build a Concord alone, so Congress chartered Joint Heavy Systems to do it. About a dozen Concords later, some of its parts have left the depots on paperwork nobody can trace.

Boreal becomes two companies trading patents through lawyers in Iceland. Mitsurugi's engineers leave for Ohio and Vladivostok before Beijing arrives. A Tangier shipyard is run by assembly. And the UN, ignored for the whole war, becomes the institution that ends it.

An ethics panel that can stop a programme, a lunar yard sworn to no bloc, keepers who won't command what they care for, a UN that has started bringing its own frames. Most of the organisations that outlast the war have that in common.
Every power splits its offices in two

After the war each power runs its business with the rest of the system through two institutions: one for diplomacy and trade, one for war, spies and research. The UNEL builds the slowest and most consistent pair. The Hegemony hides inside the Ascendancy's. And off Earth, every space faction's maker starts as a repair shed for Earth frames.

The nations that held Berlin refound the Union as a concert of equals, none of which will let another lead. Anyone can rise, whatever their skin, by joining a national elite; Toronto and Eros show what happens to those who refuse.

The UNEL was built to hold the lanes shut and step back. A generation later it licenses every launch, seals every reactor near Earth and can switch off any frame on its relays, and its careers belong to the Earthward's heirs.
A court, an audit and a bribe
2312 tests every institution at once. The Solar Court opens, the Lunar Spire is audited, and the MRD's Innovation Bureau buys a cyberweapon from a captain Colony One's own fleet had thrown away.
Offices built so it can't happen again
The Constitutionalists' offices and arsenal are designed so that Mars can never again drag Washington into a war it didn't choose: every weapon they build carries a lock only Washington can open.
fams: The US, Union and Canadian companies behind the West's frames.
State combines, design bureaus and Japan's capacitor maker.
From desert workshops to two design offices of Africa's own.
The offices each Earth power fights, spies and trades through after the war, and the faction hiding inside one of them.
Geneva's agencies, its borrowed white frames, and the institution the war forces on everyone.
A consortium, its workers and the houses beyond its reach; after the war, the anchorages just past the Moon where the seals come off.
Colony One's and the Directorate's offices and works, and the Constitutionalists after them.
The Syndicate's clans and enforcers, and the outer system's councils and makers.
Where the supers were made, and the bodies that answer for them.
Mercenaries, miners, and a canal that started opening containers.

profile.t: The Office of Strategic Influence and the Department of War; Halcyon, Brannock-Hale and the Hampton Roads yard still build for them. Their ships lose their seals at the Far Roads, at L2, and at the Phobos Forgeworks.

The External Commerce Commission and the Strategic Security Institute; Vauclair-Ehrlich, Castellani, Funkenwerk, Boreal East and the Malapert docks build for them. Beyond the Moon: berths on Deimos, then the Trojan anchorages.
The Ministry of External Harmony and the Bureau of Strategic Development; Tianlong, Tianshu, Khiimori and Mitsurugi under Beijing's protection. Beyond the Moon: a berth at Juno it never gave up.
OKB-7 and Nashik Works build for the Oath; the Hegemony waits inside the ministries. Beyond the Moon: a small dock at Mercury, and the joint anchorage at Europa.
Qadira sells to half of Earth from Khartoum, and the Tunis Works builds the Charter's medic frames. Beyond the Moon: the Eros dock, and the joint anchorage at Europa.
The Office of Global Stewardship and the Directorate of Unified Security; the Solar Court from 2312; the Spire on the far side; the lunar yards and Shackleton Works build for everyone licensed.
The Expeditionary Directorate and the Intelligence and Analysis Directorate, a state until 2312 and a fleet and a network after it; Dustline Works in the hidden docks.
The Civic Government and the Corporate Liaison Office; New Philadelphia Arsenal builds everything with Washington's lock.
External and Defensive Affairs and the Innovation Bureau, every programme before a panel; Vesta Works publishes every drawing.
The Celestial Concord and Voidborne Security, for clans that answer to no one; Skycut Foundry at Pallas; Albedo Industries sells crews that never sleep.
The Hafun Lodges that lead it, the councils that thread through every tribe, and the Vatworks that grow its frames.
The veche that argues, the akharas that ride out, and Garuda Works, built on Nashik's pairs and the Mitsurugi exiles' actuators.
The Hearthwrights, who keep a century-old frame walking.

nodes.t: Fighter maker turned frame maker
nodes.x: America's fighter and ground-attack jet maker before mechs, and still the source of every Halcyon frame's wing binders, avionics and flight-control software. It licensed Brannock's Garrison as the Sparrowhawk, then built the variable frames that US doctrine has been written around ever since: the Merlin, the Kestrel and the Harrier. Since the Partnership Act it has designed, built, crewed and maintained its own frames, and its engineers hold reserve commissions alongside their company badges.

nodes.t: Tanks, construction walkers, then the Garrison
nodes.x: America's tank and heavy-equipment maker. It put a construction walker's legs under a tank's armour and built the first mech to see combat, the M4 Garrison, which nearly everyone has licensed, copied or rebuilt since. The Army's frames are Brannock's, from the Teamster to the Bulwark, and so is most of the Army's lobbying.

nodes.t: The Union's frame maker
nodes.x: A European maker of armoured reconnaissance vehicles, whose sensor masts and habit of quiet running went on to shape every frame it built. It licence-built the Garrison as the Écuyer, and then designed the standard-hardpoint Haubert, the frame on which the whole of the Union's modular doctrine still rests.

nodes.t: Cold-weather frames from between the blocs
nodes.x: Canada's maker of snow tractors and ice-road haulers, and then, by stages, of frames: first licensed Garrisons built in Calgary, then Arctic designs of its own on US chassis carrying Union sensors. It sells to Norway as readily as to Ottawa, and its plants, as it happens, already sit on either side of the line along which the partition will later run.

nodes.t: Brannock-Hale and Halcyon, chartered by Congress
nodes.x: The joint venture Congress chartered to do what neither company could manage alone, which was to build the Concord. It took the first full-scale HT-20 plant, Bulwark armour and Harrier avionics and scaled them up to 40 m. About a dozen Concords on, its depot records show parts leaving on paperwork that its own auditors can't trace.

nodes.t: A workers' cooperative in a squatted hangar
nodes.x: Founded in 2172 by Kassel engineers and Blitz crews who walked out when Vauclair-Ehrlich standardised on the Haubert and scrapped every Blitz. They squatted a disused hangar at Tempelhof and registered as a cooperative, so that no consortium could ever buy them, and took their name from the callsign of the last Blitz pair still running in the Maghreb Depot Strikes. Every member has one vote and every drawing is published. That has made for some long meetings with the Union procurement office, though the German contingents buy their frames regardless. In 2185 a narrow vote took a contract from Berlin itself, and the cooperative split over it; the thirty-nine percent who lost took the Querschläger drawings with them to Mongolia.

nodes.t: Herder-mechanics, then Berlin's splinter
nodes.x: Named for the wind horse on the prayer flags. It began around 2175 as a cooperative of rail workshops in Darkhan, building the fast frames for the Steppe outriders that Tianlong wouldn't build. In 2185 it took in a few hundred Funkenwerk members who had walked out over the Berlin contract, and it still holds one vote per member, now in three languages. Berlin treats the walkout as desertion, which the members find rather odd, since as far as they're concerned they have only kept the vote they always had. Beijing puts up with them because the outriders vouch for them and because Tianshu can't predict them, and it has decided, on balance, that the second of those is useful to it.

nodes.t: Hand-built frames for named aces
nodes.x: An Italian atelier that builds a handful of frames a year on Vauclair-Ehrlich bones, each one for a single named ace: the Falco, the Saetta and, most recently, Roland, which remains the only super the ethics panel has approved.
